title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
The first thing I remember is the smell of the tin. It was a small, flat tin of pilchards in tomato sauce, and my uncle had been using it to hold his weights and hooks for so long that the metal had taken on the scent of brine and old oil. He never spoke much, my uncle. He was a tall, quiet man with hands like knotted rope, and when he handed me the rod, it was with a nod, not a word. The rod was old, a split-cane thing that had belonged to his father, and it felt heavy and alive in my small grip. The loch lay before us, a flat, grey mirror under a sky the colour of a bruise. It was early, so early that the midges were still sluggish, hanging in the heather like tiny specks of soot.

We sat on a flat rock that jutted out over the water, the kind of rock that had been sat on for a hundred years. He showed me how to bait the hook, his thick fingers moving with a delicate precision that seemed impossible. He took a worm from the tin, threaded it onto the hook with a series of small, deft movements, and then passed the rod back to me. He pointed to a spot on the water, maybe twenty feet out, where the surface was disturbed by a faint ripple. Then he sat back, lit his pipe, and became a part of the landscape.

The silence was the first lesson. It wasn't an empty silence, but a full one. It was the silence of the water lapping against the rock, the distant, mournful cry of a curlew, the soft hiss of his pipe. It was a silence that demanded you pay attention. I tried to fill it at first, with questions about the fish, about the loch, about the strange, dark clouds gathering over the far hills. He answered with a grunt, a shrug, a slight inclination of his head. Eventually, I understood. The silence wasn't a wall; it was a door. You had to be quiet to hear what was on the other side.

My casting was a disaster. The line whipped back and tangled in the heather, or landed with a clumsy splash that sent ripples of alarm across the loch. Each time, he would put down his pipe, retrieve the line, untangle the knot with the same patient fingers, and hand it back. He never sighed, never showed a flicker of frustration. His calm was a physical thing, a blanket that settled over my own rising panic. He was teaching me that the loch didn't care about my impatience. It had its own time, a time measured in the slow drift of clouds and the patient growth of reeds.

Hours passed. The sun, a pale, watery disc, climbed higher, burning off the mist. The midges grew bolder. My arms ached. I had almost forgotten what we were there for, lulled by the rhythm of the water and the immense, patient quiet of the man beside me. I was watching a dragonfly, its wings a shimmer of blue glass, when the rod tip twitched. It was a tiny movement, so small I thought I had imagined it. But my uncle’s head turned, just a fraction. His eyes, which had been half-closed, were now fixed on the line.

I gripped the rod. The twitch came again, a definite pull. My heart hammered against my ribs. I looked at him, my eyes wide with a question. He gave a single, slow nod. That was all. No shouted instructions, no frantic gestures. Just that one nod, an affirmation that I was to do it myself. I remembered what he’d shown me, the way to strike, not too hard, not too soft. I lifted the rod. The line went taut, and the rod bent in a beautiful, terrifying arc. The fish fought, a wild, silver flash deep in the peaty water. It was a small brown trout, no bigger than my hand, but it felt like a monster from the deep.

He was there then, his hand over mine, not to take over, but to steady me. He showed me how to bring it in, to let it run when it wanted to run, to reel when it tired. The net was a whisper in the water, and then the fish was on the rock, gasping, its scales a mosaic of bronze and gold and crimson spots. He showed me how to hold it, the cool, firm body, the surprising strength of it. He took the hook out with a small, practised twist and held the fish in the water, his hand cupped gently around it, until it gave a flick of its tail and was gone.

He didn't clap me on the back. He didn't say "well done." He simply packed his pipe, his movements as unhurried as ever, and nodded towards the water again. The lesson was over. The silence returned, but it was different now. It was a shared silence, a companionable one. We sat until the light began to fail, the sky turning to slate and then to a soft, bruised purple. We caught nothing else. As we walked back through the heather, the scent of damp earth and pine rising around us, he rested a hand on my shoulder for a moment. It was a heavy hand, a warm hand. We didn't speak. We didn't need to. The loch had said everything.

title: legend|a drowned village whose church bell still rings at low tide
text:
The hydroelectric dam was completed in 1962, and the village of Harlow’s Reach has been underwater ever since. This is a matter of public record. You can find the engineering specs, the relocation notices, the grainy photographs of the last residents standing on the steps of the general store, their faces a study in stoic resignation. The water rose, as it was meant to, and the valley became a lake. The maps were redrawn. This is the story the archives tell.

What the archives do not tell you is that the bell still rings. It rings at low tide, which is a strange thing to say about a lake, but that is what the old-timers on the reservoir’s edge call it, borrowing the language of the sea they’ve never seen. They mean the periods of drawdown, when the dam’s gates are opened to manage the spring melt or the autumn rains and the water level drops by ten, sometimes fifteen feet. The bathtub ring of pale, exposed rock widens, and the drowned world comes into view. The mud is a slick, black soup. The stumps of the old-growth hemlocks stand like rotten teeth. And then, if the wind is right and the air is still, you can hear it.

I heard it first when I was eleven, staying with my grandmother, who had lived in Harlow’s Reach as a girl but had moved to the county seat the year before the flooding. She never spoke of it directly, only in fragments, like a cook dropping pieces of a broken plate into the bin. She told me the water was a thief, but a polite one, that it had asked for permission first, in the form of lawyers and notarized letters. She said the best place to hear the bell was from the point of land near the old cemetery, the part that had been on a hill and was now a peninsula.

I went there one evening in late October. The air was cold and carried the smell of wet earth and decay. The lake was a flat, gunmetal gray, and the water was low, exposing the drowned channel of the river that had once run through the town. I sat on a granite outcrop, its surface scrubbed clean by ice, and I waited. I felt foolish, a child chasing a ghost story. But then the sun dipped below the ridge, the temperature dropped, and the wind died. In the profound quiet, I heard it.

It was not a clangorous, joyful peal. It was a single, muffled note, a dull bronze thud that seemed to travel not through the air but up through the rock I was sitting on, into my bones. It was followed by a faint, metallic groan, the sound of immense pressure and slow decay. It was the sound of something vast and forgotten shifting in its sleep. It was the bell, I knew, ringing in the drowned steeple of the Harlow’s Reach Congregational Church.

My grandmother, when I told her, didn’t scoff. She just nodded, her eyes fixed on the window. “It’s the water,” she said. “It gets into everything. The silt, the mud, the rust. It works on the metal. The pressure, the currents… they make it move. It’s just physics.” But her voice lacked conviction. She was trying to explain away a thing she knew could not be explained away.

The scientists, of course, have their theories. A local hydrologist I spoke to suggested it was a phenomenon of cavitation, bubbles of vapor forming and collapsing against the bell’s metal, creating a percussive sound. Another proposed it was the shifting of the waterlogged foundation, a slow-motion settling that caused the bell to strike its housing. The theories are plausible. They are also sterile. They explain the mechanism but not the persistent, mournful quality of the sound, nor the way it seems to carry a memory.

The bell was cast in 1888, a gift from a wealthy parishioner whose son had died at sea. It was rung for fires, for weddings, for the armistice. My grandmother remembered being lifted by her father to touch the cool bronze after a Christmas service, the cold metal a shock against her bare hand. She said the whole town could feel the bell’s vibration in their chests. It was the town’s heartbeat. Now, that heart beats only when the water allows it, a sporadic, arrhythmic pulse from a corpse.

People still go to listen. There are a few, a handful of descendants and curiosity-seekers who gather on the reservoir’s shore during the drawdown, their cars parked on the gravel verge, their thermoses of coffee steaming in the twilight. We stand there, a ragged congregation of the displaced and the obsessed, waiting. We don’t talk much. We don’t need to. We are listening for a sound that is an absence, a note struck in a room no one can enter. It is the sound of a promise that was broken, a place that was erased. When it comes, a low, shivering tone from the depths, we all look at each other, a flicker of recognition in our eyes. We hear it. We know it’s there. And then the water begins to rise again, the dam closes its gates, and the bell is silenced for another season. The town is gone, but its voice, borrowed by the water, remains. And we, its scattered children, keep returning to the shore, not to hear it ring, but to make sure it hasn't stopped.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
My first word, my mother swore, was “more.” Not “mama,” not “papa.” My father, who liked to tell this story at dinner parties in Guangzhou, would lean back and say, “See? She is a child of two appetites.” My mother would correct him: “Two languages, you mean.” I was eighteen months old, sitting in a high chair in a white-tiled kitchen in Sham Shui Po, reaching for a second helping of rice porridge while my grandmother, Ah Ma, clucked her tongue and said in Cantonese, “Gau, gau, gau—enough.” But I had already learned the trick of pointing and saying “more,” the word that worked in both worlds.

Those worlds were Hong Kong and Texas, though for a long time they were less places than weathers. From September to June I lived in Kowloon with my parents and Ah Ma in a fifth-floor walk-up above a dried-seafood shop. The air smelled of salted fish and jasmine from the balcony where my mother hung the laundry. At six I could name every shop on Tai Po Road by its smell: the bakery with its hot pineapple buns, the herbalist with his bitter roots, the stationery store where Mr. Chan kept the erasers in a glass jar and would let me hold one if I promised not to chew it.

Then every July, my mother and I flew to Houston, where my father worked for most of the year as an engineer. We stayed in a brick apartment complex called Willow Creek, and the air there smelled of chlorine and mown grass. In Hong Kong I was “Wei-Wei,” a name that meant little, a name my grandmother called out from the kitchen window when I stayed too long playing downstairs. In Houston I was “Vivian,” which the teacher at the summer camp pronounced with a flat, friendly twang—Vi-vi-an—as if my name were three separate pieces of candy.

The split did something to my tongue. In Hong Kong I spoke Cantonese with Ah Ma and English with my mother, who had learned it in secretarial school and was proud of it. In Houston I spoke English with everyone, and Cantonese only on the telephone, when my father would dial the long-distance number on Sunday nights and hand me the receiver. “Ah Ma,” I would say, and she would answer, “Wei-Wei, nei hou ma?”—are you well?—and I would say “Hou,” fine, and then run out of things to say. My father would take the phone back and speak for twenty minutes about the price of gold and the neighbor’s son who had gotten into medical school. I would sit on the linoleum floor and listen to the static, which sounded to me like the ocean between us.

The real trouble came in the third grade, when my mother decided we should stay in Houston for a full year. My father had been offered a promotion; my grandmother had fallen and needed a hip operation; the timing was bad. “One year,” my mother said, as if it were a sentence she had rehearsed. “Then we go back.” She enrolled me at Piney Point Elementary, where Mrs. Delgado, the ESL teacher, pulled me out of class twice a week and made me read aloud from a book about a dog named Spot. I could read the words, but I couldn’t hear the music in them. In Cantonese, a question rises at the end like a bird lifting off. In English, everything flattened out, and I missed the bird.

I remember a fight with a boy named Derek on the playground. He had called me “Chinese eyes,” and I had shoved him, and we both landed in the principal’s office. When the principal asked what happened, I opened my mouth and nothing came out—not because I didn’t know the words, but because I knew too many. I wanted to say “He called me a name,” but in my head I was also composing the Cantonese version for my mother, the one where I would have to explain why I had been fighting at all, and the English version felt thin, like a shirt without starch. I finally said, “He was mean.” The principal nodded. Derek got a warning. I got a lecture about using my words. I wanted to tell her that my words were the problem.

That Christmas, Ah Ma flew to Houston for three weeks. She brought a suitcase full of dried scallops and a jar of fermented bean curd wrapped in newspaper, and she stood in our kitchen in Willow Creek, squinting at the electric stove as if it were a malfunctioning appliance. “No fire,” she said. “How you cook?” We made do. Every night she cooked, and the apartment filled with the smell of soy and ginger, and my mother and I spoke Cantonese at the dinner table even though my father was there, even though he understood. It was a small rebellion, a way of making the room ours.

The night before Ah Ma left, she sat on the edge of my bed and asked, “Nei hai bin dou yan?”—which people are you from? I knew the answer she wanted. I said, “Hong Kong yan.” She patted my hand. Then she said, in her broken English, “You have two home. No problem. Two home better.” I don’t know if she believed it. I don’t know if I did. But I have carried that sentence with me for thirty years, and on the good days it sounds like a blessing, and on the bad days it sounds like a question I am still trying to answer.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The first thing you learn is that the water does not care how old you are. It doesn’t care that you have a mortgage, or that your left knee clicks when you stand up from a chair, or that you have, for forty years, considered yourself a person who does not swim. The water is busy being water. It has no opinions. This is either the most terrifying thing about it or the most comforting, and I still haven’t decided.

I was forty-one, actually, when I finally signed up, but I’d been telling people “forty” for so long it stuck. There’s a form you fill out at the community pool—emergency contact, any medical conditions, a line that asks for your swimming level. Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced. I stood at the counter with a golf pencil and felt my face go hot. Beginner. A word for toddlers and shipwreck survivors.

The instructor’s name was Denise. She had a whistle on a lanyard and the specific cheerfulness of someone who has taught a lot of frightened adults. She told me—and I have thought about this a lot—that most of her students are over thirty-five. “Kids just jump in,” she said. “Adults have to be talked into it.” She said it like a compliment, but it landed somewhere between a diagnosis and a eulogy.

The pool smelled like chlorine and, faintly, like a dentist’s office. I wore a swimsuit I’d bought at a sporting goods store the day before, still had the tag in my bag, and a pair of goggles that pinched the bridge of my nose. The shallow end was four feet. Four feet. I could stand up. I knew this intellectually. But knowing a thing and believing it are different organs, I think.

Here is a partial list of things I was afraid of, in no particular order: drowning, obviously; looking ridiculous; the moment when my feet left the bottom; the moment when they touched it again; the other people in the lane, all of whom seemed to be eight or seventy-five; the way water gets in your ears and stays there; the way it gets in your nose. The way it gets in your mouth when you are trying to breathe the way Denise was telling me to breathe, which was out through the nose, in through the mouth, or maybe the other way around, I honestly never got it straight and just sort of improvised, which is, I suspect, how most adults do everything.

The first time I put my face in the water I lasted maybe three seconds. I came up gasping like a character in a movie. Denise said, “Good,” in a tone that suggested she had seen worse. I wanted to say, I am a grown woman, I have filed taxes, I have held a dying dog in my lap, and I cannot put my face in four feet of water. Instead I nodded and did it again.

It got better. That’s the boring truth. It got better slowly, in the way that most things do, which is to say imperceptibly, and then all at once. One Tuesday I realized I had swum a full length without stopping and without thinking about stopping. The water was still water. I was still me. But something had shifted, some small hinge had oiled itself.

I still can’t dive. I still get water up my nose sometimes and have to cough it out at the wall like a malfunctioning sprinkler. But I can swim now, in a manner of speaking. I go on Thursday evenings. There’s a man there, maybe seventy, who does the backstroke with his eyes closed and a look of tremendous peace. I want to ask him how long it took him. I want to tell him I’m new. But I just nod, and he nods, and we get in our separate lanes, and the water goes on not caring, which is, I have decided, the most comforting thing about it.

title: fable|a crow who collects lost keys
text:
The crow’s name was Corvus, and his nest was a museum of misplaced potential. He had just returned from the human world, a place of endless, cluttered forgetting, and he carried a new prize in his beak: a small, silver key, its head shaped like a tiny, stylized heart. He landed on the edge of his nest, a sprawling, chaotic structure of twigs, moss, and stolen treasures, and carefully placed the key beside the others. There was a long, brass key, green with age; a black, chunky key for a car; and a dozen smaller, anonymous keys that could have opened a diary, a suitcase, or a forgotten padlock.

To Corvus, these were not just objects. They were stories. He would spend hours watching the humans from his high perch in the old oak tree. He saw them pat their pockets with growing panic, their faces contorting from confusion to frustration, and finally to a resigned despair as they retraced their steps. He saw them drop keys from overloaded bags, leave them in the locks of their front doors, or toss them aside in a moment of carelessness, never to be seen again. Corvus was not a thief; he was a collector of these moments of loss. He was the silent, feathered archivist of human carelessness.

His collection had grown famous among the local wildlife. The squirrels, who valued shiny things for their own chaotic nests, would sometimes try to barter. A particularly bold jay once offered a stolen earring for the heart-shaped key, but Corvus had simply stared at him, his head tilted, until the jay, feeling inexplicably judged, hopped away. The keys were not for trade. They were his purpose.

One afternoon, a young fox, his coat the colour of autumn leaves, trotted to the base of the oak tree. He watched Corvus for a long time, his intelligent eyes fixed on the glittering hoard. “Crow,” the fox finally called up, his voice polite but curious. “You have so many keys. Do you know what they open?”

Corvus ruffled his feathers, a low, guttural sound rumbling in his throat. He didn’t speak the language of the forest creatures often; his voice was a harsh caw, better suited for the empty spaces between human words. But he understood. He hopped to the edge of the nest and looked down at the fox.

“They open nothing,” he cawed, the sound sharp and definitive. “They are lost. That is what they are.”

The fox’s ears twitched. “But a key’s purpose is to open a lock. To have a key that opens nothing… it seems a sad thing.”

“Is it?” Corvus countered, his head bobbing. “The human who lost it feels a pang of sadness, yes. A moment of disruption. But then they get a new key, or they call a locksmith, and they forget. The key, however, remains. It is a monument to that small, forgotten moment. It is more honest than a key that is used every day, a slave to its lock. These keys are free.”

The fox considered this, his brushy tail sweeping the fallen leaves. “So you are a keeper of… freedom?”

“I am a keeper of what is left behind,” Corvus said, a note of pride in his raspy voice. He gestured with a wing to his collection. “Look at the heart-shaped one. I saw a young woman drop it outside a house with a ‘For Sale’ sign. She was crying. She was leaving a home, and in her haste, she lost the key to her old life. Now, it is here. It is not a key to a house anymore. It is a key to a memory. A sad one, but a memory nonetheless.”

The fox was silent for a moment, his gaze shifting from the crow to the glittering pile of metal and back again. He seemed to be wrestling with a new idea. “But what if someone was looking for one of them? What if the crying woman came back, searching?”

Corvus let out a short, sharp caw that was almost a laugh. “They never come back. They look down at the ground, they search their pockets, they blame the wind or a child. They never look up. They never think to ask the crow in the oak tree. Their loss is my gain. It is a simple, natural order.”

The fox nodded slowly, not entirely convinced but unwilling to challenge the crow’s strange philosophy. He turned and trotted back into the undergrowth, leaving Corvus alone with his thoughts and his treasures. The crow turned back to his collection, nudging the new heart-shaped key into a more prominent position. It caught the last light of the setting sun, a tiny, silver gleam against the rough brown twigs. He felt a profound sense of satisfaction. The world was full of people rushing to and fro, opening and closing, locking and unlocking. And here he was, high above it all, the silent curator of their forgotten moments, the guardian of a thousand locked doors that no longer existed.

title: short story|a night bus driver and a passenger who never gets off
text:
The route is a long silver thread through the city’s outskirts, and I am the needle. 214. I drive it six nights a week, from the depot in the east to the loop out past the airport and back again. The bus is a creature of the small hours, a lit-up box of stale air and weary souls, and I am its shepherd.

Most of them are ghosts. The nurse from the hospice, her shoes squeaking on the lino, her face a mask of exhaustion. The two men from the meatpacking plant who smell of cold and iron. The girl who gets on at the university stop, always with a book, always reading the same page, as if she’s trapped in a single paragraph of her life. They get on, they pay, they sit, they get off. A rhythm as predictable as the thrum of the engine.

And then there was the man in the grey coat.

He first appeared on a Tuesday, a night of thin, persistent rain that made the windows slick and the world outside a blur of coloured light. He got on at the stop by the old cemetery, a place no one ever gets on. He was neat, unremarkable, with a face you’d forget in the time it took to look away. He paid his fare with exact change, the coins dropping into the box with a final, definitive clink. He didn’t meet my eyes. He walked to the back, sat on the left-hand side, and stared out the window.

I didn’t think much of it. People have their reasons. A long way home, a need to be alone, a journey to nowhere in particular. But then he was there the next night. And the next. Always at the cemetery stop, always with the exact change, always in the same seat. He never pulled the cord. He never got off.

The first week, I’d glance in the mirror. He was a silhouette against the passing streetlights, a solid, unmoving shape. The second week, I started to feel a prickle of something—not quite unease, but a low hum of wrongness. He was a stone in the river of my routine, and the water was beginning to eddy around him. I began to invent lives for him. A man who’d lost everything and was just riding the last loop before the end. A spook, a memory the city had forgotten to exorcise.

One night, the bus was empty save for him and me. The rain was a steady hiss against the roof. I was running early, so I pulled over at the terminus, the big empty loop by the airport fence, and killed the engine. The silence was sudden and enormous. I sat there for a minute, listening to the tick of the cooling metal. Then I got up.

I walked down the aisle. He didn’t turn. I sat in the seat across from him.

“End of the line,” I said. My voice sounded loud in the quiet.

He turned his head slowly, as if waking from a deep sleep. His eyes were the colour of the sky before dawn. There was no surprise in them, no fear. Just a vast, quiet tiredness.

“I know,” he said. His voice was soft, rusted from disuse.

“You have to get off.”

He looked at me then, really looked, and I felt a strange sense of being seen, of being weighed. “Do I?”

I didn’t have an answer. We sat in the humming silence. The airport’s distant lights blinked, a slow, mechanical respiration. He wasn’t a threat. He wasn’t a puzzle to be solved. He was just a man on a bus. And I was just a driver.

“I’m going to start the engine,” I said, finally. “You can stay if you want. But I’m going back.”

He nodded, a barely perceptible dip of his chin, and turned back to the window. I returned to my seat, the bus seeming to sway slightly under my feet as I walked. I started the engine. The lights flickered on, the heater groaned to life. We drove the route in reverse, the city assembling itself out of the dark. A few passengers got on, a few got off. He remained.

When we reached the cemetery stop, he stood. He walked to the front, paused by my seat. I thought he might say something. He just gave me a small, almost imperceptible nod. Then he stepped down into the wet night and was gone.

He was back the next night. And the night after that. He never spoke again. He never got off.

Now, when I see him at the cemetery stop, a part of the tension in my shoulders eases. He is the last passenger of the night, the final entry in the logbook, the one who sees the route to its end. I don’t know his name or his story. I don’t know where he goes when the bus stops and the doors hiss open. I don’t think he knows either.

Sometimes, on the long, dark stretch past the airport, I’ll look in the mirror and meet his eyes. We don’t smile. We don’t nod. We just look at each other, two men on a bus that is going nowhere, and for a moment, the silence between us feels like the only true thing in the city. Then the light changes, and I have to watch the road again.

title: prose poem|a kitchen at four in the morning
text:
The faucet in 4B dripped in a rhythm that Marisol had come to think of as the building’s slow, irregular heartbeat. It was four in the morning on a Tuesday in November, the kind of hour that belongs to no one, and she was standing in her kitchen on the fourth floor of a walk-up on Tillman Street in the Bushwick section of Brooklyn, waiting for the water to boil. The radiator clanked twice and then subsided, as if it had made its point. On the counter, a blue bowl held three eggs and a heel of rye bread from the bakery on Knickerbocker that sold day-old loaves for a dollar after six. She had bought the bread at 6:15 the previous evening, which felt like a different geological era.

The kitchen was narrow—galley-style, the landlord had called it, as though that made it nautical rather than cramped—and the window over the sink looked out onto the airshaft, where a single bulb burned all night in the stairwell of the building behind. Marisol had never met anyone in that building. She knew only their silhouettes: the man who smoked on the third-floor landing at odd hours, the woman who practiced scales on a violin that sounded like it was being played underwater. Tonight the violinist was silent. The smoker was not. A thin curl of cigarette smoke rose past her window, and she watched it dissolve into the dark the way she watched everything at this hour—without urgency, without judgment, as if the world were a television left on in an empty room.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. A text from her brother, Tomás, in Phoenix: *you up?* She typed back: *always.* He called. His voice had the gravel of someone who had also not slept.

“I’m telling you, Mari, the guy is a ghost. No lease, no mail, no nothing. But every morning there’s a newspaper on his step. The *Arizona Republic.* Who reads a physical newspaper anymore?”

“Maybe he’s old.”

“He’s not old. I saw him once. Forties, maybe. Wore a suit. At six in the morning. In July. A suit.”

She laughed, quietly, so as not to wake the neighbor below, Mrs. Kowalski, who had complained twice about noise and once about the smell of garlic. “Maybe he’s a spy.”

“That’s what I said. To Rosa. She said I watch too many movies. But I’m telling you, the man is a ghost.”

The kettle began to whistle, a low, building note. She lifted it off the flame and poured the water over the instant coffee in her mug—the good mug, the one with the chip in the handle that she refused to throw away because Tomás had made it in a pottery class in Tucson in 2016. The coffee was not good. It was not meant to be good. It was meant to be hot and to have caffeine in it, and it succeeded on both counts.

“How’s Ma?” she asked.

“She’s Ma. She asked about you. She said, ‘Tell Marisol the figs are coming in.’ Like you were going to drive over and pick them.”

“Tell her I’ll make jam next summer.”

“You say that every year.”

“And every year I mean it.”

They were quiet for a moment. She could hear the traffic on the BQE, a distant, oceanic sound, the city’s own tide. Tomás breathed on the other end of the line. She pictured him in his kitchen in Phoenix, the one with the cactus-shaped salt and pepper shakers Rosa had bought at a yard sale, the linoleum floor he had never replaced, the window that looked out onto a parking lot. She had never been to Phoenix. She had seen it only in photographs and in the way Tomás described it, which was always in terms of what it lacked: no seasons, no walkability, no good bagels.

“You should sleep,” he said.

“I should.”

“You’re not going to.”

“I’m not going to.”

He laughed, and it was the laugh she remembered from childhood, from the kitchen in their mother’s house in Caguas, where they had eaten rice and beans at a table with a wobbly leg, and the tree frogs had sung outside the window, and the world had felt enormous and close at the same time. That kitchen had smelled of sofrito and coffee and the lemon-scented cleaner their mother used on Saturdays. This kitchen smelled of steam and dust and the faint, sweetish trace of the mouse that had lived behind the stove last winter and then, one day, simply stopped.

“I love you, Mari.”

“I love you too. Tell Rosa I said hi. Tell Ma I said hi.”

“I will. Go drink your coffee.”

“It’s terrible coffee.”

“I know.”

They hung up. She stood at the window with the mug in her hands and watched the sky begin to change—not lighten, exactly, but soften, the black giving way to a deep, bruised blue, the color of a plum held up to a flashlight. The smoker had gone inside. The violinist had not yet begun. Somewhere in the building, a toilet flushed. The city was waking up, or it had never really been asleep, and Marisol, who had been awake for hours, felt suddenly, absurdly grateful for the drip of the faucet, the clank of the radiator, the bad coffee, the chipped mug, the voice of her brother in her ear, the whole ragged, imperfect machinery of being alive at four in the morning, which is to say, of being alive at all.

title: legend|a drowned village whose church bell still rings at low tide
text:
They say you can hear it on the lowest tides of the year, the ones that pull the water back so far the mudflats shine like wet slate. A single bell, tolling slow and steady from under the silt. St. Morwenna’s, they call it, though there’s no saint by that name in any calendar I’ve ever seen. My grandmother swore the name was older than the church itself, that it came from a woman who walked out of the sea one morning with kelp in her hair and a warning on her lips, and the village built a chapel on the spot out of pure fright.

The village was called Tregarrow. You won’t find it on a map. It sat in the crook of the estuary where the river meets the bay, and by all accounts it was a decent enough place—a few dozen families, a fish market, a mill that ran on the tide. Rich soil, too, which is rare that close to the salt. They grew early potatoes and sold them up-country. There are records. Tax rolls, parish registers, a letter from a merchant in 1602 complaining about the quality of the pilchards. Ordinary things. That’s what makes it worse, I think. It wasn’t a wicked village. It wasn’t Sodom. It was just a village that happened to be in the wrong place when the sea decided to take it.

The stories disagree on how it happened. Some say a storm—a real one, the kind that comes once a century, with waves like moving hills. Others say it wasn’t a storm at all but a slow drowning, the ground sinking year by year, the wells turning brackish, the cellars flooding at spring tides until finally the whole place gave up and slid under. My grandmother held to a third version, the one she heard from her own grandmother: that the village was cursed by a beggar woman turned away from a christening, and that the sea came up the streets like a thief in the night, quiet as you please, and swallowed every house and every soul except one child who’d been sent to the next parish for medicine. That child grew up, married, had children. Half the families in the county claim descent from her. Probably they’re all lying.

What’s certain is that the village is gone. At extreme low tide you can still see the bones of it—a few stumps of wall, the blackened footings of the mill, a stone cross knocked flat. The mud is treacherous. People have died out there, sunk to the waist and then the chest before anyone could reach them. The coastguard posts warnings. Nobody pays attention. You go out at the lowest ebb of the year, when the moon is right, and you wait, and if the wind is offshore and the water is still, you’ll hear it.

The bell.

It doesn’t ring fast. It doesn’t ring loud. It’s a dull sound, muffled, like someone striking a pot under a blanket. One toll. A long pause. Another toll. Nobody knows who’s ringing it. The bell was cast in 1489—there’s a record of the payment, three pounds six shillings to a founder in Bodmin—and it hung in the tower until the tower went under. Bronze doesn’t ring itself. But there it is.

Some say it’s the drowned ringing for their own funeral. Some say it’s a warning, that the bell rings when the sea is coming for another village and we’d do well to listen. A few—the ones who’ve spent too long on the mud—say it’s not a bell at all, just the tide working through some hollow in the wreck, some trick of stone and water. That’s the sensible explanation. I’ve heard sensible explanations all my life and none of them ever made me feel better about the sound.

I went out once. Years ago now, with my uncle’s boat and a lantern and a flask of something to keep the cold off. The tide was as low as I’ve ever seen it. I stood on the mud where the market square must have been and I listened. And I heard it. Two tolls, then nothing. Then one more, so faint I might have imagined it. My uncle swore he heard nothing at all, and he was a man who didn’t lie. But I heard it. I know I heard it.

The water came back fast, the way it does. We barely made the boat. And on the way in, my uncle said something I’ve never forgotten. He said, “They don’t ring it for us. They ring it so they know each other’s still there.”

title: personal essay|why I keep a notebook of overheard sentences
text:
—and the woman at the next table said, “I only cry in parking lots,” and I wrote it down.

I didn’t look up. That’s the first rule of the notebook: you never look up. You keep your eyes on your coffee or your shoes or the middle distance, and you move your hand slowly, like you’re checking the time, like you’re doing nothing at all. The woman was maybe forty, talking to a friend across a plate of eggs she wasn’t eating. She said it the way people say things they’ve said before, a line worn smooth from repeating. *I only cry in parking lots.* Then she laughed, and her friend laughed, and the conversation moved on to a coworker named Denise, and I sat there with my pen moving and thought: there it is. That’s the whole thing. A life in eleven words.

I started the notebook years ago, though I couldn’t tell you the exact day. What I remember is the feeling of hearing something I wasn’t supposed to hear—not a secret, exactly, nothing scandalous, just a sentence that had escaped—and wanting to keep it. The first entry I can still find is from a bus: a man on his phone saying, “No, I’m not mad, I’m just tired of being the one who remembers.” I wrote it on the back of a receipt and shoved it in my pocket, and for three days I carried it around like a stone in my shoe. It bothered me. It still bothers me. Who was he talking to? What did they forget?

That’s what the notebook is, I’ve come to think: a collection of things that bother me in the right way. Not gossip. I’m not interested in who did what to whom. I’m interested in the sentences people say when they think no one is listening, or when they forget that the world is full of ears. The fragments. The throwaway lines that turn out, on inspection, to be load-bearing.

There’s a man in a hardware store, holding two different lengths of pipe, saying to no one: “I’ve been wrong before, but I’ve never been this wrong.” There’s a teenager on a bench telling her friend, “My mom says I have a tone. I don’t have a tone.” There’s an old man at a pharmacy counter, very quietly, to the pharmacist: “I don’t want to be a burden, but I don’t want to be alone either.” I wrote that one down and then sat in my car for a while before I drove home. Some entries you have to recover from.

People ask—when they find out, usually by accident, usually by spotting the notebook and asking what it is—why I do it. The honest answer is that I don’t entirely know, and the answers I give are all partly true. I say it’s a writer thing, which is true but lazy. I say it’s a way of paying attention, which is true but sounds nobler than it is. I say it’s cheaper than therapy, which gets a laugh and ends the conversation.

But here’s what I think it actually is. I think we live most of our lives inside our own heads, narrating ourselves, and it’s easy to believe that everyone else is doing the same—that they’re all as contained and coherent as we feel, or as we imagine we feel. Then you hear a stranger say, “I only cry in parking lots,” and the whole illusion cracks. She wasn’t narrating herself. She was just leaking. And what leaked was more honest than anything I’ve ever carefully composed about my own life.

The notebook keeps me honest in the other direction, too. When I’m writing and I reach for a feeling, I can flip through and find one that’s real. Not my idea of sadness—someone else’s actual sadness, caught in the wild. “I don’t want to be a burden, but I don’t want to be alone either.” You can’t invent that. You can only overhear it.

I don’t record names. I don’t record places, mostly. I’m not building a dossier; I’m building a chorus. The notebook is full of voices that don’t know they’re in a book together, and if they did know, they’d probably be embarrassed, or angry, or confused. I think about that sometimes. I think about the woman in the parking lot, and whether she’d mind that a stranger has carried her sentence around for years, that it’s become a kind of scripture to me. I hope she wouldn’t mind. I hope she’d understand that I wasn’t stealing anything. I was just trying to remember what it sounds like when a person tells the truth without meaning to.

The server came by and asked if I wanted more coffee, and I said yes, and the woman at the next table paid her bill and left. I watched her go—the first rule has an exception, which is that you may look up after they’ve stood—and she walked out into the lot and got into her car and sat there for a moment before she pulled away. I didn’t write that down. Some things you don’t need to.

title: short story|a piano tuner who visits the same blind client for thirty years
text:
The streetcar’s groan was the first thing he heard, a sound like a metal animal clearing its throat, and it announced the corner of Rue des Martyrs before the smell of the bakery did. Every third Thursday for thirty years, this had been the ritual. He would step off the tram, a small leather satchel of tools in his left hand, and walk the remaining three blocks. The building was unremarkable, a pale stone facade with a heavy blue door that had not changed its shade of paint in all that time. He would press the brass button for the fourth floor, and a buzzer, always a little too loud, would grant him entry.

The climb was a slow, deliberate ascent. The stairs were wooden, worn into shallow bowls by a century of footsteps. He knew the eleventh step creaked, and the twenty-second had a deeper, more mournful groan. He would arrive at the landing, slightly out of breath, and knock twice. The door would open, and there she was, Madame Elise. She had not aged in his mind, though he knew the lines on her face had deepened, the silver in her hair had become a total white. Her blindness was a settled fact, a condition of her existence that was as unremarkable to him as the colour of her door.

“Monsieur Ferrand,” she would say, her voice a dry rustle of leaves. “You are punctual.”

“The streetcar, Madame, is a reliable beast,” he would reply, the same exchange they had shared for decades.

Her apartment was a world of sound and touch. The air was thick with the scent of old paper and beeswax. A clock in the hallway ticked with a precise, metallic click. He would follow her into the salon, his feet knowing the path around the low table and the armchair without needing to look. And there it was. The piano. A Pleyel grand from the 1890s, its rosewood case holding a deep, dark sheen. It was the reason for his visit, the silent third party in their long acquaintance.

He would open his satchel and lay his tools on the felt cloth he always brought: the tuning hammer, a set of mutes, a small fork. He would strike the A, and listen. For thirty years, he had listened to the sound of this piano decay. He knew its every idiosyncrasy. The slight nasal quality of the upper register, the way the bass strings, when struck too hard, would produce a faint, sympathetic rattle from a loose soundboard screw he could never quite reach. He knew the history of its wear, the notes she played most often, the ones that had been loved into a state of gentle exhaustion.

She would sit in her armchair, a dark shape against the window’s diffuse light, and wait. The first few minutes were always for listening. He would play a slow, chromatic scale, his fingers gentle on the keys. Then he would begin. The turning of the pins was a quiet, rhythmic music of its own. A slight creak, a metallic sigh, and then the note would be coaxed back into its proper place. He would play a fifth, then a fourth, then a major third, building the intervals, weaving the fabric of the sound back into a coherent whole.

She never spoke while he worked. The silence between them was not empty; it was filled with the sound of the piano being restored. It was a conversation. He would offer a note, and she would receive it. He was the physician, and she was the patient’s most devoted guardian.

Once, years ago, when he was younger and more foolish, he had asked her if she missed the music. He meant, of course, the act of playing. He had heard from the concierge that she had been a formidable pianist before the glaucoma had taken her sight. She had been silent for a long time, and he had felt the weight of his own clumsiness. Then she had said, “I do not miss the music, Monsieur Ferrand. I remember it. I remember the feel of the keys, the vibration in the wood. When you tune it, I can hear its shape. It is enough.”

He had never asked again. He understood. The piano was not an instrument for her to play, but a living thing she communed with. His job was not just to tune it, but to keep its voice true, to preserve its integrity so that her memory of it would not be betrayed by decay. He was the caretaker of her memory’s vessel.

He finished the middle register and moved to the treble. The notes were bright, almost brittle, like thin crystal. He softened one, then another, bringing them into a shimmering, silvery balance. He thought of the first time he had come here, a young man nervous in the presence of a legend. He had been recommended by a friend of a friend, and he had been terrified of the silent, sightless woman who had sat so still in her chair. Now, the silence was a comfort. It was the shared silence of two people who know each other’s rhythms.

The final check was a series of chords, a slow progression from the lowest bass to the highest treble. He played a C major chord, letting it ring. The sound was full, round, and true. It filled the room, pressing against the walls, a testament to his quiet, meticulous work. He closed his satchel. The click of the latch was the signal.

She rose from her chair. “It is done.”

“It is done, Madame.”

He walked to the door. He never asked for payment. A cheque would arrive in the mail a week later, always for the correct amount, always with a small, handwritten note of thanks. He would descend the stairs, the eleventh step creaking, the twenty-second groaning, and step back out into the Paris afternoon. The streetcar’s groan would greet him, and he would head home. For thirty years, he had been the keeper of a single, silent sound, a promise made to a woman he had never truly seen, and who had never seen him. He had kept the piano, and in doing so, had kept her world from falling out of tune.

title: free verse poem sequence|a year of weather in one valley
text:
I  
The river came down in a hurry that March,  
brown and loud, carrying somebody’s fence post  
past the Co-op where Earl Fisk was stacking seed corn.  
“She’ll crest by Tuesday,” he said,  
not looking up from the pallet.  
He was right. By Tuesday the low field  
behind the Methodist church was a lake  
with a mailbox in it,  
and the herons stood in the shallows  
like gray men who had lost their argument with the water.  
Marla Deene brought coffee to the volunteers  
in her late husband’s thermos,  
the one with the dent in the lid,  
and nobody mentioned the dent.  

II  
April was wind.  
It took the shingles off the Bergstrom barn  
one at a time, like a man dealing cards,  
and Lyle Bergstrom stood in the yard  
with his hat in his hand  
watching the sky do its work.  
“That’s the third roof in twenty years,” he said  
to nobody, to the dog,  
to the red-winged blackbirds stitching the fence line.  
The lilacs came anyway.  
They always come anyway.  
Marla cut a branch and put it in a mason jar  
on the counter at the diner,  
and for a week the whole place smelled like 1974,  
which is the year she met him,  
which she did not say out loud.  

III  
June: the heat came early and stayed.  
The creek behind the VFW went down to stones,  
and the stones got warm,  
and the boys fished anyway,  
catching nothing,  
throwing rocks at nothing,  
their laughter carrying up the hill  
to where old Ruth Ann Kessler sat on her porch  
shelling peas into a metal bowl.  
“Sound carries when it’s dry,” she told me.  
“You can hear a dog bark in Aldrich  
if the wind’s right.”  
The wind was not right.  
The wind was nowhere.  
The peas clicked in the bowl like small dry bones.  

IV  
July the storm came at four in the afternoon  
and took the power with it.  
We sat in the dark of the Bluebird Café  
and ate melting ice cream out of paper cups  
because it was going to melt anyway.  
Earl Fisk said, “I seen a storm in ’58  
took the steeple off the Lutheran church  
and set it down in the cemetery,  
upright, like it was planted.”  
Nobody believed him.  
Nobody called him a liar.  
The rain came sideways and the screen door banged  
and Marla lit candles that had been in the drawer  
since the Christmas pageant,  
and we were all, for an hour,  
the only people in the world.  

V  
August: the corn got tall and then got taller.  
You could stand at the edge of Lyle’s field  
and hear it growing,  
or that’s what he said,  
and maybe it was just the wind,  
but he said it with such certainty  
that I stood there anyway,  
listening,  
the way you listen to a man who has lost three roofs  
and is still standing in his yard  
with his hat in his hand.  
The cicadas were loud that year.  
Louder than usual, Ruth Ann said.  
“Means a hard winter.”  
She was right about most things.  
She was wrong about that one.  

VI  
October the leaves turned and the hunters came.  
Out-of-state plates, orange vests,  
the smell of gun oil and coffee  
in the aisle at the hardware store.  
Earl Fisk sold them licenses and said,  
“Mind the fence line on the ridge.”  
One of them asked where the big buck was  
and Earl said, “He’s where he wants to be,”  
which is the kind of thing Earl says  
that sounds like nothing  
and is not nothing.  
The valley got quiet after they left.  
The deer came back down.  
They always come back down.  

VII  
The first snow came the week of Thanksgiving,  
early, before the turkey,  
and Marla put the storm windows up herself  
because she always did,  
and Lyle came over to help  
and she let him,  
and they stood on the porch afterward  
drinking coffee from the dented thermos  
and not saying much.  
“Looks like a long one,” Lyle said.  
“Looks like,” Marla said.  
The snow came down past the streetlight  
like the whole sky was getting quieter.  

VIII  
February, the ice on the river  
and the ice on the road  
and the ice in the words we used with each other,  
short, careful,  
everybody waiting for the thaw.  
Ruth Ann Kessler died on a Tuesday.  
The ground was too hard to dig,  
so they waited,  
and the whole valley waited with her,  
and when they finally laid her down in April,  
the lilacs were coming,  
and the river was loud again,  
and Earl Fisk said, “She’d have liked this weather,”  
and Marla said, “She’d have said it was going to rain,”  
and it did,  
a little,  
just enough to settle the dust.

title: short story|a night bus driver and a passenger who never gets off
text:
The 11:40 to Waltham is a route for the dead and the newly employed. I’ve been driving it six years. You get the nurses coming off shift, staring at nothing. You get the guys who smell of bleach and regret. You get me, Earl, with a thermos of coffee that’s mostly sugar and a radio that only picks up the country station.

The bus is a 2009 Nova LFS. The back door hisses like an old man getting out of a chair. There’s a stain on the ceiling above seat 14 that looks, if you squint, like the state of Ohio, and I’ve had a lot of time to squint.

She got on at the hospital stop. Third stop of the night. Blue coat, the kind that’s for show more than warmth. Carried a plastic bag from a pharmacy, the logo worn off. Didn’t look at me. Just tapped her card and went to the middle, sat on the left side, and put the bag on the seat next to her like it was a sleeping cat.

People do that. They get on, they ride, they get off. The rhythm of it. You learn to feel the pull of the bell before you hear it. The shift in a person’s weight when they stand.

But she didn’t move.

We went through the retail park. The neon signs of the 24-hour gym and the discount carpet warehouse. A fox trotting along the pavement, bold as brass. She just looked out the window.

Downtown next. A couple of lads got on, all noise and cheap cologne, and I had to tell them to turn the music down. One of them glanced at her, then looked away. She was doing that thing people do when they don’t want to be seen. Not hiding. Just… absent.

The lads got off at The Swan. A woman got on, cried quietly for four stops, then got off. The bus emptied and filled, emptied and filled. And still, the blue coat. The plastic bag.

By the time we hit the ring road, the bus was empty. Just me, the hum of the engine, the ghost of her in the mirror. The sodium lights were making stripes across the seats. I kept glancing back. Habit. You check your mirror, you check your passengers. She was still there.

I had a supervisor once, old Bob, he said, “Earl, you’re a driver, not a social worker. You drive. They ride. That’s the deal.” Bob was a miserable sod, but he was mostly right. Mostly.

I pulled into the terminus. End of the line. Waltham. A dead-end estate with one shop and a pub that’s been closed for a decade. I killed the engine. The silence was sudden and thick. I just sat there for a minute, listening to the tick of the cooling metal. Then I got up.

“End of the line, love,” I said. My voice sounded too loud.

She didn’t flinch. Just kept looking out the window at the blank brick wall of the laundrette.

“Miss?”

I walked down the aisle. The floor was sticky with something I didn’t want to identify. I got closer. I could smell her now. Not bad. Just… nothing. Like the air in a room nobody’s used for a long time.

“This is the last stop. Waltham.”

She turned her head. Slowly. Her face was the kind you forget while you’re looking at it. Pale. Eyes the colour of dishwater. She didn’t look sad. She didn’t look anything.

“I know,” she said. Her voice was quiet, but clear. “I’m just going to sit here a while.”

“You can’t,” I said. “I’ve got to take the bus back to the depot. I have to lock up.”

“I’ll be gone by then,” she said. And then she smiled. It was a small, tired thing. “Don’t worry. You won’t even notice.”

And what do you do with that? Call the police? For what? Sitting on a bus? I stood there, feeling the absurdity of it all. The thermos in my hand, the sticky floor, the ghost in the blue coat. I had a Sudoku book at home with one puzzle left. I had a cat that needed feeding.

I went back to the front. Sat in the driver’s seat. Started the engine.

I drove the empty bus all the way back to the depot. Didn’t look in the mirror once. Parked it. Swept the floor. Found a hairgrip and a bus ticket from 2018. And when I walked past seat 14, it was empty.

The plastic bag was gone too.

I don’t know. Maybe she was just a person. Maybe she was a story I tell myself to get through the quiet nights. But some nights, when the fog’s down and the radio’s just static, I’ll be driving the 11:40 and I’ll feel the bus get a little heavier. Just for a second. And I’ll think, *She’s still riding.*

And I just keep driving.

title: short story|a beekeeper's widow deciding whether to keep the hives
text:
The suit still smelled of him. That was the worst of it—not the empty chair at the table or the cold side of the bed, but the way the canvas holdall in the mudroom breathed out his sweat and smoke and the faint sweetness of propolis every time she walked past. Ellen stood in the yard with the veil pushed back, the spring sun already too warm on her shoulders, and listened to the low hum coming from the twelve white boxes lined up along the fence.

Arthur had kept bees for thirty-one years. He had kept them through droughts and varroa and the year the county sprayed for mosquitoes and half the colonies died. He had kept them through his own bad back and the winter he broke his wrist and Ellen had to drive him out to the hives because he refused to miss a check. He had not, however, arranged to keep them through dying, and so the question had landed in her lap like a dropped frame, heavy and full of noise.

The first inspection had been a disaster. She'd waited too long, afraid of it, and by the time she opened the first box the bees had drawn comb across the inner cover and she couldn't get the lid off without tearing it. They boiled up around her, not angry exactly, but confused, and she'd stood there in the smoke with her heart going and her hands shaking and thought: I am sixty-three years old and I do not know what I am doing. She'd closed it up and gone inside and cried at the kitchen sink, which was a thing she had not done since the funeral.

But the bees had not died. That was the thing. She had neglected them for six weeks and they had gone on doing what they did, gathering what the fields offered, raising their young in the dark. There was something almost insulting about it, and something comforting too. The world did not require her to hold it up.

Frank from the next farm over had offered to take them. He had a hundred and forty hives and a flatbed and a nephew who helped with the heavy lifting. "No sense you getting stung," he'd said, standing in her kitchen with his cap in his hands, and she knew he meant it kindly. She had said she'd think about it. She had been thinking about it for eleven days.

The truth was she didn't need the money, not badly. Arthur's pension and the life insurance would keep the lights on. The honey had never been a living, only a habit—jars for the church fair, jars for the neighbors at Christmas, a few hundred dollars at the farmers market in a good year. What she needed was a reason to be outside at seven in the morning with the dew soaking through her boots.

She lit the smoker the way he had taught her, a twist of newspaper and a handful of pine shavings, and pumped the bellows until the smoke came white and cool. The first hive was the gentlest—Arthur had always said the quiet ones were the ones to watch, that a calm colony was a colony with a good queen and no worries. She lifted the lid and the smell came up at her, that warm waxy breath, and the bees went on with their work, unbothered, crawling over the frames in their slow amber traffic.

She found the queen on the fourth frame. She knew it was her because of the small court around her, the way the others turned toward her, and because she was longer than the rest, her abdomen tapering to a point. Ellen had never been able to find the queen before. Arthur could spot one in three seconds flat, could tell you which hive she'd come from by the color of her, but Ellen had always just nodded and pretended to see. Now here she was, plain as day, laying her eggs in a neat spiral, and Ellen felt a small unreasonable pride, as if she'd been the one to put her there.

She worked through the rest of the hives slowly, the way he used to, taking her time. The seventh was light on stores and she made a note to feed it. The ninth had a queen cell on the bottom bar, swollen and peanut-shaped, and she stood looking at it a long moment, trying to remember what he would have done—leave it, probably, let them swarm, let them decide. The tenth had a drone layer, the brood bumpy and scattered, and that one would need a new queen or it would dwindle and die. She wrote it down on the pad in her pocket in handwriting that was not his.

By the time she finished the sun was properly up and the field beyond the fence was loud with insects. She set the smoker down in the grass and pulled off her gloves and stood there with her hands on her hips, looking at the twelve boxes. Frank's nephew could be here by Thursday. She could have the whole thing gone before the blackberries came in.

She thought about the jars in the pantry, the ones Arthur had labeled in his careful block capitals, and about the way he used to come in from the yard at dusk with his veil under his arm and say, "They're all right, El. They're all right today." She thought about the queen on the fourth frame, turning in her slow court.

She picked up the smoker and walked back toward the house to call Frank and tell him no.

title: creation myth|how the northern lights were woven
text:
In the beginning, there was no sky, only the Great Dark, and within it, the First Weaver, whose name was Aja, sat at a loom made of starlight and silence. She was not a woman, nor a spirit, nor a god as they are later understood, but a patient and deliberate force, and her hands were the color of deep water. For ages beyond counting, she did nothing but feel the threads between her fingers, learning their tension, their give, the low hum each one made when plucked. These were the threads of what would become everything: the heavy, slow-twisting cord of stone; the cool, slippery filament of water; the dry, brittle strand of air. She wove them into being, and the world took shape below her, a heavy and quiet place.

But the world was without light, and Aja saw that the threads of air and water, though beautiful, were invisible in the Great Dark. They had no voice. She reached into the folds of the void and drew out a new material, one she had been saving. It was not a thread or a cord, but something finer, like the dust from a moth’s wing, and it held the memory of fire without its heat. It was light, but it was a wild, untamed light, and it would not be woven. It slipped from the shuttle, it frayed at the edges of the loom, it refused to be bound.

Aja knew she could not force it. So she sat for another age, simply holding this strange, luminous material, letting it learn the shape of her hands. She saw that it responded not to force, but to feeling. When she was calm, the light settled into a soft, steady glow. When she remembered the loneliness of the Great Dark, it pulsed with a deep and sorrowful blue. When she felt the joy of the world she had made, it flared into a brilliant, silent green. She was not its master, but its partner.

With this understanding, she began her greatest work. She did not try to weave the light into the fabric of the world, for it was too vast and too wild for such a small pattern. Instead, she took the very first threads she had ever spun—the ones that had made the sky—and she began to unweave them, ever so gently. She pulled them apart, creating a vast, soft canopy of unwoven threads, a place of potential, a loom for the sky itself.

Into this canopy, she began to work the light. She used her fingers as the shuttle, her breath as the weft. She took a strand of the deep blue from her sorrow and laid it across the sky. Then, with a flick of her wrist, she threw a handful of the wild, green light against it, and it clung, not like dye to cloth, but like frost to a windowpane. She worked for a hundred years on the first ribbon, a great, shimmering curtain of green that rippled as if in a breeze that did not exist. It was not a solid thing; it was a suggestion of a color, a motion caught in the act of happening.

She saw that the light was lonely in its vastness, so she drew upon the memory of the world below. She remembered the slow, patient crawl of the glaciers and wove that feeling into the fabric, giving the lights their slow, majestic dance. She remembered the sudden crack of ice on a winter river and threaded that sharp, sudden flash of white and violet through the green. She remembered the quiet hush that falls over a snow-covered forest and gave the lights their profound and utter silence.

These were not just colors; they were the echoes of her own experience. The fierce, exultant red that sometimes tore through the curtain was the memory of the first time a thread had held fast in her loom. The soft, rose-pink fringe that sometimes edged the green was the feeling of tenderness she had for her creation. The lights were a tapestry of her own memory, a diary written in the sky.

When she was finished, she did not tie off the ends. She left them loose, to unravel and re-weave themselves with the turning of the ages. She stepped back from the loom of the sky, and for the first time, the world below was lit by something other than the cold, distant stars. It was a light that moved, that breathed, that remembered. It was a light that was woven, not from force, but from feeling; not to illuminate the world, but to remind it that it was not alone. And so the lights have danced ever since, a vast and silent weaving, a story told in color and motion, a memory of the first quiet joy and the first deep sorrow, hanging in the air between the world and the stars.

title: literary novel|an elderly translator finishing her last book
text:
The manuscript arrived in a cardboard box, as they always did, but this one was lighter than most. I had cleared a space for it on the long oak table that has been the center of my life for forty years. The table is scarred with the rings of countless cups of tea, the gouges of a letter opener I once dropped, the faint, ghostly rectangles where stacks of paper have sat for months at a time. I am a translator. Or, I was. The distinction feels less like a matter of retirement and more like a gradual erosion, a coastline receding inch by inch until one day you look and the sea is somewhere else entirely.

This book was to be my last. A slim novel by a writer I had never heard of, a man from a country whose language I have spent my entire adult life trying to convince myself I understand. The publisher’s note was brief, almost apologetic. A minor work, they said. A coda. I ran my fingers over the cover page, the title in a typeface that felt aggressively modern. *The Glass Orchard*. I already disliked it.

For a week, I did nothing. I let the box sit there, a quiet accusation. I made tea, I watched the rain streak the windows, I listened to the house settle around me. My husband, Henrik, has been dead for seven years. His presence is still the most substantial thing in this house, a silence that has its own weight and texture. He used to call my translations “acts of benevolent treason.” He would read the final proofs aloud, his voice a low counterpoint to the rhythm of the original text in my head. Now, there is only my own voice, and it has grown querulous and thin.

On the eighth day, I opened the box. The paper smelled of dust and distant ink. I began to read. The prose was spare, almost grudging. It was not a difficult text, not in the way of the philosophical treatises I translated in my thirties, or the dense, knotty poetry of my fifties. It was simple. A man returns to his childhood village. He walks through the rooms of his dead parents’ house. He remembers. That was all. It was the kind of book I might have dismissed once, as lacking in intellectual rigor. But now, at seventy-eight, I found its simplicity terrifying. It was like looking at a photograph of a place you know intimately and finding that all the familiar landmarks have been removed.

I began to work. My method has not changed in decades. First, a complete reading, pen in hand, marking nothing but the places where the language resists me. Then, a literal, ugly, word-for-word transcription into a notebook. This is the skeleton. Then, the slow, painstaking work of giving it flesh, of finding the English rhythm that corresponds to the original’s heartbeat. It is a process of listening, of waiting for the whisper of the author’s intent to become audible in another tongue.

But the whisper would not come. The man in the book, the returning son, was a stranger to me. His nostalgia felt like a performance. His observations were precise but cold. I would sit at my table for hours, the original text on my left, my notebook on my right, and feel a profound, unsettling emptiness. Who was I to be this man’s voice? What could I, an old woman in a quiet house, possibly know of his particular grief?

One afternoon, I came across a sentence. It described the man standing in his mother’s kitchen, the light coming through the window. The original was something like, “The sun lay on the floor like a tired animal.” It is a good line, but it is not mine. I wrote it down. Then I sat back and looked at it. A tired animal. I thought of our old dog, a greyhound named Icarus, who in his final years would find a patch of sun in this very room and collapse into it with a sigh that seemed to hold the sum of all his disappointments. The memory was not a story; it was a physical sensation, a warmth on my own skin, the smell of dust and dog.

I crossed out my first attempt. I wrote, “The sun was on the floor.” Then, after a long moment, I added, “and the house was quiet.” It was not a translation. It was a betrayal. A small, quiet act of treason.

I have not written another word since. The manuscript is still there, open to that page. The deadline, which once felt like a distant threat, is now a near certainty. I will not finish it. I will not translate this man’s book. I will sit here, in the failing light, with the ghost of a dog at my feet and the weight of a thousand other people’s words in the air, and I will listen to the silence of my own. It is, I think, the only honest thing left to do.

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
The ledger was in the bottom of his tackle box. Not with the bills and the tax stuff, which my mother had already gone through with a glass of wine and a roll of trash bags. The tackle box. The one that still smelled of gasoline and old rubber and something sweet underneath, like bait gone bad in a hot garage.

I almost threw it out. I want to be honest about that. I had a trash bag in one hand and the box in the other and I thought, who needs thirty-year-old fish hooks. But it was heavy in a way that didn't make sense. Hooks are light. Sinkers aren't that heavy. So I opened it, and there, under a tray of rusty spoons and a dried-out minnow trap, was a black-and-white composition notebook. The kind you buy at a drugstore for ninety-nine cents. The kind I used in fifth grade for spelling words.

He'd written on every page. Both sides. In pencil, mostly, going soft where his hand had rested.

It wasn't a diary. That's the thing. I kept waiting for a diary. Some word about me, about us, about anything that happened. Instead it was numbers. Columns. Dates. "Apr 12 — gas 4.10, coffee .75, tipped the kid at the carwash a dollar, why, I don't know." That kind of thing. Groceries itemized down to the onion. "Onions. Two. Looked good."

I sat on the garage floor for maybe an hour. Cold concrete, the door open to the driveway, a neighbor's dog barking at nothing the way dogs do. I read it front to back and then back to front looking for something I'd missed.

The entries went back to 1978. Before me. Before the house. He wrote down the price of a haircut in a town I'd never heard of, and next to it, in the margin, a single word: "Bad." That was the closest he came to complaining. About anything. Ever. I laughed out loud in that garage, which is a strange thing to do alone.

There were digressions. Rare, but there. "Saw a hawk today. Big. Sat on the fence for ten minutes." No further comment. Ten minutes. He timed it. That's my father. He wrote down the hawk like it was a purchase.

I found the year I was born. He recorded the hospital parking, the vending machine coffee, and then a gap of two blank pages before the entries pick up again. Two blank pages. I don't know what that means. Maybe nothing. Maybe he was just tired.

Here's the part I keep coming back to. In 1993, for about six weeks, he wrote down every penny he spent on me. Not everything — just the extras. The cleats, the book fair money, the two dollars for the school dance I didn't want to go to. Each one has a little checkmark next to it. Not a tally. A checkmark. Like he was crossing something off a list of things he owed the world, and the world was me.

I never asked him for that two dollars. He offered. He just handed it over at the kitchen table and said, "In case."

The last entry is three weeks before he died. "Pens. Two. Blue." Nothing after. No hawk. No tipped dollar. The pencil resting in the crease where he'd closed it.

My mother wanted to know what was in the box. I told her fishing stuff. I don't know why I lied. Maybe because she'd have wanted to throw the notebook out too — she was very efficient that week, in a way I understand now and couldn't then. Maybe because it felt like the one thing he'd left that was only mine. Or only his. Hard to say where the line is.

The notebook's in my desk drawer now. I don't take it out much. When I do, I don't read it, really. I just flip through it and look at the pencil marks, the way his handwriting leaned harder in some places than others. The man kept a ledger for forty years and never once wrote down a feeling. But you can read it anyway. You can read it just fine.

I still have the tackle box too. I can't fish. Never could.

title: literary novel|a lighthouse keeper's daughter returning after the light is automated
text:
The kitchen smelled of cold ash and the sea. Mara set the kettle on the propane burner and listened to the hiss, the tick of the metal expanding. Outside, the light—no longer *her* light, no longer anyone’s—swept its pale, mechanical gaze across the water. It had been automated for a year, but she still felt its rhythm in her bones, a phantom pulse. She had come back to pack the last of her father’s things, a task she had postponed through a winter of excuses, through a spring of silence.

The cottage was a time capsule of a life measured in weather. Barometers hung on the walls like icons, their brass faces green with age. A tide table from 1998 was still pinned by the door, its corners curled and brittle. She ran a finger over the spine of a navigation manual, the leather cracked like a dried riverbed. Her father had taught her to read the sea from this room, to name the clouds and the winds, to understand that the light was not just a beacon but a promise. *We are here,* it said. *You are not alone.* Now the promise was kept by a computer chip and a backup battery, a silent, unfaltering sentry that never grew tired, never grew lonely.

She climbed the spiral stairs to the lamp room, her footsteps echoing in the hollow tower. The great lens, the Fresnel masterpiece her grandfather had polished with velvet and reverence, stood silent and dark. The automation crew had left the old lamp in place, a museum piece beneath the new, efficient LED unit that squatted above it like a cuckoo in a sparrow’s nest. Mara remembered the heat of the old lamp, the smell of vaporized kerosene, the way her father’s face would glow as he wound the clockwork mechanism, a ritual as sacred as prayer. She would sit on the top step, wrapped in a wool blanket, and watch him work, his hands sure and steady. He was the keeper of the light, and she was the keeper of him.

The new light was a cold, blue-white thing. It had no warmth, no scent. It did not need her. It did not need anyone.

Downstairs, she began to empty the drawers. In the bottom of a heavy oak dresser, she found a small, tin box. Inside were buttons, a dry fountain pen, and a photograph. It was of her mother, standing on the rocks below the lighthouse, her hair whipping across her face, her laughter a silent, joyful thing caught in sepia. Mara had been six when her mother left, and her father had never spoken of it, his grief a locked room she was never allowed to enter. He had simply become more devoted to the light, as if trying to atone for a darkness he couldn't name.

She held the photograph, and for the first time in years, she felt a hot, sudden anger at the sea, at the light, at the stubborn, unyielding man who had raised her. He had given his life to a tower, to a machine that now rendered him obsolete. He had taught her to be self-sufficient, to be a keeper, but he had never taught her how to leave. Or how to stay.

Later, she walked down to the water’s edge. The tide was out, and the rocks were slick with weed. The wind was a sharp, clean blade. She looked up at the tower, its whitewash stark against the bruising sky. The beam swung around, indifferent, touching her for a moment before moving on, illuminating the empty expanse of the Atlantic. She had spent her childhood inside that beam, safe and defined. Now she was outside it, in the dark, and the world felt vast and terrifyingly free.

Her father had died in the spring, quietly, in the village infirmary, not in the tower he loved. His last words to her, on the phone, had been about the weather. "Storm coming in from the west," he'd said, his voice thin as paper. "You should check your gutters." He had been checking the gutters of a house she hadn't lived in for a decade. He had been keeping watch, as always, from a place where he could no longer see the sea.

She didn't cry. The tears were a luxury she couldn't afford, a crack in the dam she had built around herself. Instead, she picked up a smooth, flat stone and skimmed it across the water. It skipped once, twice, three times before sinking. She thought of her father's hands, the calluses from the ropes and the brass polish, the way they had held hers when she was small, teaching her to tie a bowline. *A knot that never slips,* he'd said. *But it can always be untied.*

A foghorn sounded in the distance, a low, mournful note. It was not her horn. It belonged to a freighter, a world of commerce and progress that had no use for keepers. The beam swept past again, and in its brief, ghostly light, she saw the ghost of a girl on the stairs, a ghost of a man at the lamp. They were fading, becoming part of the stone and the salt and the story. She was the last one left to remember.

She turned her back on the tower and walked toward the cottage. The door was open, a rectangle of warm light in the gathering dusk. It was not the lighthouse beam, but it was enough. It was a light she had made herself. The automation had taken the light, but it had not taken the keeper. She would pack the boxes. She would lock the door. And in the morning, she would leave. The sea would keep its own counsel, and the light would go on turning, faithful to no one but the night.

title: myth retelling|a river goddess who refuses to flood the valley
text:
The river came down from the mountains with the spring melt, and it came down singing. It sang through the high passes where the snow still held in the shadows, it sang over the smooth grey stones of the upper reaches, and by the time it reached the first terraces of the valley it had found its full voice—a low, brown, churning note that carried the smell of iron and crushed green things. The people in the valley heard it and were glad, for the river was the valley’s blood, and its song meant the fields would drink.
