Now, the hives were hers. Six of them, lined up like white tombstones at the edge of the meadow. The county extension agent had called, a polite young man with a clipboard who’d offered to “help her liquidate the assets.” The word had stuck in her craw. Assets. As if the bees were stocks and bonds, and not the buzzing, temperamental, strangely elegant creatures Tom had loved more than he’d loved most people.

She walked closer, the grass wetting the hem of her jeans. The bees were busy, oblivious to her sorrow or her indecision. They flew in and out of the small entrances with a purpose that felt obscene. They were making honey. They were raising brood. They were doing exactly what they were supposed to do, and Tom’s absence meant nothing to them. Their indifference was a cold slap.

She thought of the alternatives. The agent had explained it all. She could sell the whole operation—hives, extractor, the shed full of supers and frames and the faint, sweet smell of beeswax that she couldn’t bear to enter. A man from the next county was interested. He’d have them loaded on a flatbed and hauled away in an afternoon. The meadow would be just a meadow again. Quiet. She could sell the honey, too, the dozens of jars Tom had already put up, their golden color catching the light in the pantry. She could be free of it all. The thought was a cool, clean draught of air in the suffocating house.

But then there was the honey. Not the jars, but the memory of it. Tom, his hands sticky with propolis, holding out a spoon of honeycomb for her to taste. The first time, early in their marriage, the flavor had been a shock—not just sweet, but complex, with notes of the wild mint that grew by the creek and something else, something dark and bitter she couldn’t name. “That’s the willow,” he’d said, his eyes crinkling. “Bees are like winemakers. They tell you a story about the land.” He could taste the season in it, the specific week of the summer, the sun and the rain.

Martha didn’t know the story of the land. She knew the story of Tom. She knew the way he’d be up at dawn to check the hives, the quiet joy in his face when he found the queen, that single, marked dot in the seething mass of her subjects. She knew the way he’d talk to them, a low murmur she could never quite make out, as if he were sharing secrets.

She stood before Hive 2. It was the gentlest colony, Tom had always said. The bees rose and fell around her, a living curtain. A single forager landed on the back of her hand. She didn’t flinch. It walked a few steps, its antennae twitching, tasting her skin. Did she smell like him? she wondered. The thought was a sudden, sharp ache. The bee lifted off, a speck against the flat white sky.

To keep them, she would have to learn. She would have to open the hives, to read the frames, to find the queen. She would have to know when to add a super, when to treat for mites, when to worry. She would have to become the keeper. The responsibility felt immense, a physical weight on her shoulders, heavy as a full super. And what if she failed? What if the hives weakened, or swarmed, or succumbed to the winter? It would be her failure, a betrayal of his memory.

But to sell them, to watch them loaded onto that flatbed, to see the meadow empty… it would be like losing him a second time. She would be selling not just the bees, but the story he told with them. The wild mint and the willow, the specific sun of that specific summer. She would be letting the hum die out.

She took a few steps back. The bees continued their work, a tapestry of motion. They were not hers. They were not Tom’s. They were their own, a wild, fierce, self-contained universe. But he had been their shepherd. He had tended them, and now he was gone, and the meadow was silent in a way she’d never noticed before.

She turned back toward the house, the low hum still vibrating through her. It was a question, a thousand questions, hanging in the sweet, heavy air. She would not call the agent today. Not tomorrow, either. She would go inside and she would find his notebook, the one with the cracked leather cover and the pages filled with his neat, looping scrawl. She would read the story of the land. And then, maybe, she would learn how to listen.

title: short story|a piano tuner who visits the same blind client for thirty years
text:
The rain had stopped by the time Arthur Pemberton reached the corner of Maple and Third, but the gutters still ran with it, carrying a brown soup of leaves and cigarette ends past the shuttered bakery. He shifted the leather satchel to his other shoulder and checked his watch—ten past two, twelve minutes late. He had never been late before.

The house was a narrow Victorian wedged between a laundromat and a dental office, its clapboard painted a faded green that had once been fashionable in the seventies. A brass plate beside the door read M. HOLLOWAY, PIANO INSTRUCTION, though no student had climbed those steps in years. Arthur wiped his shoes on the mat and knocked twice.

“It’s open,” came the voice from inside, thin but certain.

He found her in the parlor, seated in the wing chair by the window as always, a wool blanket across her knees. Margaret Holloway was eighty-three now, though she’d never told him that directly; he’d pieced it together from the dates on the recital programs she kept in a drawer, the ones from before the glaucoma had taken the last of her sight. Her white hair was pinned back with a tortoiseshell comb, and her hands rested on the arms of the chair, fingers slightly curved, as though still expecting keys beneath them.

“Mr. Pemberton,” she said. “You’re wet.”

“It’s raining, Mrs. Holloway.”

“I know it’s raining. I can hear it in the walls. But you’re wetter than the rain would make you. You walked from the station.”

He smiled, though she couldn’t see it. “The bus was late.”

“Liar. You always walk when you’re thinking about something. Sit down. The kettle’s on.”

He set his satchel on the floor and took the chair opposite her, the one with the worn velvet seat that had been his for thirty years. The parlor smelled of dust and lemon polish and the faint, sweet decay of old paper. The Steinway stood in the corner, its mahogany lid closed, a lace runner across the top holding a photograph of a man in a navy uniform—her husband, dead since 1978.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I said the bus—”

“Not the bus. You’re late in yourself. You’ve been late in yourself for months now, Mr. Pemberton. I hear it in the way you tune. You rush the middle octaves. You used to linger there.”

Arthur looked at his hands. They were seventy-one years old, spotted and stiff, the knuckles swollen with arthritis that made the fine work harder each year. He’d been tuning pianos since he was twenty-two, and Margaret Holloway’s Steinway since the spring of 1994, when her regular man had retired and left her his name in a letter.

“I’m thinking of retiring,” he said.

The kettle whistled from the kitchen. Margaret didn’t move.

“I’m seventy-one,” he went on. “My daughter wants me to move to Portland. She says the winters here are too hard on me. She’s probably right.”

“Probably,” Margaret said. “People are usually right about the winters.”

She rose then, her hand finding the edge of the side table, then the doorframe, then the counter. He watched her make the tea—two cups, one sugar in his, none in hers—with the unhesitating grace of a woman who had lived in the same house for fifty years and could navigate it in her sleep. She set his cup on the table beside him and returned to her chair.

“You know what I’ll miss?” she said. “Not the tuning. The tuning I can get from anyone. It’s the way you talk while you work. You tell me about the weather, about your daughter, about the cats in your neighborhood. You tell me things you probably don’t tell anyone else, because you know I can’t see your face and judge you.”

Arthur wrapped his hands around the warm cup. “I tell you things because you listen.”

“I listen because you’re interesting. Most people aren’t.” She sipped her tea. “Do you remember the first time you came? You were so nervous. You dropped your wrench twice. You kept apologizing for the noise.”

“I remember.”

“You tuned the whole thing in forty minutes. Fastest anyone’s ever done it. And then you sat down and played a little Chopin. I hadn’t heard that nocturne in years. I cried. You were mortified.”

“I thought I’d offended you.”

“You gave me back something I’d lost.” She set her cup down. “That’s not a thing you retire from, Mr. Pemberton. That’s a thing you do until you can’t.”

He looked at the Steinway. The lid was closed, but he knew the inside by heart—the rusted strings, the worn hammers, the felt that had compressed under decades of her students’ hands. He knew the way the third A above middle C went flat in humid weather, the way the pedals squeaked in January, the way the whole instrument seemed to breathe when she played it, which she still did, every morning, though she could no longer read the music and had to play from memory.

“I’ll tune it today,” he said. “One more time.”

“You’ll tune it today,” she agreed. “And next spring, when the weather turns, you’ll tune it again. And you’ll complain about the bus, and I’ll know you walked, and we’ll have tea. That’s how it works.”

Arthur opened his satchel and took out his tools. The light through the window had turned the color of weak honey. He crossed the room and lifted the lid, and the strings caught the light, and Margaret Holloway sat back in her chair and folded her hands, and for a moment the house was so quiet he could hear the rain drying on the roof.

“Start with the middle octaves,” she said. “Linger there.”

He did.

title: memoir|growing up above a family laundry in a northern English town
text:
The thing about living above a laundry is the heat. Not the dry, aggressive heat of a radiator, but a wet, woolly heat that crept up through the floorboards and settled in the walls. It was a presence. Our flat, on the two floors above Bradley’s Wash-o-Mat, was never truly cold, even in the January of 1984 when the pipes froze solid and Dad swore for a full ten minutes without repeating himself. The flat just got a different kind of damp, a sort of disappointed mustiness, like a dog that’s been shut out of a room.

You’d wake up to the smell of it. Not just clean linen, which is what people imagine. It was more specific than that. It was the sharp, chemical tang of industrial detergent, the soapy ghost of a thousand other people’s socks and shirts, and the underlying, deeply ingrained scent of the starch they used on the big hotel contracts. My school shirts always smelled faintly of it. For years, I thought that was just what clean meant.

The laundry itself was a cavern. A low-slung brick building that squatted at the end of our terraced street, a full stop at the end of a long, grimy sentence. The windows were always steamed up, even in summer, so you could never really see in. Just shapes. Vague, shifting figures moving between the great metal drums of the washers, which were the size of small cars and made a noise like a continuously breaking wave. My mother was one of those shapes. She worked the presses, feeding sheets into the great mangle that would flatten them into submission, her face flushed and her hair frizzing in the steam.

My job, from about the age of six, was the lost property. I’d sit on the counter by the till, a chipped Formica slab, and go through the bins of things people had left behind. Odd socks, mostly. A child’s cardigan. A single, lace-trimmed handkerchief. But sometimes, treasures. I found a ten-pound note once, folded so small it was like a little secret. Dad let me keep it. I bought a Rubik’s Cube and a whole selection box of chocolate bars, and felt sick for two days. There was a book once, too, a paperback with a torn cover, called *The Passion of New Eve*. I was far too young for it, of course, but I read it anyway, hidden under the covers with a torch, the smell of bleach from the sheets below me mixing with the imaginary, terrifying London in the book.

There’s a rhythm to that life. A rhythm you don’t get in a normal house. Monday was the day the hospital linens came, so the whole place smelled of antiseptic. Friday was the big push for the weekend trade, the local restaurants and B&Bs, and Dad would be up till midnight getting the last of it done. You’d fall asleep to the thump and thrum of the machines. It was a lullaby, really. A mechanical, reliable heart.

The best thing was the roof. There was a flat section of it, outside my bedroom window, that you could shimmy onto if you were careful. From up there, you could see the whole town. The dark, satanic mills, long since dead, their chimneys like broken fingers pointing at the sky. The bus station. The grey ribbon of the canal. And the people, scurrying about their business, none of them knowing that they were being watched by a boy who smelled of soap powder. I’d sit up there for hours, reading, or just watching. It felt like being a king of a very small, very damp kingdom.

I left when I was eighteen. University. The first thing I noticed in my halls of residence was the silence. And the cold. A dry, papery cold that was always with you. I’d lie in bed, and my body would be waiting for the floor to start humming, for the heat to rise, for the smell of clean clothes to wash over me. It never came. My flatmates thought I was strange because I’d sometimes go and sit in the launderette on the corner, just to watch the washing go round. They thought I was doing my washing. I was. But it was more than that. I was listening for a heartbeat I’d known my whole life, and I could never quite hear it in that place. It was always just out of earshot, like a song you can’t remember the tune to.

title: literary essay|silence and omission in short fiction
text:
The waiter clears the plates, and for a moment the table is a small stage of absence: the ring his cup left, the fork laid at an angle, the napkin crumpled like a failed draft. My friend is telling me about a story she read—I have already forgotten the author—in which a woman learns of her husband’s death and does not speak for three pages. “Nothing happens,” my friend says, meaning everything happens. She means the kettle boils, the neighbor knocks, the dog needs walking, and the woman moves through these small obligations with a precision that is itself a kind of scream. The story omits the scream. That is the scream.

This is the oldest trick in the short story’s narrow book, and it never stops working: the reader is asked to supply what the page withholds. Fiction is an art of the ellipsis, and the ellipsis is an invitation. When Hemingway writes that a thing is “nice” and leaves the word to rot in its context, he is trusting us to smell the rot. When Mansfield ends “The Lady’s Maid” with a servant’s cheerful “I don’t know,” the two words are a door slammed on a room we have already seen. The omission is not a gap in the meaning; it is the meaning’s engine. The white space on the page is not empty—it is pressurized.

Consider the mechanics of it. A story can say a character is grief-stricken, or it can show her folding her husband’s shirts into a drawer and then, a line later, unfolding them and folding them again. The second version omits the word “grief” and thereby admits it more fully. This is what Chekhov meant when he told his brother that one must not write “the moon shone” but rather “the neck of a broken bottle glittered.” The glitter carries the moon; the moon is never named. Omission is not a subtraction but a transfer of labor—from the writer’s description to the reader’s inference, where it becomes more intimate, more durable, more true.

And silence, in fiction, is never merely the absence of speech. It is a material with weight and grain. Think of the silences in Carver, which are not peaceful but load-bearing, holding up whole marriages of resentment. Think of the final silence in “The Dead,” where Gabriel’s soul swoons while snow falls “faintly” through the universe—the adverb doing the work of a whole orchestra. Or think of the child in “Araby,” who arrives at the bazaar too late and hears a voice call “O love! O love!” in a tone that is merely commercial, and the story closes on his eyes burning with anguish and anger. Joyce does not explain the boy’s disillusionment. He omits the explanation, and the omission is the disillusionment.

There is a risk, of course. Omission can be mere coyness, silence can be a writer’s evasion dressed as restraint. The difference is whether the withheld thing is present in the texture of the prose—whether the absence has a shape. A good story leaves a hole the exact size of what is missing. A bad one leaves a hole the size of the author’s uncertainty. The reader can tell. We are all, as readers, experts in the archaeology of gaps; we know when a silence has been earned and when it has merely been permitted.

My friend stirs her coffee and says the thing I have been circling: “The story never tells you what she and her husband fought about. You just know it was the same fight, every time.” Exactly. The omission is not a secret withheld from the reader; it is a secret the reader is made to keep on the characters’ behalf. That is the peculiar intimacy of the form. The short story, compressed and ruthless, cannot afford to explain everything, and so it recruits us. We become accomplices in the unsaid. We finish the sentence the character cannot.

The waiter returns with the check, and my friend and I do what people do: we talk about something else. But the story stays with me, the way a room stays with you after the light is switched off—the furniture still there in the dark, exactly where we left it, waiting for someone to describe it.

title: fable|a crow who collects lost keys
text:
The crow’s name was Corvus, though no one had called him that for a very long time. He lived in the hollow of an ancient oak at the edge of a town that was always losing things. Corvus did not collect what others collected. He had no interest in the bright foil of gum wrappers or the smooth, cool weight of a discarded bottle cap. His passion, his singular and obsessive art, was keys.

His collection began by chance. He had been a young bird, foolish and loud, when he spotted a glint in the wet grass of a park. It was a small, silver key, the kind for a diary or a small wooden box. He took it to his nest, not for any reason he could name, but because it was perfect and small and held a secret he would never know. The weight of it in his beak was a satisfaction. The feel of it beneath his claw was a promise.

From that day, he became a hunter of lost access. He learned the rhythms of the town. He knew that on Tuesdays, the baker, a flustered man named Elias, would invariably pat his flour-dusted apron and sigh, having left his shop key in the lock of his back door. Corvus would wait until the man was busy with a customer, then swoop down and pluck the brass key from its resting place. He knew that the children who played by the river would often lose the keys to their bicycles, and he would find them half-buried in the mud, their tiny teeth clogged with grit.

His collection grew. He kept them in a hollowed-out branch, a secret gallery of forgotten portals. There were long, elegant keys of tarnished brass for houses with ivy climbing the walls. There were flat, utilitarian keys for padlocks on garden sheds. There were car keys, heavy and black with plastic buttons, which he found most puzzling and therefore most fascinating. He would arrange them by size, by shape, by the dullness or brilliance of their metal. He was a connoisseur. A key was not just a key; it was the story of a moment of carelessness, a small human drama of frustration and regret. He was the silent curator of these frozen moments.

He never used them. The idea of opening a door was anathema to him. The value was in the potential, the locked-away *what if*. A key that opened a door was a key whose mystery was spent. A key in his collection was a key that opened nothing but the vast, dark space of his own imagining. He would sometimes hold a small, ornate key in his beak and feel a tremor of pure possibility. What did it open? A music box that played a forgotten lullaby? A chest of letters from a long-dead lover? The cage of a singing bird? The not-knowing was the point.

One afternoon, a great storm lashed the town. The wind was a howling animal, tearing at shingles and snapping branches. Corvus, safe in his oak, watched the chaos. The next morning, the world was washed clean. The river had breached its banks, and the town was a mess of mud and debris. As Corvus flew over the ruins of a small, collapsed toolshed, he saw it. A key, larger than any he had ever seen, half-buried in the silt. It was not for a house or a car. It was immense, forged of black iron, and its head was shaped like a tangled knot of serpents. It was a key for a gate, a fortress, a dungeon. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen.

He wrestled it from the mud, the weight of it straining his neck. He flew it back to his oak with immense effort, his wings burning. He placed it at the center of his collection, the crowning jewel. For weeks, he was obsessed with it. He would stare at it for hours. It was a key that held the weight of history. It was a key that could command an army, or unseal a tomb, or open the door to a world of shadows. Its silence was louder than any other key’s. Its story was the grandest, the most terrifying.

But as the seasons turned, a strange thing happened. The black iron key began to feel less like a treasure and more like a burden. Its silence was not a promise but a void. The weight of its imagined stories began to press on him. The other keys, the small, domestic ones, seemed to whisper their simple tales of forgotten lunches and misplaced mail. They were humble and true. The iron key was a tyrant. It demanded a story so vast that it consumed all the others.

One evening, as the sun set and painted the sky in hues of bruised purple and gold, Corvus took the black iron key from his collection. He held its cold, heavy length in his claws. He felt not the thrill of possibility, but a profound weariness. He flew to the deepest part of the river, where the water ran dark and swift. He hovered for a moment, the great key dangling from his beak, and then he let it go. It fell with a silent, heavy plunge and was gone.

He returned to his oak. The collection felt lighter, more like itself. He picked up a small, silver key, the first one he had ever found, and felt its familiar, delicate weight. It was just a key. It was enough. He tucked his head beneath his wing, surrounded by his quiet, unlocked world.

title: short story|two sisters clearing out their mother's flat
text:
The flat smelled of old paper and the particular lavender soap she used, a scent that had always seemed to me to be the very essence of her, now revealed as something you could buy in a bulk pack of six. We had been at it for three hours. The silence between us was not companionable; it was a solid, thick thing, punctuated only by the sound of tape being peeled from cardboard and the soft thud of books into a box.

My sister, Claire, was ruthless. She moved through the rooms with the efficiency of a surgeon, her movements precise and unsentimental. She was sorting the kitchenware. I could hear the clink of cutlery as she wrapped each piece in newspaper, a sound as regular and final as a ticking clock.

I was in the bedroom, surrounded by the soft, faded geography of my mother’s clothes. I had started with the wardrobe, my hands moving through the fabrics as if reading a life in braille. Here was the heavy wool coat she wore for funerals. Here, the silk blouse with the coffee stain on the cuff, a badge of some forgotten, minor catastrophe. I wasn’t sorting. I was just touching. I was looking for a sign, a message, some hidden compartment in the lining of her life that would explain the last, quiet, retreating years.

“Found the photo albums,” Claire said from the doorway. She didn’t come in. She never liked this room, said it was too small.

“Right,” I said, my voice raspy from dust and disuse.

“They’re heavy. We should probably just take them. No time to go through them now.”

“No,” I agreed. “No time.”

She hovered for a moment, her gaze scanning the room, assessing its contents as volume, as weight, as a problem to be solved. “I’m going to start on the living room next. The books.”

“She loved her books,” I said, a stupid, obvious thing to say.

Claire’s expression didn’t change. “They’re just books now. They’re making the place damp.” She turned and left, her footsteps firm on the hallway floorboards.

I went back to the wardrobe. At the bottom, pushed to the back, was a small, wooden box, the kind that once held a cheap watch or a fountain pen. It wasn’t locked. Inside, there were no secrets, no letters from a clandestine lover, no key to a safety deposit box. There were just buttons. A whole collection of them, sorted into small, clear plastic bags. Horn buttons, glass buttons, little pearlescent ones from a child’s cardigan. She had labelled them in her tiny, precise handwriting: ‘Coat buttons – blue’, ‘Shirt buttons – white, small’.

I sat on the floor, the box in my lap. This was the most my mother thing I had ever found. A meticulous, pointless act of order. A quiet, obsessive cataloguing of the mundane. It was a language I understood, a genetic inheritance of anxiety. I felt a sudden, sharp urge to cry, but it was for the buttons, for their pathetic, hopeful tidiness, not for her. Not exactly for her. It was for the sheer, exhausting weight of a life lived in such small, careful increments.

Claire came back in. “What’s that?”

“Buttons.”

She came closer and peered into the box. She gave a short, sharp sigh. “For God’s sake. Just throw them out. What are we going to do with a box of buttons?”

“I don’t know.”

“We can’t keep everything. We can’t keep *anything*,” she said, her voice tight. “That’s the point. We have to empty it.”

I knew she was right. I knew the landlord was coming on Friday, that the flat needed to be returned to a state of anonymous, characterless neutrality. I knew that holding onto a box of buttons was a fool’s errand, a sentimental anchor to a ship that had already sunk.

“I’ll do it,” I said, closing the lid.

She watched me for a second, her face unreadable. Then she nodded and went back to the living room. I heard the first heavy book drop into a box with a dull, final boom. Then another. And another.

I didn’t throw the buttons away. I tucked the box into my own bag, nestled between my wallet and a half-eaten packet of mints. It was a small, pointless act of defiance, a secret I would keep from Claire, and from myself for as long as I could. I stood up, my knees cracking in the silence. The air in the flat was getting colder, the light from the window thinner. It wasn't a home anymore. It was just a set of rooms we were emptying, one box at a time.

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
The ledger was at the back of his closet, under a box of shotgun shells and a single gray Florsheim pump. My mother’s shoe. She lost the other one in the move to the condo, or maybe it was eaten by a dog we never had. That’s the kind of thing you find when you’re cleaning out a dead man’s closet. A single shoe. A box of shells for a gun he sold in 1987. And a ledger.

It wasn’t a fancy thing. A black-and-red composite notebook, the kind you buy at Office Depot for three ninety-nine. The cover was soft at the corners, furred from handling. I thought it was a check register at first. He was a man who balanced his checkbook to the penny, who would call the bank over a twelve-cent discrepancy and stay on hold for twenty minutes just to prove a point.

But it wasn’t checks. It was everything else.

The first page started in 1974. *Jan 4 — coffee, 15¢. Jan 4 — pack of Winstons, 45¢. Jan 5 — haircut, $3.* The handwriting was his, that tight, slanted scrawl that always looked like it was leaning into a wind. I could hear him breathing through his nose as he wrote it. He did that when he concentrated.

I sat down on the floor of the closet, right there on the beige carpet that smelled like mothballs and old wool, and I read.

He recorded everything. Not just money. That’s what got me. It wasn’t a financial document. It was a life, itemized. *Feb 2 — J. sick. Chicken soup, 59¢. Feb 3 — J. still sick. Ginger ale, 39¢. Feb 4 — J. better. New comic book, 25¢.* I was J. I was six years old and had the flu, and he bought me a comic book. I don’t remember the comic. I don’t remember being sick. But I remember the way he used to put his hand on my forehead to check for fever, his palm rough and cool at the same time. He never said much. Just *hmm* and then he’d go to the store.

The entries went on. *Mar 12 — new tires, $87.50. Mar 15 — M. mad about tires.* M. was my mother. He wrote *M. mad* like it was a line item. A budget category. I laughed out loud in that closet, a dry, barking sound that surprised me. Then I felt bad for laughing.

There were gaps. Whole months missing in ’78. I don’t know why. Maybe he got tired. Maybe he was happy and didn’t need to write it down. The next entry was *Sept 2 — J. starts second grade. Lunchbox, $2.49.* A red plastic lunchbox with a Thermos. I remember that one. I lost the Thermos by October. He never mentioned it. But here it was. A two-dollar-and-forty-nine-cent fact.

I kept turning pages. The ’80s were sparse. *Oct 14, 1983 — J. breaks arm. Hospital, $200 deductible.* I remember the arm. I remember the cast, the smell of the plaster, the way he signed it *Dad* with a little frowny face. He didn’t write *frowny face* in the ledger. Just the deductible.

Then, 1991. *June 8 — J. graduates. * That’s all. No amount. No commentary. Just a period. And then, a few lines down, *June 9 — too quiet in the house.*

I closed the book. I couldn’t read anymore. The beige carpet was making my knees ache. I thought about him sitting at the kitchen table, the one with the Formica top that always felt slightly sticky no matter how much you wiped it, writing in this notebook. His glasses pushed up on his forehead. A cup of Sanka going cold. Recording a fifty-nine-cent can of soup. Recording the quiet.

I put the ledger back in the closet, under the shotgun shells. I didn’t throw it away. I didn’t take it with me. It felt like it belonged there, in the dark, with the single shoe and the smell of mothballs. A man’s whole life, reduced to what he thought was worth remembering. A can of ginger ale. A pair of tires. A too-quiet house.

I still think about that last entry sometimes. *Too quiet.* He never told me that. He never said the house felt empty or that he missed me. He just wrote it in a three-dollar notebook and put it in the closet. That was his way, I guess. To keep the books. To balance the ledger. To let the numbers say what he couldn’t.

title: narrative poem|a ferry crossing in a storm
text:
The lantern’s swing a pendulum of light
that carved a cave of gold from solid night,
and in that cave, a hundred faces, pale
as drowned men’s fingers, huddled in the gale.
A woman clutched a bundle to her breast—
a sleeping child, or bread, or nothing. Best
not ask. A drover’s cattle lowed in fear,
a sound that curdled in the atmosphere
and mixed with creak of timber, snap of sail,
the hiss of spray like serpents on the rail.
The ferryman, a knot of salt-stiff rope,
stood at the wheel, his back to every hope
and terror on the deck. He did not turn
to watch the black waves rise and crash and churn.
His eyes were fixed upon a point ahead
where nothing but the storm and darkness spread.
He knew the channel by the feel of swell,
a lore his father taught him, and his father’s father. Well
he knew the hidden sandbar’s grinding teeth,
the reef that waited like a thief beneath
the innocent black water. In his mind
he held a map of dangers, undefined
by any ink, a cartography of dread
that kept them all from joining with the dead.

A sudden lurch. The deck canted and threw
a stumbling sailor hard against the crew
of praying women. Someone screamed. The lamp
swung wild and for a moment, cold and damp,
the darkness had a texture, thick and deep,
a blanket woven for a final sleep.
The child began to cry, a thin, sharp wail
that cut against the roaring of the gale.
The mother’s hush was swallowed by the wind,
a comfort offered, instantly rescinded.
A man in oilskins, face like weathered stone,
let out a groan that was not quite his own,
and gripped the rail with knuckles white as bone.
He’d seen the water rise, a liquid wall,
and watched it hang, suspended, ere its fall
upon the bow. He’d felt the vessel groan
in every joint, as if to say *alone*
*we are, and frail, and this is not our sea.*
He turned his face away and tried to be
a smaller thing, a thing the storm would spare,
a man who’d paid his fare and had no care
for gods or monsters, only for the shore
that waited, dark and solid, just before
the edge of sight. He prayed to feel its grit
beneath his boots, and have the strength to spit
the salt from out his mouth and curse the wave
that brought him to the threshold of his grave.

And in the midst of all this, one man laughed.
A madman, or a saint, or one who’d quaffed
too deep of something stronger than the spray.
He stood amidships, arms out wide, and swayed
with every pitch and roll, a grin of joy
upon his face, as though this grim destroy-
er of all comfort was a long-lost friend.
He shouted something to the howling wind,
a word that none could hear, a name, a plea,
a challenge, or a thanks for being free
of solid ground and all its tedious laws.
The others stared, and in their fear, the pause
of his strange laughter gave them pause as well.
A flicker in the heart of their dark hell.
For if a man could stand and laugh at this,
then maybe there was something not amiss
with laughing too, with finding in the dread
a thread of something else, a thing unsaid
that held them all together on the wave,
a fragile, foolish courage, brave and grave.

title: literary novel|an elderly translator finishing her last book
text:
The light through the window was the colour of weak tea, and it fell across the page in a way that made the letters seem to float, untethered from the paper. Elara had been staring at the same sentence for twenty minutes. It was a good sentence, a fine sentence, one that had given the original author no end of trouble, she suspected, and it was giving her a similar amount of grief now. The verb was the issue. It sat at the end of the clause, a stubborn, Teutonic knot of a word, and it refused to yield to the clean, forward-marching rhythm of the English she was trying to coax it into. In her mind, she had already translated it a dozen ways. *He succumbed to the weariness.* Too passive. *Weariness overcame him.* Too simple, too neat. The original had a texture, a sense of slow, grinding inevitability. It was the weariness of a man who has been carrying a stone up a hill for a lifetime, only to find another hill at the top.

She removed her glasses, the wire frames leaving two small, red indentations on the bridge of her nose. The world outside the window dissolved into a soft blur. The garden was a palimpsest of her late husband’s work and her own subsequent neglect. The roses he had pruned with such precision were now leggy and wild, their blooms small and infrequent. The stone birdbath, which he had always kept scrubbed and filled, was filmed with a green slick of algae. She could hear the rustle of a blackbird in the dry leaves under the hedge, a busy, scratching sound that was the only company she’d had all morning.

The book was *Die Letzte Brücke*, by a writer named Konstantin Richter, a man who had died in obscurity in 1962. It was his final novel, a slim, melancholic thing about a bridge engineer in a shattered post-war city. It was not a masterpiece. Elara knew that. It was too slow, too inward, its plot a mere thread on which to hang the heavy ornaments of its protagonist’s despair. But she had loved it since she was a young woman, had found in its quiet, stubborn prose a reflection of something she couldn’t name. To translate it now, at the end of her life, felt less like a career choice and more like a final, necessary act of devotion.

Her fingers, the knuckles prominent and roped with veins, rested on the keyboard of her typewriter. An electric one, a concession to her arthritis, though she still missed the satisfying, mechanical *thwack* of her old Olympia. She had typed the first draft on that machine, decades ago, a different book, a different life. Now, the soft, electronic chatter of the keys felt impersonal. She typed the sentence again, her chosen version, and the neat, black letters appeared on the page. *A weariness he could not name settled upon him, the weight of all the bridges he had built and all the rivers they had failed to tame.*

She read it. It was not perfect. It was a translation, after all, a well-intentioned betrayal. But it was true to the spirit of the thing, to the man on the page and the man who had written him. She pulled the sheet from the typewriter and placed it face down on a stack of paper that was, she estimated, a good four inches thick. Four inches of her life, of Richter’s life, of the bridge engineer’s life. The end was in sight. Another fifty pages, perhaps sixty. A week’s work, if her hands held out.

She stood up, her joints protesting with a series of small, dry clicks. The house was very quiet. She moved to the kitchen to put the kettle on, her slippers whispering against the worn linoleum. The ritual of tea was a comfort, a punctuation mark in the long, silent sentences of her days. She measured the loose leaves into the pot, a smoky Earl Grey her husband had favoured, though she had never much cared for it herself. She drank it now for the same reason she kept his old cardigan hanging on the back of the door: it was a way of keeping the shape of him in the room.

Waiting for the water to boil, she looked at the bookshelf in the hallway. Her own translations occupied a whole shelf, a parade of spines in various states of undress, some bright with new jackets, others faded and cracked. Next to them were the German originals, including Richter’s first editions, bought with money she had saved from tutoring. She thought of all the words she had moved from one language to another, an ant carrying grains of sand from one pile to another. It seemed, from this vantage point, a strange way to have spent a life. And yet. To have held another person’s thoughts, to have turned them over in her mind, to have found the precise, fragile vessel for them in her own tongue—it was a kind of intimacy no other act could replicate.

The kettle clicked off. The steam rose, and for a moment, the window was clouded, hiding the tangled garden from view. She would finish the book. She would type the final sentence, write the final word. And then the quiet would be different. It would no longer be a space to be filled with the voices of the dead, but simply a void. She poured the hot water over the leaves and watched them unfurl, a slow, dark blossoming in the ceramic pot. Then she carried her tea back to the desk, sat down, and pulled a fresh sheet of paper into the typewriter.

title: narrative poem|a ferry crossing in a storm
text:
The ticket booth light bled a sodium orange
into the rain-slicked asphalt, and the man
inside didn't look up from his magazine,
just slid the tokens back beneath the glass.
We were the last car, maybe, or the only one
foolish enough. The harbor black as a dropped stone.

The deckhand waved us forward with a flashlight
that stuttered, and I rolled the window down
to the smell of diesel and the first hard slap
of water against the pilings. The ramp
groaned like something waking from a long sleep.
I killed the engine. The silence that came after
was not peaceful. It was the silence
of a held breath.

The ferry pushed off, and the dock lights
shrank to a necklace of drowned beads.
The wind found us then. It came across the bow
like a hand flat against a chest, and the hull
took the first swell with a sound
I felt in my teeth. The deckhand,
a kid with a ponytail and a jacket too thin,
walked the lane between the cars, checking
the chains, his face a white oval
in the dark. He didn't look at me.
He looked at the water.

The rain came sideways. It wasn't rain
so much as the sea deciding to stand up
and walk. The windows streamed. I could see
the other passengers in their cars—a woman
with her forehead against the glass,
a man eating something from a foil wrapper
with a methodical, unbothered rhythm.
We were a little village of lit cells
adrift on a black table.

The ferry climbed a swell and hung there,
a long second, the engines straining,
and then it fell. My stomach rose.
The car creaked on its chains. I thought
of the man in the booth, his magazine.
I thought of the word *capsize* and pushed it away
like a plate I wasn't hungry for.

Somewhere in the middle—if there is a middle
to a thing like this—the storm settled
into a rhythm. Not kindness. Just a pattern
you could brace against. The deckhand
had disappeared. The woman in the next car
had turned her interior light on and was reading.
The man with the foil wrapper was asleep.

I don't know what I expected. A sign?
A voice? The sea doesn't offer those things.
It only offers its own weight, and the small
persistent fact of the hull, and the engine's
dull insistence that we were still moving,
still aimed at something, even if the dark
gave no evidence of a shore.

I thought about the word *faith* and how
it's mostly just refusing to panic
in a room you can't leave. I thought
about the ticket booth, the tokens,
the small transaction that had put me here.
I thought about nothing at all for a while.
That was the best part.

Then the rain thinned. Not stopped—thinned,
like a curtain drawn back an inch.
And the horizon did something I hadn't
dared to hope for: it separated from the sea.
A gray line. A smudge. The suggestion
of a hill.

The deckhand came back, his ponytail
plastered to his neck, and he stood
at the rail and lit a cigarette
with a lighter that took three tries.
He looked at me through the windshield
and nodded, once, the way you nod
at someone who has seen the same thing
you have and doesn't need to talk about it.

The dock came up out of the murk
like a memory. The pilings, the ropes,
the wet black tires hung along the side.
The ramp lowered with its old groan.
I started the engine. The car rolled forward
onto the solid, indifferent earth.

I didn't look back at the water.
I didn't need to. It was still there.
It is always still there.
I drove up the hill into the town,
past the closed shops, past the one lit window
of a diner, and I didn't stop.
I didn't have anywhere to be.
I just drove, and the rain
kept falling, and the road
kept going, and the sea
stayed behind me,
patient,
keeping its own counsel.

title: memoir|the year spent caring for a grandmother with dementia
text:
The winter I turned twenty-six, my grandmother forgot how to make her famous apple cake. I was standing in her kitchen in Ballydehob, a small town in West Cork where the rain came sideways and the fields stayed green even in January, watching her hands hover over the flour bin like two birds uncertain where to land. “Eleanor,” she said—my name, though she’d called me Nellie my whole life—“would you pass me the… the…” Her voice trailed off into the hum of the refrigerator.

“The cinnamon, Gran,” I said. “It’s in the cupboard above the kettle.”

She looked at me with the polite confusion of a stranger asking directions. “Do I know you?”

That was the first time. By March, it happened daily.

I had moved from Dublin to care for her after my mother, her only daughter, died of a stroke that autumn. My father had offered to hire someone, but I was between jobs and between lives, and Ballydehob in winter felt like the right place to be sad. Gran’s cottage sat at the end of a boreen lined with fuchsia hedges, and from her back window you could see the ruins of an old abbey and, beyond that, the gray slice of the sea. She had lived there for fifty-one years. She had buried her husband, my grandfather Jack, in the churchyard up the hill. She had taught half the town’s children to read. Now she couldn’t remember which drawer held the spoons.

The first weeks were a kind of grief I hadn’t expected. She would ask about Jack, and I would have to tell her he was dead, and she would cry fresh tears each time, as if hearing it for the first. Then, one afternoon in April, she asked me to drive her to the post office. “I need stamps,” she said. “For my sister.”

Her sister, Auntie Peg, had died in 2009. But I said, “Alright, Gran. Let’s go.”

In the car, she hummed a song I didn’t recognize. The rain had stopped, and the low sun turned the wet road to silver. She looked out the window and said, “I used to walk this road with my mother. She’d carry a basket of eggs to trade for tea.”

“That’s right,” I said. “You told me about that.”

“Did I?” She seemed pleased. “I have a good memory, you know.”

“You do.”

At the post office, Mrs. O’Donovan behind the counter said, “Morning, Mrs. Murphy. How’s the form?”

Gran smiled her old smile, the one that had won her a husband and a hundred parent-teacher conferences. “Grand, Mary. Just grand. I’ll take a book of stamps, please.”

“Sixty cents each, or the book of ten for five-fifty.”

Gran opened her purse. Inside were three euro coins and a photograph of me at age seven, missing my front teeth. She stared at the coins for a long moment. Then she looked up at Mrs. O’Donovan and said, very clearly, “I’m sorry. I don’t have any money.”

I stepped forward. “I’ve got it, Gran.”

She turned to me, and for a second her eyes were sharp and lucid. “You’re a good girl, Nellie,” she said. “You always were.”

That night, she forgot my name again. But she remembered the song she’d hummed in the car—a rebel ballad called “The Foggy Dew”—and she sang it to me while I washed the dishes. Her voice was thin but true. When she got to the line about the bravest of hearts, she stopped and said, “Jack used to sing this. He had a terrible voice. Like a cat in a bucket.”

I laughed. She laughed. For a moment, the kitchen was the same as it had always been.

By August, she had stopped walking. By October, she needed help with everything. I learned to change sheets while she sat in a chair, to cut her food into small pieces, to answer the same question eleven times in an hour without sighing. I learned that dementia is not a straight line. Some days she was my grandmother, sharp and funny and full of stories about the nuns who taught her in school. Other days she was a frightened woman in a strange house, asking for her mother.

One evening in November, as I helped her into bed, she grabbed my wrist. “You’re not my daughter,” she said. “My daughter is dead.”

“I know, Gran. I’m Eleanor. Your granddaughter.”

She studied my face for a long time. Then she said, “You have her eyes.”

“I know.”

“She was a good girl.”

“She was.”

“And you’re a good girl too.” She let go of my wrist. “Don’t forget to turn off the immersion.”

I laughed, and then I cried, and then I turned off the immersion.

She died in February, just before the daffodils came up along the boreen. I still make her apple cake sometimes, though I’ve never gotten the cinnamon right. I use too much or too little, and the kitchen never smells quite the way it did when she was the one holding the spoon. But I keep trying. It’s the only way I know to remember a woman who spent a year forgetting everything—and still, somehow, taught me how to pay attention.

title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
The rod tip dipped, a subtle, almost apologetic nod, and my heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. Uncle Ian’s hand, resting on his own knee, didn’t move. His eyes, the colour of the loch under a clouded sky, remained fixed on the far shore. He had taught me the rhythm without a single word: the slow, patient reel, the flick of the wrist, the wait. The silence between us was a physical thing, a third presence in the small wooden boat, woven from the lap of water against the hull and the distant, mournful cry of a curlew.

We had been out for hours, the sun a pale, heatless disc that had travelled across the sky without ever truly warming the air. The loch was a vast, dark mirror, holding the brooding shapes of the hills in its depths. My initial excitement had long since curdled into a numb, damp boredom. My fingers were cold, smelling of worms and metal, and my back ached from the enforced stillness. I was eleven, and the concept of a quiet, shared purpose was alien to me. I wanted to talk, to ask questions, to break the oppressive stillness with the sound of my own voice. But Ian’s silence was a command, a wall I dared not breach.

Then came the nod. It was so slight I might have imagined it. But the line, which had been a slack curve in the water, tightened. The silence shattered, not with sound, but with a sudden, violent tension that shot up the monofilament and into my very bones. The rod bent, a deep, beautiful arc, and the reel began to scream, a high-pitched, frantic sound that was the most exciting thing I had ever heard. My instinct was to yank back, to fight it with brute force, but a memory of Ian’s hands—showing me, not telling me—flashed in my mind. A firm, steady pressure. Let him run. Let him tire.

The fish, a phantom in the black water, pulled with a strength that felt ancient and immense. My small arms trembled with the effort of holding the rod high. I could feel the thrum of its life through the line, a frantic, desperate energy. Ian finally moved. He leaned forward, his old tweed jacket creaking, and placed a steadying hand on my shoulder. He didn't speak, but the weight of his hand was a sentence: *You are not alone in this. Hold fast.* The warmth of his palm seeped through my jumper, a silent anchor in the frantic dance.

The fight was a conversation conducted in pulls and runs, in the screaming of the reel and the groaning of the rod. I was no longer a bored boy in a boat; I was a conduit for a struggle that had been playing out in these dark waters for millennia. The fish made a final, desperate surge for freedom, boring deep, and for a terrifying moment, the line went slack. My stomach dropped. I had lost him. But Ian’s hand tightened on my shoulder, a silent, firm *no*. Reel. Keep the tension. I obeyed, my movements clumsy with panic, and the line went taut again. The fight was back on.

Slowly, inexorably, I brought him towards the boat. The shape resolved in the peat-stained water, a flash of silver and a furious red eye. He was a brown trout, not huge, but in that moment, he was a leviathan. Ian reached out with the net, a silent, deft movement, and scooped him from the water. The sudden absence of weight on the line was disorienting. The fish lay in the net, gasping, its flanks heaving, its scales a miracle of iridescence.

Ian didn’t congratulate me. He simply nodded once, his gaze meeting mine for a fleeting second. In his eyes, I saw not just approval, but a profound recognition. He was seeing not a boy, but a fellow initiate. He carefully unhooked the fish, his gnarled fingers gentle, and held it up for me to see. It was then that I understood. The silence wasn't an absence; it was a space filled with a different kind of language—the language of patience, of respect, of a shared understanding that didn't need to be articulated. It was the language of the loch itself. He slipped the fish back into the water, and it vanished with a flick of its tail, a secret returned to the deep. The silence settled over us again, but it was different now. It was no longer a wall, but a blanket.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The water was the color of old glass, green and thick with the reflection of the oak trees that ringed the pond. I stood at the edge, my toes curling into the cool mud, and I felt the familiar, childish vertigo. I was forty years old, and I was afraid of the deep end. Not the ocean, not a pool, but this specific, murky pond on a friend’s property in upstate New York, where the bottom was a mystery of silt and submerged branches. My wife, a woman who moves through water like a seal, was already fifty yards out, her arms carving clean arcs. My ten-year-old son was cannonballing off the dock, his laughter sharp and bright. They were natives; I was a tourist in their element.

My own history with water is a catalogue of near-misses. As a child, I was the one who stayed in the shallow end, my hands gripping the rough concrete of the pool’s edge until my knuckles were white, watching the other kids become sleek, amphibious creatures. I had taken lessons—group lessons where I was the oldest by decades, a lanky, self-conscious teenager among the toddlers. I learned to float, to kick, to dog-paddle with a frantic, joyless efficiency. But the deep end, the place where the bottom fell away and the water turned a darker, more serious blue, remained a foreign country. I could not surrender to it. The act of swimming requires a kind of faith, a belief that the water will hold you if you just stop fighting it. I never had that faith.

So for years, I was a wader. I was the man at the beach who stood knee-deep, holding the towels, watching the horizon. I was fine. I was comfortable. But comfort, I was beginning to learn, is a very small room.

The catalyst wasn't a midlife crisis in the clichéd sense—no sports car, no sudden urge to climb a mountain. It was quieter. It was the sight of my son, effortlessly treading water, asking me to come out further. It was the look on his face, a mixture of hope and expectation, that I recognized as the same look I’d given my own father when I was a boy. I didn’t want to be the father who stood on the shore. I wanted to be in the story with him.

My first attempts in that pond were pathetic. I’d push off from the dock and immediately my body would betray me. My legs would sink, my breathing would become shallow and panicked, and my mind would scream *down, down, down*. I’d flail my way back to the ladder, my heart hammering against my ribs, tasting the metallic tang of fear mixed with the pond water. My wife, ever patient, tried to coach me. “Just relax,” she’d say, her voice calm and infuriatingly serene. “The water wants to hold you.” But I couldn’t believe her. The water, to me, was a neutral, indifferent force, not a supportive one.

One afternoon, I was alone. The family had gone into town. I stood on the dock, the sun warm on my shoulders, and I looked at the water. I was tired of being afraid. I was tired of the constant, low-grade hum of anxiety that vibrated just beneath the surface of my life. I dove in, not with any grace, but with a clumsy, desperate lunge.

I didn’t try to swim. I just tried to be. I let my body sink for a moment, the green silence closing over my head. Then, I kicked my legs, not in a panic, but in a slow, deliberate rhythm. I moved my arms, not to propel myself, but to feel the resistance of the water. I focused on my breath, on the simple mechanics of turning my head to the side to inhale, then exhaling slowly into the murk. For the first few minutes, it was a negotiation. My body screamed for the safety of the bottom, for the solid certainty of the dock. But I kept going, a noisy, inefficient mess of limbs.

And then, something shifted. It wasn’t a moment of epiphany, a sudden mastery. It was a gradual, quiet acquiescence. I stopped thinking about the depth. I stopped picturing the dark, formless bottom. I began to feel the water not as an adversary, but as a medium. It was supporting me. My legs, which had always felt like lead weights, were now buoyant. My breathing, once a ragged gasp, found a rhythm. I was moving. I was actually swimming. I turned my head to breathe and saw the far shore, the trees, the sky. I was in the middle of the pond. I was in the deep end.

I didn’t suddenly become a great swimmer. My stroke is still clumsy, my endurance limited. But the fear is gone. It was replaced by a profound sense of physical humility. My body, which I had always thought of as a vessel for my mind, a tool for work and carrying children, had its own wisdom, its own capacity for trust. I had spent forty years building walls of competence and control, and the water had simply washed them away. Now, when I swim, I feel a part of the landscape. I am not just looking at the water; I am in it. And in that immersion, there is a quiet, profound peace.

title: literary novel|a lighthouse keeper's daughter returning after the light is automated
text:
The light had been out for three years by the time I came back, but the silence of it was a physical thing, a pressure against the eardrums. I stood on the gravel where the road ended and the sea began, and I listened. The wind was there, of course, and the suck and drag of the tide on the shingle, the distant, petulant cry of a gull. But the great, rhythmic breath of the place was gone. The lens, that heart of glass and clockwork, no longer turned. Its absence was a hole in the world.

My father had died in the spring. The solicitor’s letter was formal, efficient, and had smelled faintly of toner. It spoke of probate and a key, held for me at the village post office. It did not speak of the forty years my father had spent winding the mechanism, nor of the way the light, in its slow, sweeping arc, had been the last thing I saw before sleep and the first thing I saw if I woke in the dark. It was just an asset, now, a decommissioned building on a rocky headland.

The key was heavy and cold in my palm. The lock on the tower door was stiff with rust and sea-salt, and it took a moment of wrestling before it gave, with a groan that sounded like a complaint. The air inside was still and cold, holding the scent of dust, old brass, and the ghost of my father’s pipe tobacco. It was a smell I had not known I remembered until it hit me, a clean, sharp blow to the sternum.

I didn’t go up to the lamp room at first. I went into the keeper’s cottage, our home. It was emptier than I expected. The furniture was there—the horsehair sofa, the scarred oak table—but the life had been vacuumed out of it. The coastguard or whoever had come to clear things had been tidy. They had taken the photographs from the walls, leaving pale rectangles like unhealed scars on the wallpaper. They had emptied the bookshelves. The house was a museum of its own absence.

My father was not a sentimental man. He was a man of barometers and tide tables, of oil and wicks and, later, of the finicky electronics of the automated system he had distrusted to the end. He spoke in facts. The wind is backing, force six. The glass is falling. There is a ship.

I found his logbooks in a cupboard, stacked in neat, chronological piles. I pulled one from the year I was twelve. His handwriting was small, cramped, and precise. *4 a.m. Wind WSW, fresh. Visibility good. Light exhibited.* And then, later that day: *0930. Daughter found a dead Manx shearwater on the rocks. Buried it.*

That was it. That was the entire entry. He had recorded the death of a seabird with the same dispassion as the weather. I remembered that bird. I remembered its ridiculous, needle-thin beak and the strange, waxy look of its closed eyes. I had cried, and he had put his hand on my head, a brief, heavy weight, and said, “Everything comes to the rock, in the end.”

I climbed the tower then, my footsteps echoing in the spiraling stone throat. The lamp room was a cage of glass and rusted iron. The great lens stood silent, its facets dulled with a film of grime. It was a beautiful, dead thing, a cyclops with its eye put out. The automated light, they’d told me, was a simple, ugly thing, a flashing LED on a steel pole just outside. A machine that needed no man.

I stood where my father had stood for four decades, my hands resting on the cold iron railing. The sea was a sheet of hammered pewter under a low, grey sky. It was the same view he’d had, the same view I’d had as a girl, but it felt like a photograph of a place I’d never been. The light was gone, and in its absence, the world had simply continued. The sea did not mourn it. The rocks did not care.

I took out the logbook from my bag, the last one he’d kept before the automation. I opened it to the final page. The last entry was in his hand, but the letters were fainter now, more spidered. *1st October. Light automated. 0800. Handed over to Trinity House. All in order.*

He had not written anything after that. No final reflection, no grand summation. Just a fact. The job was done. He had handed it over. I closed the book. The silence in the lamp room was immense, a presence. It was not an emptiness. It was the sound of a held breath, of something waiting. I did not know for what. I put the logbook back in my bag, and I went down the stairs, and I locked the door behind me. The key was still cold in my hand.

title: memoir|the year spent caring for a grandmother with dementia
text:
The summer I turned twenty-six, my grandmother forgot how to make her famous lemon bars. It happened on a Tuesday, the kind of humid July afternoon in Baton Rouge where the air feels like a wet wool blanket. I was standing in her kitchen on Magnolia Street, watching her stare at a bowl of flour and butter as if it were a trigonometry problem. “Mamaw,” I said, “you’ve made these a thousand times.” She looked at me, her blue eyes clear and untroubled, and said, “I’m sorry, sweetheart. Do I know you?”

That was the beginning. The doctors at Ochsner called it vascular dementia, likely from a series of small strokes she’d never noticed. My mother, Diane, had been handling things, but she was exhausted—she’d been driving up from New Orleans every weekend for six months. I was between jobs, a fact I’d been sheepish about until my father said, “Go. She needs somebody. You need something.” So I packed a duffel bag and moved into Mamaw’s spare bedroom, the one with the framed photo of her late husband, Earl, in his Navy uniform, and the quilt she’d sewn from his old shirts.

The first month was a geography lesson in her unraveling. She’d wake at 3 a.m. convinced it was time for church, or she’d put her purse in the refrigerator and then accuse me of stealing it. Once, she called me “Earl” for three hours straight. I learned not to correct her. Instead, I’d say, “Okay, Earl’s here. What do you need?” That seemed to calm her. The neurologist, a brisk woman named Dr. Patel, told me, “Don’t argue with the reality she’s in. Join her there.” It felt like a betrayal at first, this gentle lying. But it worked.

There were good days. On a Thursday in September, we sat on her screened porch while a thunderstorm rolled in. She was lucid, sipping sweet tea, and she told me about the time she and Earl drove to Biloxi in 1958 and got caught in a hurricane. “He held my hand so tight I lost feeling in my fingers,” she said, laughing. “He said, ‘Loretta, if we go, we go together.’” Then she looked at me sharply. “You’re not Earl.” “No, ma’am,” I said. “I’m your grandson, Daniel.” She nodded slowly. “Daniel. You were a fat baby.” I laughed so hard I nearly dropped my glass.

But the bad days came faster. In November, she wandered out the front door at dusk in her nightgown. I found her two blocks away, standing in front of the Piggly Wiggly, asking a teenager if he’d seen Earl. I brought her home and she cried for an hour, not knowing why. That night, I installed a chain lock and slept on the couch facing the door. I started keeping a notebook—not for her, for me. “Nov. 14: She remembered the name of her childhood dog, Pepper. Nov. 15: She called me a stranger and threw a shoe at my head.”

My mother visited for Christmas. We made Mamaw’s lemon bars together, following the recipe card in her spidery handwriting. Mamaw watched us from her armchair, suspicious at first, then curious. “Those look good,” she said. “My mother used to make those.” I handed her a piece. She took a bite, and her face changed—softened, like a window opening. “Oh,” she whispered. “I remember this.” For five minutes, she was back. Then she asked who’d left the flour out.

By March, she needed a nursing home. Dr. Patel said it gently, but the words hung in the air like smoke. We chose St. Clare’s, a small place off Perkins Road with a garden and a cat named Mr. Whiskers. The day we moved her in, she was confused but calm. She looked at me and said, “You’ve been so kind. Are you my son?” “No, Mamaw. I’m Daniel.” She patted my hand. “Daniel. That’s a good name.” She died in her sleep six weeks later. The last thing she said to me, two days before, was, “Tell Earl I’ll be home soon.”

I drove back to New Orleans with her recipe box on the passenger seat. I haven’t made the lemon bars yet. The card still smells faintly of butter and vanilla. Sometimes I take it out and read her handwriting, the loop of the “L” in Loretta, and I think about that hurricane in 1958, how Earl held her hand so tight. That’s what I tried to do, for one year, on Magnolia Street. I held on, even when she let go.

title: myth retelling|a river goddess who refuses to flood the valley
text:
They called her Apa, though that was not her name. Names for river goddesses are not for human mouths, not really, and what we call them is only the sound of us being polite. She lived in the green-brown water that came down out of the hills, the water that carried silt the color of old teeth and made the valley grow fat with barley. Every year, when the snows melted, Apa was supposed to rise. That was the arrangement.

The arrangement was old. Older than the shrine at the bend, which was built from stones pulled out of her own bed and which leaned, always, a little to the left. Older than the priest with the cracked hands who came down each spring with a clay bowl of milk and honey and poured it in. The flood was the point. The flood laid down new soil, drowned the rats, filled the low meadows with water so the children could spear fish in them, and when it went down, it left a smell like the inside of a bread oven. Everyone knew this. The valley was a bowl and Apa filled it, and if she didn't, the barley came up thin and tasted of dust.

But here is the thing about a river. A river remembers every stone it has ever gone around. Apa remembered the summer the water got so low you could walk across on the backs of the big flat rocks, and the children had done that, hopping, and one of them — a girl with a crooked front tooth, I want to say her name was Eshe but I might be inventing that — had fallen in and come up laughing. Apa had held her up. She hadn't meant to. It just happened, the way your hand goes out when a cup tips.

So when the year came that the snows melted all at once, and the messengers came down from the high villages saying the water was building black and angry behind the ridge, and the priest came with his bowl and his cracked hands and told her, now, now is the time, Apa did not rise.

She thought about the girl with the crooked tooth, who was a woman now, who had a baby of her own that slept in a basket by the door. She thought about the shrine stones, already leaning. She thought, a little bitterly, that nobody had asked her if she wanted to be the kind of river that drowns things.

The priest poured the milk and the honey. The honey sank. She held her water where it was, and the valley did not flood, and the barley came up thin and tasted of dust, and everyone said Apa had abandoned them.

But I have to tell you about the other thing. The thing that doesn't go in the story the way they tell it. Because while Apa was holding her water back, the water behind the ridge had nowhere to go, and it sat there, and it sat there, and finally it went the other way. Down the back side of the hills. Into the country where nobody from the valley had ever been, where the people spoke differently and kept goats and had never heard of Apa or her arrangement. And it drowned them. Not all of them. Enough.

Apa felt it happen. A river goddess feels where her water goes, even when it goes wrong. She has never said whether she would do it again.

The valley survived. The barley was thin for a generation and then it wasn't. The priest died and a new priest came, and the shrine got a new roof, and the story they tell now is that Apa is a difficult goddess who must be coaxed. They pour the milk. They pour the honey. They wait. And most years she rises, and most years it's fine, and nobody down there talks about the back side of the hills.

But the woman with the crooked tooth — if that was her name, Eshe, and if it wasn't, it should have been — she named her daughter something that means *she who holds*. Nobody knows why. She never explained it.

title: personal essay|living next to a railway line for twenty years
text:
The first thing I learned was the language of the house. It was not a language of creaks or groans, but of a deep, geological shudder that began somewhere in the floorboards and travelled up through the walls. It was a pre-verbal tremor, a warning that announced the 07:45 express from a full minute before it arrived. You could feel it in the soles of your feet, a faint, buzzing anticipation. Then came the sound, a distant, mournful horn that seemed to be calling for something it had lost, a sound that belonged more to the empty fields two miles down the track than to our suburban street. And then, the main event: the train itself. A great, clattering beast of steel and thunder that would consume the world for precisely seventeen seconds.

For the first year, I would stop what I was doing. I would look up from my book, my hand frozen over a page, and wait for it to pass. It was an intrusion, a violent reminder that my small, quiet life was bisected by a force of industry and motion. But the human animal is a creature of profound and terrifying adaptability. By the end of the second year, the 07:45 was no longer an event; it was a fact. It was the metronome of my morning, the punctuation mark at the end of my first cup of tea. I could tell the time by the rhythm of the trains. The slow, heavy freight trains that rumbled through in the dead of night were the insomniacs, their long, groaning procession a sign that it was past two in the morning. The quick, light passenger trains that flitted by every half hour were the day’s steady pulse.

The house itself became a living testament to the railway. The fine, dark grit that settled on the windowsills was not common dust but a precipitate of iron and brake-shoe ash. If you wiped it with a white cloth, it left a grey smear, like graphite. The pictures on the walls never hung quite straight; the constant, low-level vibration saw to that, giving them a permanent, slightly drunken tilt. The finest of the good china, the wedding-gift plates we kept in the cabinet, had hairline cracks that we knew, without ever speaking of it, were the railway’s slow, patient work. We were living inside a tuning fork, and our possessions were slowly learning the song.

The railway was our clock, our calendar, and our weather. A foggy morning muffled the trains, their sounds arriving strange and disembodied, like voices from another room. A hard frost made the tracks ring with a higher, clearer pitch. And the seasons were marked not just by the colour of the leaves on the embankment, but by the changing quality of the light that flashed through the carriage windows as they passed. In winter, it was a cold, sterile white. In summer, it was a warm, golden blur. We never saw the faces of the passengers, only the suggestion of them, a thousand strangers a day hurtling through our lives, their own stories momentarily flickering against our walls.

Our lives were woven into the gaps between the trains. We learned to time our conversations, to pause for a passing express, to wait for the thunder to subside before delivering the punchline of a joke. A summer barbecue was a chaotic symphony of conversation punctuated by the roar of the 18:15 to the coast. We learned to sleep through anything, our bodies attuned to ignore the familiar disruptions. The silence that fell after the last train of the night was a profound and almost unnatural thing, a void that took a moment to get used to. It was in that silence that you could finally hear the house settle, the faint tick of the central heating, the whisper of the wind in the eaves. It was the sound of the world without its mechanical heartbeat.

After twenty years, I no longer hear the trains. I feel them. They are a part of my physiology, as innate as my own pulse. When I am away from home, staying in a quiet hotel or a friend’s peaceful cottage, I find the silence unnerving. It feels thin, incomplete. I lie awake, listening for the ghost of a rumble that isn't there, missing the deep, reassuring shudder that once told me, with absolute certainty, that I was home. The railway line is no longer a boundary at the edge of my garden. It is the spine of my life, a constant, thrumming presence that holds everything else in place.

title: elegy in free verse|a closed coal mine and the men who worked it
text:
Pit Lights

The gate is chain and rust and a lock I don't test.
Behind it, the tipple stands like a held breath,
conveyor belt frozen mid-thought,
and the slag heap has gone green enough
that someone driving past might call it a hill.

I came back with no ceremony in mind.
No flowers. Nothing to lay down.
Just the hour before dark when the valley
turns the color of weak tea
and the swallows work the old slack piles
for whatever insects live there now.

---

Ray Dolan taught me to read a roof.
Not books—the ceiling of a tunnel,
where the rock talks if you know the language
of a hairline crack. He'd hold his lamp up
and go quiet, and the quiet was the lesson.
*You listen with your skin,* he said,
and I never knew if he was joking
until the day a beam sagged two inches
and he had us out before the dust could settle.
Ray died in his garden, in 1994,
of a heart that had been patient long enough.
I keep thinking he should have died underground,
that the mine owed him that much drama.
But the mine never paid what it owed anybody.

---

Here is what I remember of the work:
the cage dropping like a stone in water,
the pressure in your ears, the smell—
not what you'd think, not sulfur and doom,
but wet rock and machine oil and the sweat
of twelve men who'd rather be anywhere
and wouldn't be anywhere else.
The lamps made small yellow rooms
and the rooms moved with us.
We were each of us alone in a yellow room,
connected by noise.

Tomás Reyes sang. Badly. Constantly.
Boleros his mother had taught him,
half-remembered, wrong words,
and we threatened to bury him for it
and he sang anyway, for nineteen years.

He's in Beckley now, I hear.
Or maybe that was his brother.
The names go soft at the edges.

---

The company sealed the shafts in '09.
There was a meeting, there were figures on a screen,
there was a man from Chicago who said *transition*
like it was a word without a body in it.
Some men took the retraining money.
Some drove to the mines in Virginia until those closed too.
Some are on the hill behind the church
where the stones tilt like teeth.

I don't know what I expected, standing here.
Not ghosts. I don't believe in ghosts.
What I believe in is the way a place
holds the shape of the work done in it—
the worn rail, the path that goes nowhere now,
the way my hands still close a certain way
around a lamp that isn't there.

---

We were not heroes and I won't say we were.
We were men with mortgages and bad knees
who went down because the check cleared
and because our fathers went down
and because there is a kind of pride
in doing the thing that scares you daily
until it doesn't.

That's the part nobody puts on the signs.

The thing that scares you daily
becomes the thing you can't sleep without.
I still wake at four. Every morning. For nothing.
My wife says it's the age. It isn't the age.

---

The swallows are going in now,
stitching the dark together over the slack heap.
Somewhere under that green
is the seam we worked, the rooms we cut,
the pillars we left standing like a held breath.
It will not be opened again. The water's in it.
That's what the engineers say—the mine
is full of itself now, a slow black lake
under the hill, and the lake has no opinion.

I don't either, mostly.
I drive home with the windows down.
The valley gives up its color by degrees.
Tomorrow I'll wake at four and lie there
listening to the house, which is not a mine,
which does not need listening, which holds.

That's the elegy, I guess.
Not the gate, not the heap, not the names
going soft. Just this: the work is over,
the men are scattered, the water rises,
and the listening doesn't stop.

title: literary essay|silence and omission in short fiction
text:
The most important thing that happens in Raymond Carver’s “A Small, Good Thing” occurs when no one is speaking. Ann Weiss has been at the hospital for days, her son Scotty in a coma after being hit by a car on his birthday. A doctor has just told her that the tests are “inconclusive.” She is standing in the corridor when she sees a black family—a mother, a father, a small girl—waiting outside a room. The mother is crying without sound, her hand pressed flat against the wall. Ann wants to say something. She does not. She goes back to Scotty’s room and sits down. Carver writes: “She didn’t know what to say. She didn’t say anything.” That sentence—flat, unadorned, almost nothing—is the story’s moral center. It is also a masterclass in the use of omission. Carver does not tell us what Ann feels. He does not describe the corridor’s fluorescent hum or the smell of antiseptic. He gives us the silence and lets it do the work.

This is not a technique unique to Carver, but he is its most disciplined practitioner in the American short story after Chekhov. In “Why Don’t You Dance?”, a man sells his furniture on his front lawn after his marriage ends. A young couple stops. They drink whiskey, dance, negotiate a price for the bed. The girl says, “You must be desperate or something.” The man agrees. At the end, the girl tries to tell people about it later—“She kept talking. She told everyone. There was more to it, and she was trying to get it talked out.” But she can’t. The story ends with her giving up: “She quit talking.” Carver omits the man’s backstory, his wife’s name, the reason for the sale. What remains is the furniture, the whiskey, the dance, and the girl’s failed attempt to narrate. The silence is not a gap; it is the story’s engine.

Consider a different tradition: James Joyce’s “Eveline,” from *Dubliners* (1914). Eveline Hill stands at the North Wall quay in Dublin, holding letters to her lover Frank, who waits at the boat for Buenos Aires. She has decided to leave her abusive father, her dead mother’s memory, the dust of her childhood home. Joyce gives us the details: the yellowing photograph of the priest, the broken harmonium, the smell of dusty cretonne. Then, at the dock, she feels “all the seas of the world tumbled about her heart.” Frank calls to her. She does not answer. “She set her white face to him, passive, like a helpless animal.
