The air down here was its own climate: a permanent, humid warmth that smelled of industrial detergent, boiled starches, and the faint, metallic tang of the city’s water.

My shift started at eleven, just as the last of the evening trays were being collected. I’d tie on a heavy canvas apron, still damp from the previous wearer, and begin my rounds. There was the stockpot of chicken broth to be set to a low simmer for the morning’s soup, a vast, bubbling cauldron that became the kitchen’s slow, steady heartbeat. There were mountains of potatoes to peel, their pale flesh yielding to my knife in slick, rhythmic curls. The work was mindless, a loop of physical tasks that kept my hands busy while my mind drifted in the sterile quiet.

The night dietician, a woman named Brenda with tired eyes and a perpetual smudge of ink on her middle finger, would leave me a list. It was never a culinary challenge. It was a litany of clinical needs. “NPO for 6A,” she’d scrawl. “Clear liquids for bed 412.” “Ensure at 3 a.m. for the cardiac patient in 305.” I was not feeding people; I was refueling them, providing the necessary calories and nutrients to keep their bodies from failing. The food was a variable in a medical equation, and I was just the one solving for x. I’d measure out precise portions of Jell-O, arrange individual servings of saltines on a tray, and blend the beige, nutrient-dense shakes that looked like wet cement. It was a far cry from the fragrant, chaotic meals I imagined being cooked in the city’s real restaurants, where I fancied I might one day work.

The kitchen had its own nocturnal inhabitants. There was a porter named Gus, a man in his sixties with a lazy eye and a cart that squeaked on its left wheel. He’d come down for his break, drink his coffee from a chipped mug, and tell me about the things he’d seen on the upper floors. He was the kitchen’s link to the world above. “They lost a patient in the ICU tonight,” he’d say, his voice flat. “Young guy. ‘Nother one in the ER. Overdose.” He spoke of it not with gossipy relish, but with the weary matter-of-factness of a man who had been ferrying carts through the corridors of human suffering for decades. His words were the only thing that pierced the bubble of my stainless-steel world, a reminder that downstairs, I was preparing clear liquids for someone who might not live to drink them.

My favorite task was the 3 a.m. rounds. I’d load the insulated cart, the one with the squeaky wheel, and take the service elevator up. The hospital was ghostly then. In the hallways, the only light came from behind the nurses’ station, where a couple of night shifters would be whispering over a chart, their faces lit by the glow of a computer screen. I’d push my cart past closed doors, each one a sealed room containing its own private universe of pain, hope, or simple, restless sleep. I’d slip the trays onto the bedside tables of the patients Brenda had listed, my movements as quiet as a thief’s. An old man in 305 was always awake, a tiny, bird-like figure propped up in bed, the television on mute. He never said a word, just watched me as the blue light of the screen flickered across his face. I would place his plastic cup of chocolate Ensure on his tray, and he would give a slight, almost imperceptible nod. That nod was our entire conversation, night after night.

In those moments, I felt the immense, quiet gravity of the place. The kitchen was where you sanitized and ordered things—where you could neatly arrange peas on a plate or stack the clean, white trays. The upper floors were where things happened, where the messy, unsterilized business of life and death was conducted. I was a ghost passing through, a silent provider of midnight sustenance.

By 5:00 a.m., the first hint of dawn would filter through the small, high window where the delivery trucks would eventually dock. The day shift would begin to trickle in, bringing with them the smell of fresh coffee and the loud, jarring energy of the waking world. They’d find the stockpot simmering, the potatoes peeled, the trays stacked. I’d hang up my apron, its dampness now cooled and clammy, and take the elevator up, stepping out into the pale morning light. The city was beginning to stir, oblivious to the silent, self-contained war that had just been fought in the floors above my head. I would walk home, smelling of broth and bleach, and sleep until it was time to do it all again.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
The house in Cumbria had a name, not a number, and its walls were thick enough to hold the cold at bay. My grandmother’s house. The smell of it was a specific alchemy: coal smoke, damp wool, and the sharp, clean bite of her lemon marmalade. In the back garden, a stone wall, older than anyone could remember, separated us from a field of sheep that belonged to a farmer named Mr. Gowling. I learned the names of things there first. *Lintel*. *Gable*. *Sill*. Words that felt like the objects themselves, sturdy and Anglo-Saxon.

Then, the telephone would trill its harsh, foreign ring, and it would be my father. His voice, a low rumble from another world, would speak to my mother in the language of our other life. It was a language of long, rolling vowels and softened consonants, a language I associated with the smell of diesel fumes at the airport and the oppressive heat that met us on the other side. It was the language of my father’s parents, whose house in the Dutch polder had no name, only a number on a blue sign. Their walls were thin, and the wind that came off the flat fields seemed to pass right through them.

My life was a series of translations, not just of words, but of being. In England, I was the boy with the strange, foreign father, the one who came and went. My accent was pure Cumbrian, a fact my grandmother guarded with a quiet fierceness. In the Netherlands, I was the boy from England, my skin too pale for the sun, my clothes somehow wrong, my Dutch halting and childlike long after I should have mastered it. I was a permanent visitor in my father’s homeland, a temporary resident in my mother’s.

The ferry was our bridge, a churning, grey limbo. I would stand at the rail, the wind whipping my hair, and watch the white cliffs of Dover dissolve into a smudge, then nothing. The crossing was a physical unmaking of one identity and a slow, reluctant assembling of another. By the time we docked at Calais, the smell of the air had changed, the light was different, and I had to remember to be someone else. The transition was never clean. For days, I would dream in English and wake up confused by the Dutch voices in the kitchen.

Language was a territory I navigated with a child’s instinct for survival. I learned to keep my two selves separate, a form of mental hygiene. English was the language of my grandmother’s kitchen, of stories and comfort. Dutch was the language of the street, of school, of my father’s quiet authority. I never learned to argue in Dutch; the words for anger and hurt felt clumsy and borrowed. I never learned to pray in English; the words felt too direct, too personal. My prayers, such as they were, were mumbled in the neutral, formal cadence of the Dutch I heard in church.

There was a deep and unspoken sadness in my mother’s eyes whenever we left England. And a similar, more stoic reserve in my father’s whenever we returned to the Netherlands. They were each, in their own way, exiles. And I was the living embodiment of their compromise, a child who belonged fully to neither place, a permanent diplomat in the small, fraught nation of our family. My existence was the treaty, and I felt the weight of its terms.

Once, I tried to explain this to a friend in England. I told him that in the Netherlands, I felt like a guest in my own life. He looked at me, baffled. "But you're English," he said. It wasn't a question. It was a statement of fact, as solid and immovable as the stone wall in my grandmother's garden. He was right, of course. And he was entirely wrong. I had no language to explain the space between, the vast, grey sea that I carried inside me.

The last time I took the ferry, I was sixteen. I stood at the rail, as I always had, but the ritual felt hollow. The sea was just water. The cliffs were just chalk. The two halves of my life, which had once felt so monumental and irreconcilable, had begun to shrink. They were no longer two countries, but two sets of memories, two catalogs of sensation. The smell of coal smoke. The taste of salt on the wind. The sound of my father’s voice on the phone, a low rumble from a world that was, and was not, my own. The sea was just the sea, and I was just a boy on a boat, going from one place to another, carrying both of them, and neither of them, with me.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The first thing you need to know about learning to swim at forty is that your body has opinions. Mine did, anyway. Forty years of gravity, of walking and sitting and climbing stairs, and suddenly the water wants a different contract. The lungs want to be told what to do. The legs, which have carried me faithfully up and down the East Coast and through two pregnancies, suddenly feel like two balloons tied to a chair.

I was not a water person. Let me correct that. I was a *bathtub* person. Shallow end of the motel pool, age nine, gripping the concrete lip while my cousin did cannonballs. That was the extent of it. In seventh grade, the school took us to the municipal pool in Schenectady, and the instructor—a teenager named Dawn with a whistle and a deep and abiding contempt for the cowardly—told me to put my face in. I put my face in. Then she told me to blow bubbles. I inhaled an entire pool. It is possible this is an exaggeration. It is also possible it is not. I spent the rest of the session on the bleachers, wet and shivering in my borrowed suit, watching the other kids turn into fish.

So. Forty. My daughter is eight and she swims like she was born with gills, which, given the amount of time she spends underwater, might be true. And there was a moment at a lake in Maine, last July, when she paddled out past the rope and I felt the old panic rise up my throat. Not for her. For me. I couldn't follow.

That's the honest reason. Not fitness. Not a bucket list. I wanted to be able to follow my kid into the water.

The lessons were at the Y on Tuesday nights. Adult beginners. There were four of us. A man in his sixties who wanted to do a triathlon. A woman recovering from a car accident. A young guy who, it turned out, had never learned because his family couldn't afford lessons and he was embarrassed. And me. We stood in the shallow end like a support group for the aquatically delayed, and the instructor, a retired schoolteacher named Marguerite who wore a nose clip and a rash guard, said, "There is no such thing as sinking."

This is, of course, a lie. People sink. Ships sink. But she meant it in the sense that a human body, lungs full of air, will float if it relaxes. The problem is the relaxing. The problem is the part of the brain that says *this is not how we stay alive.*

The first thing she taught us was the back float. Sounds easy. Lie back, ears in the water, look at the ceiling. I lay back and immediately my chin came up like a turtle's and my legs dropped and I was vertical again, splashing, apologizing. Marguerite stood behind my head and cupped her hands under my skull. "Trust me," she said. "I've got you." I don't know why this undid me. Maybe it was the phrase. Maybe it was the fact that nobody had said it to me in a while. I floated. Twenty seconds. My ears filled with water and the world went muffled and distant, and I could hear my own heart.

The freestyle came later, and it was ugly. I will not pretend otherwise. I swallowed water. I got water up my nose, an experience I can only describe as inhaling a swarm of bees. I kicked too hard and ran out of breath and had to grab the lane rope and hang there like a drowned thing while the triathlon man glided past, sympathetic. There is nothing more humbling than being lapped by a sixty-two-year-old engineer from Tonawanda.

But here is the thing. Here is the part I did not expect. About six weeks in, I was doing laps—slow, ragged, real laps—and I noticed the silence. Not silence exactly. The sound of my own exhale, a long ribbon of bubbles, and the water moving past my ears, and a kind of concentrated quiet in my head that I had not felt since before I had children. I reached the wall and held on and laughed out loud. The lifeguard looked at me. A grown woman laughing at the end of a lane at nine o'clock on a Tuesday. Fine.

I'm not a strong swimmer now. I'm a competent one. I can do a length without stopping, more or less. I can tread water. I can float on my back and look at the ceiling of the YMCA and listen to the muffled world. That's enough. More than enough.

Last summer we went back to the lake. My daughter paddled out past the rope and I followed. Not fast. Not pretty. But there.

title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
The rod tip dipped, a subtle, almost apologetic nod, and my heart hammered against my ribs. Uncle Ian’s hand, resting on the gunwale, didn’t move. His eyes, the same grey as the loch, remained fixed on the distant, mist-shrouded shore. He was a man carved from silence and stone, and I had learned in the past three days that his stillness was not an absence of thought, but a concentration of it. I gripped the cork handle, my knuckles white, waiting for his command, a whisper, a nod—anything. None came. The silence stretched, filled only by the lap of water against the small wooden boat and the mournful cry of a curlew. I was eleven, and this was my first summer in the Highlands, a season I’d been sent to spend with a man I barely knew.

The loch was a vast, black mirror, holding the mountains in its depths. It was a place of immense, quiet power, and Ian was its high priest. Our days had a ritualistic rhythm: up before the sun, a breakfast of porridge and strong tea taken in silence, then out onto the water. He would row with a slow, steady economy of motion, the oars creaking in their locks, the only sound for miles. He’d chosen our spot each day not by any logic I could discern, but by a glance at the sky, the water, the direction of the wind. Then, the long, patient wait. He would fish with a Zen-like focus, his line a delicate thread connecting him to the deep. I, on the other hand, was a creature of fidgets and questions, my patience fraying within minutes. I’d watch the midges dance, trace patterns in the clouds, and will the float to move.

The float had been my idea. Ian had scoffed, a rare vocalisation that was half grunt, half sigh. He was a fly fisherman, a practitioner of grace and deception. A float, with its garish red tip and reliance on brute luck, was, I sensed, a philistine’s tool. But he’d tied one on for me without a word, his thick, calloused fingers working the line with a surprising gentleness. And now, that vulgar little red tip was bobbing, a frantic semaphore that sent a jolt of pure electricity through me.

The dip came again, more pronounced this time. The float vanished beneath the surface, and the line went taut. Instinct took over. I yanked the rod upwards, a violent, unthinking jerk. The rod bent into a terrifying arc, and the reel screamed in protest. “Ah!” I gasped, a sound of pure shock. I could feel it, a living, pulsing weight on the other end. It was terrifying and magnificent.

Ian finally moved. He didn’t shout or grab the rod. He simply leaned forward, his presence a sudden, solid anchor in the chaos of the moment. “Easy,” he murmured, his voice a low rumble barely audible over the shrieking reel. “Let him run.”

His words were a balm. I loosened my death grip, just a fraction, and the fish took off, stripping line from the reel in a furious dash for the deep. The rod bucked and strained. I was terrified it would snap, that I would lose this phantom, this sudden, vibrant connection to the unseen world below. Ian’s hand came to rest on my shoulder. It was a heavy, grounding weight. He didn’t need to say anything else. The pressure of his hand told me to hold on, to breathe, to trust the tackle and the line and, impossibly, myself.

The fight was a conversation. A series of tugs and runs, of give and take. My arms ached. The sun, now higher, burned the back of my neck. I forgot about the midges, about my boredom, about the silent, intimidating man beside me. My entire universe had shrunk to the bend of the rod and the whine of the reel. Ian guided me with the smallest of gestures: a slight pressure on my shoulder to keep the rod tip up, a nod towards the other side of the boat when the fish changed direction. He was a silent conductor, and I was the entire, frantic orchestra.

Slowly, the runs became shorter, the pulls less powerful. The fish was tiring. I could feel its strength waning, replaced by a sullen, heavy resistance. I began to gain line, my movements becoming less jerky, more attuned to the rhythm of the fight. The boat drifted, and Ian made no move to correct it, letting the fish dictate our path.

Then, I saw it. A flash of silver in the dark water, a shape, a shadow. It was a trout, a beautiful, wild brown trout, its flanks speckled with crimson and gold. The sight of it took my breath away. It was no longer a phantom, but a real, living creature, and I was the one who had tricked it.

Ian reached for the net. He moved with the same slow, deliberate grace he did everything, dipping the mesh into the water without a splash. He didn’t scoop; he waited. He guided the tired fish over the net, and with a single, smooth motion, lifted it from the loch. The fish lay in the net, gasping, its scales shimmering in the pale Highland light. It was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen.

Ian laid a hand on my back. He still didn’t speak. But as he looked from the fish to me, I saw it. A flicker in his grey eyes. A slight, almost imperceptible crinkling at the corners. It wasn’t a smile, not exactly. It was something better. It was a look of shared understanding, of quiet pride, of a lesson passed from one generation to the next without a single word being spoken. In that moment, the great, silent gulf between us closed. We were no longer a boy and his distant uncle; we were two fishermen, bound by the shared miracle of the catch.

title: memoir|growing up above a family laundry in a northern English town
text:
The smell was the first thing, and the last. It was a smell that had no single name, a complex broth of clean and dirty. From the front room, the ghost of it: the sweet, synthetic perfume of the blue and pink powders we scooped from giant drums, the sharp chemical tang of the bleach. But from the back, from the yard where the air was thick and wet, it was the smell of other people’s lives. The sourness of sweat in a cotton shirt, the faint, grassy note of a child’s mud-caked trousers, the cloying sweetness of perfume on a silk scarf. Our house was a lung, breathing in the town’s soiled linen and breathing out a hot, damp exhalation of steam and soap.

The laundry was the engine of our home, a constant, thrumming presence in the basement. Its rhythm was the rhythm of my childhood. The great cylindrical washers would groan into life, a deep, guttural sound that vibrated up through the floorboards and into the soles of my feet. Then would come the percussive clang of the dryer doors, the hiss of steam from the press, the frantic, high-pitched whine of the spin cycle that sounded like a trapped animal. My mother was the high priestess of this subterranean world, a small, formidable woman in a faded tabard, her hands permanently red and chapped, her hair frizzing in the heat. She could read a stain like a fortune teller reads tea leaves. A rust-coloured smear on a bedsheet was a story of a scraped knee; a greyish shadow on a cuff spoke of a desk job and tired elbows.

I was forbidden from the laundry floor itself, but the house was porous. The heat seeped upwards, making the kitchen windows weep with condensation. The noise was a constant lullaby. And the lint, the lint was everywhere. It was a fine, grey fluff that settled on every surface, a sediment of the town’s fibres. I would find it in my hair, on my toothbrush, and on the dark wool of my school jumper. It felt like the town itself was slowly, gently, disintegrating and sifting down onto us.

Our lives were marked by the laundry’s clock. We ate dinner when the last of the day’s wash was folded, the kitchen table cleared of receipts and safety pins. My father, who drove the delivery van, would return at dusk, his face grey with fatigue, smelling of diesel and the fresh, clean linen stacked in the back. He rarely spoke of his day, but the van’s cargo told its own stories. He delivered crisp white sheets to the big hotel on the hill, and frayed, thin towels to the old folks’ home by the river. He knew the town not by its streets, but by its washing.

The laundry was our livelihood, but it was also our secret shame. Other children’s fathers worked in offices or on building sites. Their mothers didn’t spend their days wrestling with other people’s dirt. I never invited friends back. Our house, I felt, was not like theirs. It had no quiet, no stillness. It smelled of industry and otherness. The steam from the vents in the back wall was a constant, ghostly plume, a public declaration of our strange, subterranean life. I saw it as a flag of surrender to the grime of the world.

Yet, there was a strange intimacy to it all. I knew the fabric of the town in a way no one else did. I knew that the mayor wore surprisingly threadbare vests. I knew that the formidable Mrs. Gable, who ran the post office, slept on floral poly-cotton sheets that were pilled and soft with age. I knew the particular shade of pink that a certain girl in my class favoured for her ballet tights, because I’d once found a pair, forgotten and damp, in the pocket of a coat my mother was sorting. It was a knowledge that felt illicit, a form of voyeurism that left a faintly grimy feeling on the soul.

On winter nights, when the town was muffled with fog and the sodium streetlights made halos of the damp air, our house was the warmest place in the world. The heat from the laundry below was a physical presence, a solid, comforting thing. I would lie in bed, listening to the deep, rhythmic thump of the machinery, a mechanical heartbeat. The window would be a slick of condensation, and if I pressed my finger to the glass, I could draw a line through the water, a clear streak through which I could see the dark, silent shapes of the terraced houses opposite. Their windows were dark, their lives quiet. Ours was a house that never slept, a house that was always, relentlessly, washing away the sins of the town, one load at a time.

title: nature essay|the life of an abandoned quarry
text:
The first thing was the quiet. Not a silence, which is a vacuum, but a quiet that felt inhabited, like a room left by someone who might still be in it. The quarry was a vast, scooped-out bowl of grey stone, a man-made amphitheater where the audience had long since departed. I had come to it by a path choked with vetch and wild carrot, a path that seemed to want to erase itself, and when I reached the lip of the excavation, the air changed. It was cooler, denser, carrying the mineral smell of wet rock and something else—a green, vegetable scent that was almost a taste.

The walls were sheer, terraced in some places by the old cuts, and their surface was a map of violence and time. Here were the clean, brutal lines of the drills, and there, the slow, patient signatures of lichen in rust and pale green. The stone itself was a dark, brooding schist, and when I put my palm against it, it held the night's chill. It felt not like a thing, but like an event that had stopped. The entire place was a monument to a sudden halt. One day, the men and their machines had simply left, and the world had begun the slow, meticulous work of moving back in.

In the center of the bowl, a small lake had formed. It was not a picturesque pond. Its water was the color of steeped tea, dark and peaty, and it held the sky without reflecting it, a perfect, flat black mirror. It was fed by unseen springs, a slow, constant weeping from the rock face, and its surface was littered with the pollen of the pines that now crowded the upper rim. No fish rose. It was a dead-looking eye, and yet, at its edges, where the water met the shattered rubble, there were signs of a persistent, almost furtive life. Caddisfly larvae in their little houses of sand and grit, water boatmen skating in frantic, pointless circles.

I sat on a block of stone that had been rejected, perhaps for a flaw, and watched the light change. The sun, moving across the opening, was a hand that revealed and concealed. It lit up a patch of Buddleja, the butterfly bush, its purple cones a frantic, buzzing metropolis of bees and vanessid butterflies. Then it would move on, and the bush would fall back into a dusky, silent shadow, its inhabitants hidden. The quarry was a place of这些小, discrete worlds, each in its own pocket of sun or shade. A world of mosses on the north-facing wall, a deep, velvet green that seemed to drink the light. A world of stonecrop and harebells on a thin ledge, clinging to a purchase that was half a millennium old.

There was no grand narrative here, no tidy moral about nature’s resilience. The quarry was not a wound that had healed; it was a wound that had been repurposed. The violence of its creation was the very thing that gave it its form, its shelter, its peculiar, hard-edged beauty. The ecosystem was not a return to some pristine past, but a new thing entirely, built on the ruins of industry. The fox I saw, slipping like a copper shadow between the scree, was not a symbol of wildness returning. It was just a fox, finding a den in a place where the noise of men had ceased.

As the afternoon wore on, the quality of the light deepened, turning the quarry into a study in grey and gold. The stone, which had seemed so uniform, revealed its subtleties: veins of quartz, patches of iron staining, the faint, fossilized imprints of things that had lived and died in a sea that predated the forest by an almost unimaginable span. The scale of time was vertiginous. My own presence here was a flicker, a single frame in a film that had been running for eons. The quarry would outlast me, and the fox, and the pines on the rim. It would continue its slow, patient work of being, a testament not to nature’s triumph, but to its indifference, and to the strange, accidental beauty that can arise from a hole in the ground.

title: memoir|the year spent caring for a grandmother with dementia
text:
The year I moved back to Cleveland, the snow came early and stayed late, and my grandmother, Rose, kept asking me where her husband was. He had been dead since 1998. I would find her standing at the front window of the house on West 130th Street, her hand flat against the glass, watching the empty driveway as if expecting a car that had already arrived.

“He’s on his way, Bubbe,” I’d say. “Traffic on I-71.”

She’d nod, satisfied for a moment, then turn to me with narrowed eyes. “Who are you again?”

“I’m your granddaughter. Sarah.”

“Sarah,” she’d repeat, testing the word like a stone in her mouth. “Sarah went to college in Chicago.”

“That’s me. I came back.”

She’d look at me for a long beat, then pat my cheek with a dry hand. “Well, you have her face.”

I had moved back because my mother couldn’t do it alone anymore. Rose had been diagnosed with vascular dementia two years earlier, and the progression had been steady, a slow erosion of the sharp, funny, impossible woman who had once run a kosher catering business out of her basement and could curse in three languages. My mother, Diane, was sixty-three and still working as a nurse at MetroHealth. She’d call me at night, exhausted, and say things like, “She put her shoes in the freezer today. Just tell me that’s normal.”

It wasn’t normal, but it was the new normal. I took a leave from my job at a bookstore in Chicago, packed two suitcases, and moved into the guest room that still had my old posters on the wall. The room smelled like mothballs and the lavender sachets Rose sewed by the dozen every Christmas.

The days took on a rhythm. Mornings were the worst. Rose would wake up confused, sometimes angry, sometimes frightened. She’d forget where she was, forget that my grandfather was gone, forget that she had ever been a person who knew things. I learned to approach her slowly, to say her name before touching her shoulder. “Rose,” I’d say. “It’s morning. You’re in your house. On West 130th. I’m Sarah. I’m here to help.”

One morning in February, she looked at me and said, “You’re the one who reads to me.”

I hadn’t read to her yet. But I said, “Yes. What should we read?”

“The paper,” she said. “The obituaries.”

So I read her the obituaries. Every morning for a week. She listened intently, occasionally saying, “Him I knew,” or “She was a bitch.” It was the most lucid she’d been in months. I didn’t question it. I just read.

There were good days. Days when she remembered my name, when she told me stories about her catering business, about the time she dropped a whole tray of blintzes at a wedding and blamed the groom’s mother. She’d laugh, that deep, rattling laugh, and for a moment she was Rose again, the woman who had taught me to fold kreplach when I was eight, who had slipped me five-dollar bills and told me not to tell my mother.

But the bad days came more often. She’d wander out the front door in her nightgown. She’d accuse me of stealing her jewelry. She’d cry for hours, calling for her mother, who had been dead for fifty years. I learned to sit with her in the crying, to hold her hand and say nothing. There was nothing to say.

In April, she fell in the bathroom. I found her on the floor, her hip already swelling, and she looked up at me and said, “Sarah, I’m sorry.” It was the first time she’d said my name in weeks. I called 911. The paramedics were kind and efficient. At the hospital, they told us she’d broken her hip. Surgery was an option, but at her age and with her condition, the recovery would be brutal. My mother and I sat in the hospital cafeteria, drinking bad coffee, and made the decision together. No surgery. Palliative care.

She came home on a Tuesday. Hospice set up a bed in the living room, facing the window. She slept most of the time. When she was awake, she talked to people who weren’t there. Her brother, her sister, my grandfather. “I’m coming,” she said once, clear as a bell. “I’m coming.”

She died on a Thursday in May, early in the morning, while the lilacs were blooming in the backyard. My mother was holding her hand. I was in the kitchen, making coffee, and I heard my mother say, “It’s okay, Mom. You can go.” And then a long silence. And then my mother’s quiet cry.

I don’t remember much about the funeral. I remember the smell of the deli platters, the way my mother’s friends from the hospital hugged her too tightly, the rabbi’s drone. I remember standing in the backyard afterward, looking at the lilacs, and thinking that Rose would have hated the flowers. She always said lilacs smelled like old lady perfume.

The house sold in the fall. I went back to Chicago. I still have the lavender sachets. I keep them in a drawer with my sweaters. Sometimes, when I open it, I smell that house on West 130th, and I hear her voice, sharp and clear, saying, “Who are you again?” And I say, quietly, “I’m Sarah. I’m here to help.”

title: myth retelling|the smith who forged the first bell
text:
The hammer came down, and the sound that rang out was not the flat clang of iron on iron, but a deep and mournful hum that seemed to rise from the earth itself. It hung in the air of the smithy, a vibration you could feel in your teeth, and for a long moment, neither the smith nor his apprentice dared to breathe. The boy, a lad named Corin with wide eyes and a smudge of soot on his nose, finally let his jaw drop. “Master,” he whispered, “what was that?”

The smith, a man whose back was permanently curved by a lifetime of leaning over the anvil, did not answer at once. His name was Bran, and he was known throughout the valley as a man who could coax the soul out of metal. But this was different. He had taken the strange, star-blessed ore the elders had found in the riverbed—a metal that was too soft for a blade and too stubborn for a plow—and he had shaped it into a vessel. A great, inverted cup, as tall as a man, its surface smooth and dark. He had poured into its molten heart a measure of silver, a handful of salt from the sea, and, on a whim, a lock of his own hair. Now, as it cooled, he struck it, and it sang.

“It’s a voice,” Bran said, his own voice rough with awe. He ran a calloused thumb over the lip of the great bell. It was cool now, but he could still feel the phantom thrum of its song beneath his skin. “The metal remembers something. The fire, the water, the deep places of the world. It wants to speak.”

Corin, ever practical, frowned. “Speak? To whom? It just makes a noise, Master. A strange one, to be sure. But what good is a noise that isn’t a warning cry or a call to work?”

Bran grunted. He didn’t have an answer. He only knew that the sound was not finished. It was a single note, a foundation, but it was lonely. It needed a chorus. He looked at the ore that remained, a small pile of unyielding starlight in the corner of his forge. “We need more,” he said, a feverish light kindling in his eyes. “We need a scale.”

For the next moon, the forge did not sleep. Bran and Corin worked in shifts, the boy pumping the bellows until his arms felt like water, the smith shaping smaller versions of the great bell. He experimented with the metals, adding tin for a sharper, clearer tone, lead for a duller, more sonorous one. He discovered that by changing the thickness of the bell’s lip, he could change its pitch. He crafted a set of seven, each one a different size, each one holding a different note. He hung them from a great beam in his workshop, and when he struck them in sequence, the air shimmered. It was a language without words, a story told in vibration. The lowest note spoke of the deep, patient earth. The highest, a clear, ringing tone, spoke of the first light of dawn.

The villagers, who had initially mocked Bran for wasting good metal on such a foolish endeavor, began to gather at the door of his smithy. They would stand in silence, listening as he played his strange stone-and-metal orchestra. They felt the music in their bones. It stirred something in them—a memory of a time before the fields were tilled, before the houses were built, a time when they were part of the wild, thrumming heart of the world.

It was the village elder, a woman named Elara with hair like winter frost, who finally understood. She came to Bran one evening as he was polishing the smallest bell, the one that sang like a lark. “You have not just made a noise, Bran,” she said, her voice quiet. “You have made a memory. You have forged a way for us to speak to the mountain, and for the mountain to speak back.”

Bran looked at his hands, stained with soot and scarred by sparks. He had always thought of himself as a shaper of tools, a maker of things for the hands. He had never considered he might be a maker of things for the soul. The idea was terrifying. It was also, he realized, the most important thing he had ever done.

He looked at the seven bells hanging in the gloom of his smithy, their dark surfaces catching the glow of the forge. They were no longer just metal. They were a question, a prayer, a story waiting to be told. And he, the smith, was the one who had given them a voice. He had not just forged a bell; he had forged a bridge. And he knew, with a certainty that settled deep in his gut, that the world would never be silent again.

title: folk tale|the miller's third son and the talking millstone
text:
There was a miller who lived by a river that ran slow and brown, and he had three sons. The two elder were broad-shouldered and loud, quick to laugh and quicker to claim the best of everything, and when the miller died they took the mill and the wheel and the good stone and left the third son, whose name was Corin, with nothing but the old cracked quern from the attic and a sack of tailings no one wanted. Corin did not argue. He carried the quern down to the riverbank, set it on a flat stone, and sat looking at it while the water went by.

The quern was a sorry thing, grey and pitted, with a hole in the middle and a handle worn smooth by hands long dead. Corin turned it once, idly, and heard a voice.

“Easy,” it said. “I’m not as young as I was.”

Corin took his hand away. The river went on. A heron lifted off the far bank. He looked at the quern and the quern, in its way, looked back.

“You talk,” he said.

“I grind,” said the quern. “Talking is what I do between grindings. You’ve woken me up, so you may as well be useful. What have you got?”

Corin had the sack of tailings, the chaff and dust and broken grains the brothers had swept out and left him. He poured a handful into the hole. The quern turned itself, slow and gritty, and what came out at the edge was not flour but a thin trickle of something that shone. Corin caught it in his palm. It was salt. Good salt, white and coarse, the kind that costs money in the hill towns where no sea reaches.

“That’s the trick of me,” said the quern. “I don’t make what you put in. I make what’s wanted. But mind—I’m old, and I’m tired, and I won’t be hurried. Turn me too fast and you’ll get dust and a headache.”

So Corin went to the hill towns with a sack of salt on his back, and he sold it for a good price, and came home. He did this many times, never taking more than the quern would give, always letting it rest when it asked. He bought a cart. He bought a mule. He did not buy a fine house, because the quern told him not to, and he had learned to listen.

His brothers heard of it. They came to the riverbank, the two of them, big and red-faced, and they saw the old quern and the sack of salt and they laughed. “A talking stone,” said the elder. “Our brother has gone soft in the head.” But the second brother was quieter, and he watched how Corin poured in the chaff and how the salt came out, and he went home thinking.

That night, while Corin slept, the second brother crept down to the riverbank and took the quern. He carried it to his own mill and set it on the floor and poured in a whole barrel of good wheat. “Grind,” he said. “Grind fast. I want gold.”

The quern groaned. “I’m old,” it said. “I’m tired. I won’t be hurried.”

“You’ll do as you’re told,” said the brother, and he seized the handle and turned it hard and fast, faster than it had been turned in a hundred years.

What came out was not gold. It was sand, and then gravel, and then a grey sludge that smelled of the river bottom, and it came faster and faster until it filled the mill room to the height of a man’s knee, then his waist, then his chest. The brother shouted and the quern said nothing at all. He got out through the window with the sludge at his chin, and when he looked back the mill was full to the rafters, and the wheel outside had stopped, choked with grit.

In the morning Corin came and dug the quern out. It was cracked worse than before, and when he turned it, it did not speak. He carried it back to the riverbank and sat with it a long while. Then he poured in a handful of chaff, and turned it gently, and after a moment it sighed and began, slow and gritty, and the salt came out thin and white at the edge.

“You came back for me,” it said.

“You’re mine,” said Corin. “Cracked or not.”

The quern ground on. The river went by, slow and brown. And Corin sat with his hand on the handle, turning it at the speed the old stone liked, which was the speed of a man walking, or a heart beating, or the water going down to the sea.

title: literary novel|a sound archivist who finds a confession hidden on an old tape
text:
The tape was a Scotch 203, its reel yellowed like an old tooth. It came in a lot from a house clearance in the Cascades, a box of reels smelling of mildew and cedar. My job, as an archivist for the university’s ethnomusicology department, is to digitize the analog dead. I’ve transferred field recordings of weddings, funerals, church choirs, and the agonizingly earnest strumming of folk singers who never made it. I am a ferryman for ghosts.

This tape was labeled in fountain pen, the ink faded to a brown whisper: *Hayes, M. – Family, 1968*.

The first ten minutes were what I expected. A family barbecue. The hiss and crackle of the tape was a constant, like distant static rain. A man’s voice, presumably M. Hayes, narrated with the tedious authority of a father wielding a new tape recorder. “And here’s your mother, getting the potato salad. Say hello, Janice.” A woman’s voice, tinny and distant, said something about the heat. The clatter of plates. A dog barking. The sounds of a world that had long since dissolved into memory and dust.

I was about to mark the file and move on when the scene shifted. The sounds of the party faded, replaced by the creak of a door and the muffled quiet of a different room. The father’s voice was gone. Then, a new voice, closer to the microphone, a boy’s voice, probably no older than twelve. It was tight, a wire pulled taut.

“Are you sure it’s on?” the boy asked.

“The light’s red, isn’t it?” This was another boy, older. His voice was a low, confident murmur.

There was a scuffling sound, then a sharp intake of breath. “I don’t want to,” the first boy whispered. It was a sound of pure, animal dread.

“You have to,” the older boy said. “You promised. Now tell it what you did.”

A long silence followed. I could hear the tape’s own hum, the mechanical breath of the machine. I leaned closer to my monitors, the world of my sterile office dissolving. I was no longer an archivist; I was a trespasser in a darkened room, fifty years gone.

“I… I broke it,” the young voice finally said, the words catching in his throat. “The… the thing. The bird. The one Dad got from Japan.”

“The netsuke,” the older boy corrected, his voice a prosecutor’s.

“The netsuke,” the younger boy repeated, the word a foreign stone in his mouth. “I was playing with it. It was a game. It was a hawk, and I was making it fly. And it… it fell. It broke. I tried to glue it, but the beak… the beak came off.”

“And then what?” the older boy prompted.

“And then I hid it. I put it in the back of the drawer. I told Dad I didn’t know what happened. I let him think it was lost.”

“You lied,” the older boy stated, not a question but a verdict.

“I lied,” the younger boy echoed, and then the sound of his crying began. It wasn’t a child’s loud, performative wail, but a quiet, ragged, hopeless sound. The sound of a soul being crushed under the weight of its own small, terrible secret. It went on for a minute, maybe two, before the tape clicked and the hiss returned, the silence of the room now charged with the echo of that confession.

I sat there for a long time, the headphone cups warm against my ears. The confession was profoundly mundane. A broken trinket, a childish lie. No murder, no grand betrayal. It was a sin of a scale that could only matter to a child, and to the man that child would become. But the shame in that boy’s voice was absolute. It was a foundational sin, the moment he first understood his own capacity for deceit, and the sound of his world cracking.

Who was he? Did he ever confess to his father? Or does he carry the ghost of that broken beak with him still, a tiny, sharp piece of guilt lodged in his heart? I will never know. The tape offers no resolution, only the raw, unvarnished moment.

I finished the transfer. The file is now in the digital archive, designated MS-348, Box 12, Reel 4. It is cataloged, preserved, and accessible to any researcher with a legitimate reason. It is safe. But I can’t shake the feeling that I have not saved a piece of history, but have instead exhumed a ghost and given it a new, more permanent home. I can still hear it, you know. The quiet, ragged crying of a boy who broke a bird.

title: nature essay|a winter of watching one heron on the same canal
text:
The canal freezes first at the edges, a skin of grey glass that creeps inward each night until only a dark seam of open water remains along the centre, and that is where the heron stood. I first saw it on the second of December, from the towpath below the locks at Marsworth, and I marked the date in the margin of a bird report I was carrying for no good reason. It was a grey heron, Ardea cinerea, though it took me a week to stop calling it simply the heron, as if there were no others in Buckinghamshire. There were, of course. But this one had a habit of holding its head at a slight angle, a tilt of perhaps ten degrees to the left, as though listening for something under the ice, and by the end of the month I could have picked it out of a crowd of a hundred.

My neighbour Margaret, who has walked the Wendover Arm every morning since her husband died, told me I was being ridiculous. "It's a bird," she said, on one of the mornings she stopped to watch with me, her breath clouding. "It's not a character in a novel." She said this without unkindness. Then she added, after a pause: "Though I'll grant you it's got a look about it."

The look was patience, mostly. I came to think of the winter as a lesson in it. I would arrive at half past seven, sometimes in frost so hard the puddles rang under my boots, and the heron would already be there, stationed on the same stretch of bank between the bridge at Bulbourne and the old watercress beds, motionless as a fence post. I learned to stand still myself, which is harder than it sounds. My first week I lasted four minutes before shifting my weight, and the heron lifted its head, considered me with a yellow eye, and went back to the water without any sign of alarm. It had already decided I was not worth the trouble of flying.

By January the cold had settled in properly. The canal froze solid enough that a man called Terry, who lives on a narrowboat called *Perseverance* and who I spoke to perhaps six times all winter, told me he'd seen a fox cross at the winding hole near the allotments. "Bold as brass," he said, "at four in the afternoon." The heron, meanwhile, had found a patch where a drain emptied in, keeping a coin of open water the size of a dinner plate. It stood over that coin for hours. Once I watched it take a fish — a roach, I think, though I am no icthyologist — and the whole business was over in less than a second, a jab and a swallow, and then the long stillness resumed as though nothing had happened at all. I found I had been holding my breath.

There were days it did not come. Two in a row in mid-January, after a night of hard rain, and I felt the absence the way you feel a missing tooth. I told myself this was absurd. I am fifty-three years old, I have a job and a mortgage and a mother in a care home in Aylesbury, and I was standing on a towpath worrying about a bird. But the worry was real, and when it returned on the third morning, dropping down from somewhere south with its wings held wide and its legs trailing, I heard myself say "oh, thank God" out loud, to nobody, into the cold air.

Margaret asked me in February whether I'd given it a name. "No," I said, and then, defensively: "It's a wild animal." She nodded slowly. "Quite right," she said. "Names are for things you can keep."

The thaw came late, the last week of February, and with it the noise of water moving again. The heron stayed on. I don't know when it left, exactly, or whether it left at all — I stopped going daily in March, and then I stopped going, and the winter closed over behind me the way winters do. But I find I still walk the towpath sometimes and find myself scanning the bank between the bridge and the cress beds, and I find I am disappointed, and then I find I am glad that I am. Margaret says I'm still ridiculous. She says it while walking beside me, though, which I take to mean something.

title: nature essay|a winter of watching one heron on the same canal
text:
The heron was there before I was. That’s the first thing. Every morning that winter, I’d come down the towpath with my hands jammed in my pockets and my breath hanging in the air like something I could grab, and the heron would already be in position. Same canal. Same stretch of water, the one just past the lock where the flow slows and the silt gathers and the water has that particular flat, brownish look, like old glass.

I started watching it out of boredom more than anything else. Not true. Out of a kind of stubbornness. I’d moved to that town for a job that turned out to be less of a job and more of a slow, quiet humiliation, and the canal was the only place that didn’t ask anything of me. So I walked it. Every morning. Rain or the other thing, which was mostly a fine grey drizzle that didn’t seem to fall so much as hang.

The heron didn’t care. That’s what got to me. It stood there on its ridiculous legs—too thin, honestly, like something a child had drawn—and it did not care about me, or the drizzle, or the barges that came through on weekends with their cheerful, oblivious owners. It was a machine for waiting. A grey, angular machine with a yellow eye.

For the first few weeks I tried to figure out its schedule. I thought maybe it fished at dawn and then moved on. But no. It was there at seven. It was there at ten, when I’d sometimes sneak back down for a second walk, pretending to myself that I hadn’t come specifically to check. It was there at dusk, a darker shape against the darker water. I don’t know where it went at night. I never saw it fly. That bothers me more than it should.

The canal in winter is not a beautiful place. Let’s be honest. The trees are just sticks. The water is the colour of weak tea. There’s a persistent smell, not quite bad, not quite good—something mineral and old. The only colour is the occasional plastic bag caught in the reeds, and the heron’s feet, which are a sort of dull orange, like the last bruised leaves of autumn.

I brought a notebook, eventually. I wrote things like: “Heron. 7:12. No fish. Didn’t move for forty minutes.” And then, later, more embarrassingly: “I think it knows I’m here.” Which is nonsense. It didn’t know. It didn’t care. But there’s a certain comfort in being ignored by something so completely indifferent. It’s cleaner than being ignored by people, who always seem to be doing it on purpose.

I learned its habits. It favoured the spot just downstream of the lock, where the water churned up just enough to hide the fish but not so much that the heron couldn’t see through it. It would stand with its neck folded into that S-shape, absolutely still, and then—this is the thing—it would strike. Not often. Maybe once every hour. A quick, violent uncoiling. And then it would have a fish, or it wouldn’t, and either way it would go back to being a statue. No celebration. No disappointment. Just the next wait.

I started to think of it as a colleague. We were both doing our time by the water. I’d stand on the towpath, shivering, and it would stand in the shallows, and we’d both watch the same brown surface. Sometimes I talked to it. Not out loud. Just in my head. Things like, “Any luck?” and “Bit cold today.” It never answered, which was, frankly, a relief. I’d had enough of people answering me that winter, mostly with bad news or worse sympathy.

Then, in March, it was gone. Just like that. I came down one morning and the spot was empty. The water moved the same way. The reeds were the same. But the heron wasn’t there. I waited. I walked the whole length of the canal, past the lock, past the pub with the broken sign, past the place where the path turns into mud. Nothing. I went back the next day. Nothing.

I don’t know what happened to it. Maybe it moved upstream. Maybe it died. Maybe it was just a heron, doing heron things, and I’d assigned it a significance it never asked for. But I still think about it. That grey shape in the grey water. The way it waited. The way it didn’t need anything from me, and somehow that was exactly what I needed.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The water was the color of weak tea, and it was cold in a way that felt personal. It was a Thursday morning in late September, and I was the only adult in a class of six-year-olds. We stood in the shallow end, a nervous herd of pale legs and brightly colored swimsuits, while a young woman named Chloe with a whistle around her neck told us to blow bubbles. The children, equipped with goggles and an unearned confidence, plunged their faces in immediately, erupting with triumphant gurgles. I hesitated, the chlorinated air sharp in my nose, before lowering my chin to the surface and exhaling a reluctant stream of air that felt less like a bubble and more like a sigh.

For thirty-nine years and eleven months, I had been a land animal. I was an expert at gravity. I knew the solid feel of pavement under running shoes, the reassuring click of a door latch, the weight of a book in my hands. The water was a foreign country with its own incomprehensible laws. It was a place of muffled sounds and distorted shapes, of a silence so profound it roared. My relationship with it had been one of careful avoidance, a long history of wading up to my knees at the beach, of feigning a sudden interest in reading whenever a pool party was mentioned. I was not afraid, not exactly. It was more a profound lack of trust. I didn’t trust the water not to swallow me, and I didn’t trust my body to know what to do if it tried.

The decision to learn at forty was not born of a midlife crisis or a sudden burst of athletic ambition. It was born of a quiet, creeping shame. It was the shame of being on a boat with friends and feeling a jolt of pure panic when the engine sputtered. It was the shame of my own daughter, then seven, paddling effortlessly in the deep end, calling for me to join her, and my having to invent a lie about a cramp. It was the realization that I had built a wall around a vast, beautiful part of the world and had no one to blame but myself. So, I signed up for the adult beginner class, the one scheduled at an hour when the pool was mostly empty, a time for the infirm, the elderly, and the quietly ashamed.

The first few weeks were an exercise in humiliation. My body, so competent on land, became a collection of disconnected parts. My legs, I was told, were kicking from the knee, not the hip. My arms were “windmilling,” a word that sounded both childish and chaotic. I could not coordinate my breathing. The instruction was to turn my head, inhale quickly, and turn back. What I did was inhale water, choke, and stand up sputtering, my heart hammering against my ribs. The children in the next lane over would pause their games to watch me, their small faces reflecting a mixture of curiosity and pity. I felt like a fraud, a grown man pretending to be a swimmer, my body a clumsy lie in the water.

But something began to shift. It wasn’t a breakthrough, not a single, triumphant moment of gliding effortlessly across the pool. It was a series of small, accumulating victories. One day, I managed to swim a full length of the pool without stopping, my breathing ragged but rhythmic. Another day, Chloe told me to float on my back. I panicked, the water rushing into my ears, the ceiling of the natatorium reeling above me. But then, I felt it—a gentle lift, an unexpected buoyancy. For a few seconds, I just lay there, cradled by the water, and the panic receded, replaced by a strange and profound calm. The water wasn't an adversary. It was a partner in a delicate negotiation.

The real change was subtler. It was in the way I began to look at the water, not as a threat, but as a mystery to be solved. I started to notice the way the light fractured on the surface, the intricate patterns the ripples made on the tiled floor below. I discovered the sheer, unadulterated pleasure of submersion, the world of sound and weight falling away. In the water, I was stripped of my phone, my keys, my wallet, all the talismans of my on-land identity. I was just a body, moving through a denser medium, and it was liberating.

Now, months later, I am still not a good swimmer. My freestyle is a work in progress, a graceless flail that propels me forward with more determination than finesse. I can’t do a flip turn. I have a healthy respect for the deep end. But I am no longer a land animal. I am an amphibian of a sort, a creature who moves between two worlds. Last week, I took my daughter to the pool. We raced to the other end, and she beat me, of course. But as I stood there in the chest-deep water, my breath coming in deep, satisfying pulls, I didn’t feel the familiar sting of inadequacy. I just felt wet, and tired, and a part of it all. I looked at my daughter, her hair slicked back, her smile wide and easy, and for the first time, I felt the same way—not like a visitor in her world, but like a resident.

title: personal essay|the last video rental shop in town
text:
The bell above the door of Videodrome hadn't worked properly in years. It gave a weak, asthmatic wheeze when I pushed it open, a sound that felt less like an announcement and more like a complaint. Inside, the air was thick with the scent of dust, aging paper, and the faint chemical tang of photocopier toner from the racks of laminated membership cards. It was a smell I’d known since childhood, a scent of potential, of stories contained and waiting. Now, it just smelled like a place running out of time.

The shop was a holdout, a stubborn barnacle on the hull of a city that had long since sailed into the digital sea. The walls were lined with the detritus of a bygone era: faded posters for films that were once blockbusters and were now merely cultural footnotes, a cardboard standee of a long-dead actor whose smile had been chipped away by years of incidental contact. The fluorescent lights hummed a low, constant note, illuminating dust motes dancing in the air like a slow, silent snow.

Mr. Henderson was behind the counter, as he always was. He was a man composed of quiet routines, his movements economical and precise. He was meticulously updating a spreadsheet on a laptop that looked almost as old as the shop itself, the screen’s glow casting a pale blue light on his lined face. The spreadsheet was for inventory, a task of Sisyphean absurdity given the store’s dwindling stock and clientele. He was cataloging the slow decay.

“Find everything you’re looking for?” he asked, not looking up. It was his standard greeting, a piece of script he’d delivered ten thousand times.

“Just browsing,” I replied, the same response I’d given since I was tall enough to see over the counter.

I drifted through the aisles, my fingers tracing the spines of the VHS and DVD cases. This was a tactile experience that streaming could never replicate. The plastic was cool and smooth, the covers worn soft at the corners. I wasn't looking for anything specific. I was looking for the feeling. The feeling of scanning a shelf and having a title leap out at you, a discovery born of serendipity, not an algorithm. The feeling of a shared secret, of holding a physical object that had been held by countless others, each with their own reasons for seeking it out.

The last time I had come here to actually rent something was for a friend who was sick. She’d wanted to watch *The Princess Bride*. “The VHS,” she’d specified, her voice raspy. “I want the tracking lines. I want to feel like I’m ten.” Mr. Henderson had found it for me, blowing a puff of air onto the cassette and wiping it with a soft cloth. “Good choice,” he’d said. “The tape’s a little worn. You might have to adjust the tracking.” That detail, the intimacy of it, the shared knowledge of a specific copy’s particular flaw—that was the entire point of this place. It was an heirloom, not a commodity.

Now, the shelves were pockmarked with gaps. Whole sections were gone, their contents sold off in a fire sale of nostalgia. The “Cult Classics” section was now a ghost town, save for a few lonely titles like *Eraserhead* and *Repo Man*. The emptiness was a physical presence, a testament to a world that had moved on.

A young couple came in, their laughter a jarring intrusion. They were tourists, probably, exploring the neighborhood. They wandered aimlessly, picking up cases, reading the blurbs, and putting them down with the detached curiosity of people at a museum. They drifted toward the counter. “So, like, how does this work?” the man asked, gesturing vaguely at the shelves. “Do you have a website?”

Mr. Henderson didn’t miss a beat. “No website,” he said, his voice flat. “You bring the case to the counter. I scan your card. You bring it back in three days. If it’s late, it’s a dollar a day.”

The couple exchanged a look, a silent conversation about a quaintness they found charming but incomprehensible. They didn't rent anything. They left as quickly as they’d arrived, the door wheezing shut behind them.

The silence that followed was heavier than before. Mr. Henderson looked at the door for a long moment, then returned to his spreadsheet. I felt a sudden, sharp pang of something like grief. This wasn't just a business closing. It was the erasure of a communal ritual. The act of choosing, of anticipating, of discussing what you’d watched—it was all being flattened into a solitary, frictionless scroll. The algorithm knows what you want before you do, and it offers you an infinite, sterile library of the same. It offers no surprises, no tracking lines, no worn-out tapes that require a gentle touch.

I walked up to the counter, not with a movie, but with a sense of finality. “Just these,” I said, placing a few old favorites on the counter—*Harold and Maude*, *Paris, Texas*. I didn’t need to rent them. I had them at home, digitized and pristine. But I wanted the transaction. I wanted the ritual.

Mr. Henderson scanned my card, the one I’d had since I was twelve. The photograph was a ghost of a face I barely recognized.

“Three days,” he said, not as a warning, but as a statement of fact. A unit of time that still meant something in this room.

I nodded. I took the cases, the plastic cold in my hand, and walked out. The door wheezed shut behind me. I knew I would bring them back in two days, not three. I would pay the late fee if I didn’t. It wasn't about the movies anymore. It was about the return. It was about keeping the door from closing for just one more day.

title: nature essay|the life of an abandoned quarry
text:
The first thing you notice is the silence, and then the way the silence is not really silent at all. It is a Sunday in late October, and I am standing at the lip of what the Ordnance Survey map calls Craig’s Quarry, though no one in the village of Abernyte has called it that for forty years. The last time anyone quarried stone here was 1983. Now the place belongs to the rabbits and the rain.

I had come because of a conversation with Helen Strachan, who runs the post office out of her front room and remembers when the blasting shook the jam jars off her shelves. “You want to see it now,” she said, handing me a bag of messages I had not asked for. “There’s a heron been coming. And the orchids. My word, the orchids.” She said it the way people here say most things, as if the land were a neighbour who had been ill and was now, quietly, on the mend.

The quarry is a bowl of grey rock about sixty feet deep, half a mile from the road, and the path down is a rough cut through birch and bramble. I went slowly. The walls are terraced, stepped like the seats of some enormous amphitheatre, and in the crevices the rock is stained orange with lichen. At the bottom, a flat floor of crushed stone has been colonised by moss so thick it feels like walking on a mattress. There is a pool at the far end, black and still, and a plank bridge someone has laid across the narrowest part, nailed together with rusty six-inch nails.

That is where I met Tam Laird. He was sixty-eight, a retired joiner from Dundee, and he had come out to “check the burn was running.” He had a walking stick and a flask of tea and he did not seem surprised to see me. “You’ll be the one writing about it,” he said. It was not a question.

We sat on a flat stone and he told me he had worked here for two summers as a lad, loading rubble into lorries. “The gaffer was a man called Dod Menzies. He had one eye and he kept a whippet that would sit in the cab of the digger. If you were late, he’d say, ‘The whippet’s been waiting on ye.’ That was your warning.” He laughed, and the sound went up the rock face and came back thinner.

Tam pointed out where the old crusher had stood, and the shed, and the spot where a man had lost two fingers to a conveyor belt in 1961. “They filled the shaft with concrete after,” he said. “But the water still finds a way down. You can hear it if you put your ear to the ground.” I did not put my ear to the ground. I wish now that I had.

Instead I walked the terraces. On the second level, where the rock is sheltered from the wind, there is a stand of birch that has taken twenty years to reach fifteen feet. The trunks are pale and crooked, and in the fork of one of them a plastic bag has been wedged by the wind, so old it has gone the colour of the bark. Higher up, on a ledge no wider than a doorstep, a rowan has rooted and is heavy with orange berries. No one planted it. A blackbird must have dropped the seed, and the seed must have found a teaspoon of soil in a crack, and the whole improbable business of life had gone on from there.

Helen had been right about the orchids. Near the pool, in a patch of damp grass, there were a dozen spikes of common twayblade, gone over now, and a single late-flowering helleborine, its flowers the colour of pale green glass. I crouched to look, and a frog the size of my thumbnail jumped from under my boot and swam into the shallows.

On the way back up, I passed a young couple with a dog and a rucksack. The man nodded. The woman said, “Is it deep?” I said it was. “Good,” she said. “We’re after a swim.” They went down the path hand in hand, and the dog went first, and I heard the splash a minute later, and a shout, and then laughter that rang off the terraces like something the quarry had been saving up for years.

At the top, by the gate, there is a notice board that the council put up in 1994. It says the site is a “former mineral extraction area” and advises visitors to “beware of unstable edges.” Someone has scratched a heart into the Perspex with a key, and inside the heart are two initials, and below them the date 12/8/19. The ink has faded but the scratch has not. The quarry is not unstable. It is the most stable thing for miles. It is simply waiting, the way a held breath waits, for the next thing to arrive.

title: literary novel|a sound archivist who finds a confession hidden on an old tape
text:
The tape was a Scotch 203, the kind with the green and white label that always curled at the edges if you left it on the shelf too long. I’d pulled it from a box lot I bought off a widow in Burbank — she said her husband had been a sound man on some pictures in the sixties, nothing you’d know. Most of it was what you’d expect. Room tone. Slates. A lot of dead air and somebody whistling “The Girl from Ipanema” off-key.

I almost didn’t play the thing. It was late, the building was empty except for me and the hum of the HVAC, and I had a stack of forty more reels to log before morning. But the leader was spliced wrong — a little diagonal cut, sloppy — and that bothered me. You notice things like that. So I threaded it up.

The first ninety seconds were nothing. A chair scraping. A man clearing his throat, twice. Then a voice, close to the mic, too close, the way people talk when they don’t understand that a microphone isn’t an ear. He said a name. I won’t write it here. Then he said, “I’m going to say this once, and then I’m going to erase it.”

He didn’t erase it.

I’ve been doing this work for twenty-two years. I’ve heard a lot of things on tape that weren’t meant for me. Arguments, mostly. A man practicing a proposal to a woman who, judging by the second take, said no. A kid singing to himself in a stairwell. You develop a kind of selective deafness. You have to. Otherwise you’d go home every night carrying other people’s lives around in your coat pockets.

But this was different. This was a confession. Not the legal kind, not exactly. The man — he sounded older, maybe sixties, a little phlegmy — he talked about a night in 1963. A car. A girl on a bicycle. He said the word “accident” and then he said it again, and then he said, “That’s not the right word,” and stopped talking for what felt like a full minute. I checked the counter. It was fifty-two seconds. Fifty-two seconds of a man breathing into a microphone, deciding whether to keep going.

He kept going.

The details were wrong. That’s what got me. Not wrong as in false — wrong as in too specific to be invented. He said the girl’s bicycle had a wicker basket with a broken hinge, and that the hinge had made a sound when the wheel turned, a little tick, tick, tick, and that he heard that sound for years afterward, in restaurants, in the middle of meetings, once during his own daughter’s wedding. He said he’d driven home and parked in the garage and sat there with the engine off and the radio still playing, some ad for toothpaste, and he’d listened to the whole ad. He remembered the brand. He remembered the jingle.

I rewound it. Played it again. Played it a third time with the lights off, which is a stupid thing to do, but I did it.

Here’s the thing nobody tells you about archives. Everything is a fragment. You get a man’s voice and you don’t get his face. You get a date on a label and you don’t get the weather. You spend your life assembling ghosts out of spare parts and you tell yourself it’s history, it’s preservation, it matters. And mostly it does. But sometimes you find something like this and you realize you’re not an archivist at all. You’re a witness. And witnesses have obligations.

I don’t know what I’m going to do with it. I’ve got it in a drawer in my desk, wrapped in a cloth, which is ridiculous, it’s magnetic tape, it doesn’t need a blanket. But there it is. I keep thinking about the hinge. Tick, tick, tick. I keep thinking about the toothpaste jingle. I keep thinking about a man who sat in his car and listened to an advertisement all the way through because he couldn’t make himself go inside his own house.

The widow in Burbank — she had kind eyes. She offered me lemonade. I wonder if she knew. I wonder if she’s the daughter from the wedding. I wonder a lot of things I’m not going to put on paper.

Tomorrow I’ll log the rest of the box. Room tone. Slates. Somebody whistling. The ordinary noise of people who never had to say a thing once and then erase it.

title: short story|two sisters clearing out their mother's flat
text:
The photograph was stuck to the bottom of the drawer, fused there by years of humidity and forgotten spills. Sarah worked a fingernail beneath its edge, and it came away with a sound like a peeling plaster. It was a picture of them, taken maybe thirty years ago, standing in front of a caravan with the sea a grey smudge behind them. Their mother was in the middle, her arms around their shoulders, pulling them in tight. She was laughing, her head thrown back, and even in the faded colour, you could see the flash of her white teeth. Claire was on her left, scowling at the camera, a teenager already furious with the world. Sarah was on her right, beaming, a gap-toothed seven-year-old in a swimsuit that was too big for her.

Claire took the photo from Sarah’s hand, her touch brisk and impersonal. ‘God, look at my hair,’ she said, her voice flat. ‘I was going through that awful phase.’ She turned it over, as if looking for a date, then placed it on the growing pile for the charity shop. ‘We can’t keep everything, Sarah.’

‘I know,’ Sarah said, but her voice was quiet. She looked around the living room, which was no longer a living room but a waystation for a life’s debris. Boxes marked ‘KEEP’ and ‘CHARITY’ and ‘TIP’ squatted on the carpet like silent, judgemental toads. The air smelled of dust, old paper, and the faint, sweet ghost of their mother’s lavender hand cream. It was a smell that seemed to cling to everything, to the curtains, to the armchairs, to the very walls, and Sarah felt a sudden, desperate urge to open a window and let in the cold, clean October air.

They had been at it for three days. Three days of sorting through a lifetime of accumulated things: the good china that was never used, the birthday cards from great-aunts they barely remembered, the drawers full of rubber bands and blunt pencils. Claire was a machine, efficient and unsentimental. She had a system. She worked from left to right, top to bottom, emptying cupboards and wardrobes with a ruthless energy. Sarah was slower. She kept getting snagged on the past, picking up an object and finding herself lost in the memory it held. A thimble from a forgotten sewing kit had sent her back to afternoons spent watching her mother darn socks at the kitchen table. A chipped mug had reminded her of the hot chocolate her mother made on snow days, with a mountain of squirty cream and a dusting of cocoa.

‘What about this?’ Claire asked, holding up a small, porcelain figurine of a shepherdess. It was a terrible thing, all simpering smile and pastel frills.

‘Mum loved that,’ Sarah said. ‘Dad gave it to her for their anniversary one year. She said it was the ugliest thing she’d ever seen, but she kept it on the mantelpiece for forty years.’

Claire turned it over in her hands. ‘It’s hideous. And it’s got a chip.’ She dropped it into the TIP box with a hollow clunk. Sarah flinched. It felt like a small betrayal.

They worked in silence for a while, the only sounds the rustle of paper and the soft thud of things being discarded. Sarah moved to the bookshelf. Most of the books were old paperbacks, their spines creased and faded. She pulled one out, a dog-eared copy of a romance novel with a swooning couple on the cover. A piece of paper fluttered out and landed at her feet. It was a shopping list, written in her mother’s elegant, looping handwriting. Bread, milk, eggs. And at the bottom, in a different pen, a note to herself: ‘Call Sarah. Ask about her promotion. Be encouraging.’

Sarah’s throat tightened. She remembered that call. She had been so excited, so full of her own news, and her mother had listened, had said all the right things, but Sarah had been too busy to notice the slight hesitation in her voice, the way she had said ‘that’s wonderful, darling’ a little too brightly. Now, holding this scrap of paper, she realised her mother had probably been worried, had probably thought it was a mistake, but had chosen to be supportive anyway. The small, everyday act of love hit her with the force of a physical blow.

Claire came over, a bin bag in her hand. ‘Found anything good?’

Sarah held out the shopping list. Claire glanced at it, her expression softening for just a fraction of a second before the mask of efficiency slammed back down. ‘Right,’ she said. ‘Well. That’s a nice memory.’ She took the book from Sarah’s hand and put it in the CHARITY box. ‘We should get a move on. The man from the hospice shop is coming at four.’

She moved to the sideboard, her hands already reaching for the next thing to be sorted, the next memory to be boxed, labelled, and dispatched. Sarah watched her, this sister who had always been the strong one, the one who organised the family holidays and remembered the birthdays. She was a whirlwind of purpose, and Sarah suddenly felt a profound and lonely stillness in her wake. She looked at the TIP box, at the chipped shepherdess nestled among the rubbish, and for the first time, she felt a flicker of something that wasn't sadness or nostalgia. It was anger. Not at Claire, not really, but at the sheer, brutal finality of it all. The way a life could be reduced to a series of boxes, its worth measured by its usefulness to others.

title: folk tale|the miller's third son and the talking millstone
text:
My father was a miller, and the mill was his third son. It was the thing he spoke to at night, the thing he listened to in the morning, his ear pressed to the great, groaning post that anchored the stones. We—my brothers and I—were a distant second. When he died, the mill went to my eldest brother, as was right and expected. The cart and the strong grey mare went to the second. I received a small, leather purse of coins, a new coat that was too fine for me, and the old millstone from the upper floor, the one that had been cracked for a generation and was used only for grinding the coarsest feed.

My brothers were decent about it. They helped me haul the stone to the small, damp cottage at the edge of the village that was now mine. It sat in the corner of the single room, a massive, flawed disc of grey stone, its surface scored and pitted. It was a useless inheritance, a joke the village enjoyed for a season. I found work where I could, mending fences, digging ditches, and the stone sat in the corner, a monument to my father’s strange, silent favouritism.

The first time it spoke, I was certain I had finally gone mad from the damp and the loneliness. It was a low sound, like the grinding of two distant hills, a vibration that came up through the flagstones and into my bones.

“The rats,” it said. “They are in the grain sack again.”

I froze, a half-eaten crust of bread in my hand. The voice was not a voice in the air, but a pressure in the room, a thought that was not my own. I looked at the stone. Its surface was impassive.

“You are a stone,” I said, my own voice sounding thin and foolish.

“And you are a fool,” it replied, the words settling in my mind like silt. “But a fool with ears. The sack. To your left.”

I turned. The small sack of barley I’d bought that morning was indeed moving, just slightly. I’d never have noticed. I chased the rats out and tied the sack closed. That night, I sat and stared at the millstone. It offered nothing more.

In the weeks that followed, it became a reluctant oracle. Its pronouncements were never grand, never prophetic. They were observations, delivered with a grinding indifference that I came to find more comforting than any human counsel. It told me when the thatch was leaking in a spot I couldn’t see. It told me which of the village men were cheating at cards, not out of malice, but as a simple statement of fact. It told me that the baker’s wife was unhappy, and that the blacksmith’s son was afraid of his father.

I learned to listen. I learned that the stone was not a single entity but a chorus, a slow accumulation of every sound, every secret, every whispered confidence that had ever been poured into the grain it had ground. It held the memory of the mill, and the mill held the memory of the valley. It knew the weight of every harvest, the desperation of every lean winter, the petty cruelties and small kindnesses that had seeped into the flour and the meal.
