And she wove. She wove the sea’s currents and the migration of birds and the slow creep of glaciers, but she was lonely, because nobody ever came to see what she made.”

Marta stopped to spit into the fire, a habit she had, and I knew better than to rush her.

“One night—or what would have been night, if the sun had been invented—a fox came into the cave. A silver fox, with eyes like chips of ice. It sat down and watched her shuttle go back and forth, and after a while it said, ‘That’s fine work, but it doesn’t move.’ Ása was startled, because animals didn’t talk then, or at least they didn’t talk to her. She said, ‘What do you mean, it doesn’t move?’ And the fox said, ‘Everything else moves. The sea moves. The birds move. Your cloth just sits there being beautiful and dead.’ And Ása looked at her weaving and saw that the fox was right.”

I asked if the fox had a name. Marta said, “He was called Ragndr, but don’t ask me how I know that, because I wasn’t there.” She poked the fire.

“So Ása took down her weaving and she unraveled it, which took three days and three nights, and on the fourth night she began again, but this time she used something different. She used the light from the stars—she had to climb the mountain to get it, and she carried it down in a sealskin bag—and she used the breath of the sea, which she collected in a bladder from a drowned whale, and she used the silence between heartbeats, which is the hardest thing to catch because it’s always slipping away. And she wove those together, and the cloth began to move. It rippled. It shimmered. It flowed across the loom like water over stones.

“The fox came back and said, ‘Better. But it still doesn’t do anything.’ And Ása said, ‘What should it do?’ And the fox said, ‘It should dance.’ So Ása thought about that for a long time, and then she took the cloth outside and threw it up into the sky, where the cold caught it and held it, and the wind got into it and shook it, and it began to dance. It danced green and silver and red and violet, and it’s been dancing ever since. That’s what you saw last night. That’s what you’ll see tonight, if the sky stays clear.”

I asked her if Ása was still up there, weaving. Marta shook her head. “She went back to her cave and she’s weaving something else now. Something we haven’t seen yet. Maybe something better. Maybe something worse. But she’s working, and that’s the main thing.”

I finished my milk and she took the cup from me and set it on the table. “Now go home,” she said, “before your mother sends the dog after you. And tell her the bread was dry.”

It wasn’t dry. It never was. But I said I would, and I walked down the hill in the dark, and above me the lights were moving like something alive, like something that had been made on purpose and set free. I stopped at the bottom of the hill and looked up for a long time. Then I went inside, and I didn’t tell my mother the bread was dry, because some stories you keep for yourself.

title: memoir|the year spent caring for a grandmother with dementia
text:
The thing about the word “journey” is that it implies a destination. A place you get to. What I did for those twelve months, in my grandmother’s house, was more like a slow, circular drift. We were two satellites caught in a decaying orbit around a planet that was slowly disappearing.

Her name was Elara. A good name. A name from a myth. But by the time I moved in, she was already becoming a ghost in her own mythology. The first thing I noticed was the smell. Not a bad smell, not at first. It was the smell of her: lavender soap, a faint trace of the Estée Lauder perfume she’d worn since the fifties, and underneath it all, the dusty, papery scent of old age. But as the months wore on, the perfume faded, and the smell became just soap and skin and, sometimes, the sour tang of fear.

My life before this was a one-bedroom apartment with a leaky radiator and a job I was indifferent to. I packed a duffel bag and a box of books, thinking I’d have all this time to read. I think I read maybe three pages of a Graham Greene novel in a year. The book is still there, on her nightstand, a bookmark a permanent fixture at page four.

The days had a strange, repetitive texture. A rhythm of pills and meals and naps. I became a sommelier of applesauce. I learned to tell the difference between a confused silence and an angry one. The angry ones were worse. She’d look at me, and her eyes would be full of a hot, bewildered fury. “Who are you?” she’d demand, and not in the gentle, searching way of the movies. It was an accusation. “You’re the one. The one who moved all the furniture.” I hadn’t. I never did. But in her mind, I was the architect of her chaos.

There was one good afternoon. I remember it with a weird, painful clarity. We were sitting on the porch swing, the one my grandfather had built. The light was doing that honey-gold thing it does in late September. She was quiet for a long time, just swinging. Then she said, “The hydrangeas need lime.” Her voice was her own again. Clear. Present. She looked at me, and for a moment, she was my Gran. The one who taught me how to bait a fishing hook and who thought my teenage poetry was secretly brilliant. “You have your father’s stubborn chin,” she said, and patted my hand. My throat closed up. I couldn’t speak. I just nodded, and we swung. For ten, maybe fifteen minutes, we were just there. Two people on a porch. Then she turned to me, her eyes clouded over again, and asked, “Is it time for the program?” The program was a game show that had been off the air for thirty years. The moment was gone. It was like a window had opened, let in a gust of fresh air, and then slammed shut.

You learn the geography of a person. The creaky floorboard outside her bedroom. The way she’d hold her spoon when she was agitated, turning it over and over in her fingers. The specific, guttural sound she made when she was trying to find a word that had vanished. It was a sound of pure frustration, a little animal noise from the back of her throat.

My friends would call. “How are you holding up?” they’d ask. What do you say to that? You say, “Fine.” Because to say anything else would require a map and a legend and a two-hour lecture on the difference between grief and exhaustion. They’d tell me about their weekends, their promotions, their dating disasters. Their lives were moving forward, linear. Mine was a mobius strip.

The end wasn’t dramatic. It was a Tuesday. She just stopped eating. Not in a defiant way, just… she was done. The hospice nurse was kind. She told me it was a blessing. I didn’t feel blessed. I felt hollowed out. I sat by her bed for the last two days, holding her hand. It was so small and light, like a bird’s skeleton. The lavender soap was gone now. It was just the smell of a body shutting down.

Now, I live in a new apartment. The radiator works. I finished that Graham Greene novel. But sometimes, in the quiet, I’ll hear the creak of a floorboard that isn’t there, or I’ll catch a whiff of lavender in a store and my whole body will tense up. I spent a year waiting for her to come back, and now I spend my time waiting for her to leave. She hasn’t yet. That house, that year, that slow, circular drift—it’s all still in there. It’s part of the furniture now.

title: short story|a beekeeper's widow deciding whether to keep the hives
text:
The first thing Martha noticed was the sound. It wasn't the silence she’d expected, the profound and empty quiet that had filled the house since Harold’s funeral. This was a low, resonant hum, a single note held by a thousand throats, vibrating through the kitchen windowpane. It was a sound she had lived with for forty years, as constant and unremarkable as the ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall. Now, it felt like an accusation.

She stood at the sink, her hands submerged in cold water, the suds of a single teacup dissolving on her skin. Through the glass, the apiary was a study in miniature: a dozen white boxes stacked in a neat, ordered row at the far end of the meadow, facing the morning sun. Harold’s hives. His girls, he’d called them. He would spend hours out there, moving with a slow, deliberate grace she’d never seen him use anywhere else, his veiled head bent in communion with his humming, buzzing congregation. She had been the apostate, watching from the kitchen, safe behind glass.

The decision, which had been a dull, heavy stone in her gut for weeks, now felt sharp and immediate. The hives had to go. It was a simple matter of practicality. She couldn’t lift the supers, heavy with honey and wax. She couldn’t diagnose a case of chalkbrood or spot the tell-tale signs of a varroa mite. She was terrified of the smoke, the suit, the sheer, thrumming anger of a disturbed colony. She imagined a new owner, some young enthusiast with steady hands, carting the boxes away in a truck, leaving a neat, empty rectangle of pressed-down grass. The meadow would be just a meadow again. The silence would return, and she could finally, properly, begin to grieve.

But the humming persisted. It was not an angry sound today. It was the sound of industry, of purpose, of a world continuing its ancient, intricate dance, utterly indifferent to her loss. She dried her hands on a towel that still smelled faintly of his pipe smoke and walked to the back door, her hand resting on the cool brass knob. She had not been past the garden gate since the day of the burial. The garden itself was a testament to his neglect; the roses he’d so carefully pruned were leggy and wild, their blooms blown and brown.

She pushed the door open and the hum intensified, a physical presence in the air. The scent hit her then, a complex perfume of sun-warmed wood, beeswax, and the sweet, heavy fragrance of the clover that carpeted the meadow. It was the smell of his hands, of his clothes, of the life he had built for them both. She took a few hesitant steps onto the lawn, the grass damp and cool beneath her slippers.

She didn’t go closer than the edge of the garden. She didn’t need to. From here, she could see the activity at the entrances of the hives, the constant, frantic traffic of foragers returning with their pollen baskets full, a tiny, colourful cargo. She saw the guard bees, stationed at the threshold, their antennae twitching, inspecting each new arrival. She saw, at the base of the third hive, a small cluster of bees, perhaps a dozen, surrounding a single, lifeless body. They were pulling at its wings and legs, trying to hoist it away from the entrance. Undertaker bees. Harold had told her about them once, his voice filled with admiration for the colony’s ruthless efficiency.

A sudden, surprising sob caught in her throat. It wasn’t for Harold, not exactly. It was for the bee. For the small, insignificant death in the face of all that relentless, beautiful life. For the first time, she saw it not as a machine for producing honey, but as a fragile, complex society. A world he had loved and understood, a world he had tried, in his quiet way, to share with her.

She thought of the winter. The hives would need to be wrapped against the wind, their entrances reduced. They would need to be fed if their stores ran low. She would have to learn. The thought was terrifying. It was also, she realised with a jolt, a reason to get up in the morning. A task. A duty. Not to him, but to them.

She turned and walked back to the house, the hum following her. Inside, she didn’t go to the phone to call the beekeeping association. Instead, she went to the study. On the shelf, where it had sat untouched for years, was his first beekeeping manual, its spine cracked, the pages thick with his marginalia. She pulled it down, the weight of it familiar and strange in her hands. She sat in his worn armchair, the leather creaking a welcome, and opened it. The hum outside was no longer an accusation. It was a question, waiting for her answer. And for the first time, she felt she might have one.

title: elegy in free verse|a closed coal mine and the men who worked it
text:
The road in is a seam of slag,
black and vitreous, sutured with weeds.
They’ve planted a sign where the gate was:
RECLAMATION PHASE II.
The letters are peeling. A crow
works at a seam of it with its beak,
unimpressed. I park where the lamp-house stood
and the wind comes through the valley
like a man who’s forgotten what he came for.

You could set your watch by the silence here.
It falls in shifts.

*

I hired on at nineteen.
My father signed the papers because I was underage
and because he’d done his thirty years
and believed, the way men believe in weather,
that the dark was a kind of inheritance.
The cage dropped and my stomach went with it.
Four hundred feet. The air turned to a taste—
iron and old rope and the sweat of other men
pressed into the walls like a handprint.
We called it *the face*.
Everything happened at the face.
The coal was a wall you argued with
and the argument was your whole life.

*

There was a man named Ovila.
He kept a canary long after they stopped requiring it,
a small yellow rumor in a cage of wire,
and he’d say, *She sings when she’s nervous,
and when she stops, you run.*
She never stopped. She died in her sleep
one winter, of nothing, of being a bird.
Ovila buried her in a matchbox
in the garden, and after that
he was the first one down the shaft,
the first one to test the air with his lungs.

*

The company says the mine is sealed.
What they mean is they’ve poured concrete in the throat
and capped the vent with a grate
so the methane can breathe out
and the mountain can keep its own counsel.
I’ve stood at the grate in November
and felt the warm breath come up,
the mine exhaling still, slow as a sleeper
who doesn’t know the house is sold.
Some nights I dream the whole seam is a lung
and we were the small bad thing it coughed up.

*

At the co-op they still say *the pit*
the way you’d say *the war*—
a place you were, that is over,
that is not over.
Lorne’s hands are a map of it.
He can’t straighten two fingers on the left.
He says the coal remembers you
by the shape it leaves.
He says it’s not the dust that gets you,
it’s the quiet after the last shift,
the way a man’s ears keep listening
for a cage that isn’t coming.

*

I don’t have a lesson.
The mountain doesn’t care that we loved it.
The men who went down are not underground now—
they’re in the Legion hall on Fridays,
they’re in the cemetery on the hill
with the names cut shallow so the frost can have its way,
they’re in the way I still duck
when I come through a low door.
The coal is a black mirror.
You look in it and see the face of whoever
was foolish enough to think
the dark could be a living.

*

Driving out, the headlights catch the spoil heap,
a hill made of what the hill was not.
Grass is trying. It always tries.
Somewhere under the concrete
the last shift is still walking out,
lunch pails empty, lamps going cold,
and the canary is singing
because she doesn’t know any better,
because that’s what she was for.

title: personal essay|living next to a railway line for twenty years
text:
The house on Gladstone Terrace was, according to the estate agent, “a steal.” She said it with the bright, unblinking confidence of someone who had never actually stood in the back garden at 6:47 on a Monday morning. My wife, Claire, and I bought it anyway. We were thirty-one, our daughter, Nell, was two, and we had convinced ourselves that a second bedroom and a garden shed were worth almost any compromise. The compromise, it turned out, was a four-track railway line running along the bottom of our garden, close enough that I could have thrown a cricket ball onto the 07:12 to Manchester Piccadilly.

The first night, we lay awake. Claire said, “Is it always going to be like this?” I said something reassuring about adaptation and the plasticity of the human nervous system. Then the 23:40 freight train came through—a long, groaning thing carrying something heavy and anonymous—and we both sat up in bed. The windows rattled. A picture of Claire’s mother, hung that afternoon with a spirit level, went slightly crooked.

You do adapt. That is the strange truth of it. Within six months, I had stopped hearing the trains in any conscious way. I heard them the way you hear your own breathing. But I noticed something else: I could tell the time by them. The 06:52 commuter service—four carriages, a wheeze of brakes—meant I should be up. The 15:20, a slow, heavy freight, meant Nell’s nap was nearly over. The 21:05, the last fast train to London, was my signal to pour a glass of wine.

Nell grew up with them. When she was four, she asked me, “Do the trains go to the sea?” I told her some of them did. She began waving at the 08:14 every morning from the kitchen window, and I told her it was a good thing to do. For a while, she believed the driver waved back. Perhaps he did. There was a man called Derek who drove the 08:14 for years, and one day I met him at a neighbor’s barbecue. He said, “You’re the waving family on Gladstone Terrace.” He said he had a daughter Nell’s age and that he’d started waving back. That felt like a small, decent conspiracy.

Our neighbor, an elderly woman named Margaret, had lived on the terrace since 1968. She told me once, over the fence, that the trains had changed. “In the old days,” she said, “you’d get the steam ones, and the washing on the line would go black. We didn’t mind. We’d stand out here and watch them go by.” She said the noise was better then, too—a proper, living noise, not the electric sort. I asked her if she’d ever wanted to move. She looked at me as if I’d asked whether she’d ever wanted to change her name. “Why would I move?” she said. “I know everyone on this street, and I know every train. What else is there to know?”

There were bad nights. The 03:10 freight, the one that carried something metallic and clanking, could wake the dead. When Nell was six, she had a phase of nightmares and I would sit by her bed until the 03:10 had passed, then creep back to my own room. I remember standing at her window one February night, the garden silvered with frost, and watching the train go by—a single pale light in the dark, the carriages a dark smear—and thinking, This is the sound of other people’s lives. Someone is driving that train. Someone is going somewhere I will never go. It was a strangely comforting thought.

Claire left in 2019. Not because of the trains—she used to say the trains were the only honest thing about the house—but for reasons that took us both by surprise. Nell and I stayed. The house felt bigger and the trains felt louder for a while. But then the spring came, and the garden filled with the noise of blackbirds and the 07:12, and Nell said, “Dad, listen, the 07:12 is late,” and she was right. We stood at the window together and waited for it, and it came, and everything felt, for a moment, exactly as it should be.

I still live there. Nell is twenty-one now and at university in Leeds, and she texts me sometimes when she hears a train go by in the distance. “Was that the 21:05?” she asks. And I listen, and I say yes, though I’m not always sure.
